22059-balthasar-and-other-works-1909:
Anatole France, the great French man of letters, wrote the tales gathered in Balthasar and Other Works. Mrs. John Lane's English translation appeared in 1909. The title story concerns Balthasar, one of the three wise men of the Christmas story. France presents him as a king in Ethiopia, learned in the stars.

Other pieces include The Curé's Mignonette, The Daughter of Lilith, and The Red Egg. France treats saints, devils, and scholars with the same gentle irony. His prose is smooth, his learning worn lightly, and his sympathy always with the weak. These short works show the humane wit that later won him the Nobel Prize.
amphitheatrvm-sapientiae-aeternae-solius: Heinrich Khunrath engraved his vision of eternal wisdom in 1609. Circular plates show the alchemist's laboratory and Christ. The Rosicrucian showpiece. Its pages add to the record of the past. This book preserves that esoteric work for future readers.
angela-foligno-divine-consolation-1909:
Angela of Foligno told her Book of Divine Consolation to her priest. Mary G. Steegmann gave the work English dress in 1909. Angela was a rich wife in Umbria who lost her kin and turned to God. She joined the third order of St. Francis in her grief.

Step by step, she tells how God drew her from a lax life to deep pain and light. Visions of Christ in His pain crowd the mid parts. Her words are raw, bold, and free of all soft gloss. The book is a chief text of women's soul lore of the mid ages.
apuleius-apologia-florida-butler-1909:
Harold E. Butler translated Apuleius's Apologia and Florida into English in 1909. Apuleius, the Roman novelist, had been tried for practicing magic in North Africa. His defense speech survives as the Apologia.

Prosecutors claimed he won his rich wife through spells and enchantments. Apuleius answers with wit, philosophy, and ridicule of his accusers' ignorance. He discusses fish, mirrors, and poetry to show his interests were scholarly. The Florida collects showpieces of his public speaking beside the defense. Together they form the great surviving record of a Roman witchcraft trial. Butler's translation keeps the legal fireworks readable. The speech is long, bold, and full of wit from the first page to the last.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-09:
Volume nine of Burton's Thousand Nights and a Night appeared in 1885, the penultimate book of the main set. Shahrazad's store seems endless even as its appointed end draws near. Kings in her tales keep meeting clever wives, lost sons, and fortunes reversed in a single night.

Burton, nearing his own finish line, still refuses every shortcut in the text. His renderings of verse stay verse, and his notes stay frank about manners and belief. The Gutenberg text of this volume is ebook 55587, set apart from its neighbors in numbering. That quirk aside, the volume matches the rest in dress. One volume more completes Shahrazad's bargain in the main series.
arxiv-2512-00209:
Bayesian networks lay out how random variables depend on each other, which makes reasoning under uncertainty manageable. Bart Jacobs, Márk Széles, and Dario Stein study compositional inference for such networks and for causality in 2025. Inference means updating some variables with evidence and computing outcomes elsewhere.

When a joint distribution is represented by a network, its structure lets inference proceed piece by piece, with great benefits. Compositional methods scale better and are easier to verify than one global computation. The approach matters for medical, legal, and engineering reasoning, where transparent probability updates are essential. Causal reasoning adds direction to those updates, asking what changes when a variable is forced. For teams who build tools for doctors, judges, or plant staff, the gain is speed with care. Fast sums that still show how each fact moved the end result.
arxiv-2512-00309:
Biao Dong and Bin Cao study distributed sensing joined with edge artificial intelligence in 2025. In their system, scattered devices sense a target and send locally estimated features to an access point. The access point then performs collaborative inference from those features.

Performance is set at two levels: how well the devices sense, and how well they communicate. Exploiting prior information is the lever the authors use to improve the combined system. Such integrated designs matter for surveillance, environmental monitoring, and smart infrastructure, where sending raw data from every device would flood the network. Prior information is the resource the design exploits at both sensing and inference levels.
arxiv-2512-00409:
Josephson junctions carry supercurrents between superconductors, and their behavior depends on phase coherence. Polevoy and a team of co-authors report a multiterminal ballistic Josephson effect in monocrystalline gold in 2025. They built a planar junction array inside a micron-sized single crystal of gold.

The system shows a nonlocal effect: the supercurrent between any two superconducting leads is governed by phase coherence across the entire crystal. Such multiterminal devices interest physicists building novel superconducting circuits and probes of quantum transport. A single clean crystal hosting the whole array reduces the disorder that usually clouds these effects. Phase coherence across a whole crystal is the striking feature the array demonstrates.
arxiv-2512-00509:
Non-orthogonal multiple access lets several users share the same channel, which makes separating them difficult. Sumita Majhi and co-authors improve channel estimation for such systems using Gold sequences in 2025. Superimposed signals on shared subcarriers are the core obstacle.

Gold sequences have orthogonality features that may enhance user separation and channel estimation. The proposed approach uses fractional power allocation and partially decoded data symbols to refine estimates. Better estimation in shared-channel systems means more users served on the same spectrum, a direct concern for crowded wireless networks. Partially decoded symbols recycle information the receiver already has, improving the estimate cheaply. The comparison includes a conventional V-BLAST receiver design. For folks who build phone nets, the gain is more calls on the same band. There is less fuzz in the link when crowds of phones share one base site.
arxiv-2512-00609:
Wireless users sharing a channel interfere with each other, and outage probability measures how often service fails. Fernando Almeida García and co-authors analyze outage in transmit-antenna-selection NOMA systems with multi-antenna users in 2025. The fading channel follows a flexible distribution with two shape parameters.

The analysis covers maximal-ratio and equal-gain combining at the receivers. Imperfect successive interference cancellation is modeled explicitly, since real receivers never cancel perfectly. Outage formulas like these guide the design of dense wireless networks that stack users onto the same spectrum. The fading model used is flexible enough to cover many real channel conditions. Antenna selection is a cheap diversity trick, using the best antenna rather than all at once.
arxiv-2512-00809:
Zhanna Kuznetsova and Francesco Toppan build a new algebraic frame for quantum systems in a 2025 paper. They introduce color Heisenberg-Lie superalgebras, graded by small abelian groups. Grading sorts the algebra's parts by labels, and the color version adds twists to how parts combine.

Working at the third root of unity, they study the multi-particle quantum paraoscillators tied to these algebras. Paraoscillators are cousins of the oscillators used across quantum physics, with richer rules. The framework connects to Majorana qubits, a kind of quantum bit prized for stability. New algebra like this can suggest fresh ways to build and control quantum states.
arxiv-2512-00909:
Alireza Javanmardi and a team from a German AI research center present TalkingPose in a 2025 computer vision paper. Diffusion models can now animate a character from one still image plus a set of driving poses, with strong realism. Faces and gestures must move together for the result to feel alive.

Long videos remain hard, since motion can drift and lose coherence over time. TalkingPose adds feedback guidance to the diffusion process to keep face and gesture animation efficient and consistent. Better long-form animation could help virtual presenters, sign language avatars, and film pre-visualization, where a single photo must carry a whole performance.
arxiv-2512-01209:
Yadan Duan and seven coauthors resolve a solar reconnection event in fine detail in a 2025 paper. Interchange reconnection happens where open and closed magnetic field lines in the Sun's corona swap partners. It is thought to play a significant role in producing solar jets and the solar wind.

The dynamics in the low corona may be more complex than recognized, especially at the higher time and spatial resolution now available. Using Solar Orbiter observations, the team studies an event in a fan-spine-like magnetic topology. Resolving such events helps explain how the corona feeds the wind that fills the solar system.
arxiv-2512-01509:
Patrick Odagiu and co-authors shrink data so quantum classifiers can use it. Quantum methods stall when data has too many traits. Most real sets do. Cutting traits first is the plain fix. The cut must keep what the quantum step needs.

The team learns reduced forms of the data for that step. A good form keeps class gaps while traits drop. That opens quantum learning to larger real sets. It also cuts circuit size, which helps today's noisy quantum hardware run deeper tasks with fewer errors. Feature cuts learned once can be reused across classifiers, which spreads the cost of the quantum-ready form over many later tasks.
arxiv-2512-01709:
Eyal Buks studies a ferrimagnetic sphere resonator under parametric drive. The sphere's response to a pumped signal is measured in the lab. A theoretical model predicts that response. Its base claim is that disentanglement occurs spontaneously in quantum systems.

Measurements are set against those predictions. Agreement or gaps both teach something. A match would back the spontaneous disentanglement claim. A gap would bound where the model fails. Sphere resonators serve in magnon and quantum sensing work, so their drive response matters broadly. Sphere resonators couple to microwaves cleanly, so the same setup links this test to magnon devices used in hybrid quantum systems.
arxiv-2512-01809:
Chaoyi Pan and co-authors probe why flow and diffusion policies work well in robotics. Generative policies have become popular and effective for robot control. Their edge is often credited to multimodal action capture. Complex behavior expression is another claimed cause. Hard evidence for each claim is thin.

The team runs controlled tests to separate those factors. Knowing the true driver guides policy design choices. If multimodality is key, data collection should stress diverse demos. If not, simpler policies may match at lower cost. Controlled factors include data scale and policy class, so the verdict states which knob matters under which robot task family.
arxiv-2512-01909:
Why a large language model gives one answer rather than another is hidden inside its calculations, and wrong answers, or hallucinations, are hard to diagnose. Lihu Chen, Xiang Yin, and Francesca Toni introduce a framework in 2025 that reads a model's prediction as the outcome of an inner debate.

Called latent debate, the framework treats the model's internal activity as implicit arguments for and against possible answers. Making those hidden arguments visible gives researchers a handle on where a prediction came from and why it may have gone wrong. The approach adds a new tool to the effort to make language models interpretable rather than opaque.
arxiv-2512-02109:
Cosmic chronometers date the cosmos by the ages of old, calm galaxies seen at unlike ranges. The method gives the rate of expansion in a direct way. E. Tomasetti and a large team stretch the method in 2025 to whole clusters of galaxies. They gauge the past expansion near the mid-point of cosmic history.

They use fine spectra from the MUSE tool on the Very Large Telescope. Three clusters sit in close redshift bins. Cluster galaxies give many clocks in one field of view, all under shared terms. A fresh, free measure of expansion counts for much, since the main methods still clash on the rate.
arxiv-2512-02209:
The muon, a heavier cousin of the electron, wobbles in a magnetic field at a rate theory predicts with extreme precision. Dinko Počanić reviews in 2025 the experimental status of that wobble, the muon magnetic anomaly, and the prospects for sharpening it further.

The past five years brought major new measurements, and the dominant uncertainty now comes from hadronic vacuum polarization, a strong-force contribution that is hard to compute. Any lasting gap between measurement and prediction would point to unknown particles. The review gathers where the field stands in one of particle physics' longest-running and most sensitive tests of the Standard Model.
arxiv-2512-02609:
Shengkai Wu and nine co-authors teach robots to grasp one chosen object when several valid targets sit in view. Imitation learning copies human demonstrations, but demonstrations may grasp different objects in the same scene. Averaging those conflicting lessons yields one blurred, invalid action.

Their SAM2Grasp method uses prompts to say which object is meant, then predicts the grasp over time. Conditioning on the prompt resolves the multimodal confusion instead of averaging it away. Robots that grasp the intended item reliably are safer and more useful in homes, warehouses, and care settings. A prompt that names the goal turns a vague reach into the right reach, time after time.
arxiv-2512-02809:
Etienne Granet and Michael Levin test whether topological qubits survive long range forces between particles. Topological ground states are prized because their degeneracy can store quantum information robustly. Known stability theorems cover short range forces, or long range ones that fade fast.

Slowly decaying forces, falling like a power law weaker than the space dimension, escape those theorems. The authors study robustness exactly in that uncovered regime. The answer matters for quantum memory designs, where stray long range coupling is hard to remove from real materials and devices. Slow tails are the norm in real stuff, so a proof that owns them is worth more than one that bans them.
arxiv-2512-03009:
Ava Shahbazi Sooraki and Ahmad Sheykhi use the universe's matter surplus to bound a smallest possible length. String theory and quantum gravity suggest a zero point length, a minimal scale of spacetime. That length modifies the entropy tied to cosmic horizons, which feeds back into the Friedmann equations of expansion.

Gravitational baryogenesis, one story for why matter beat antimatter, depends on that expansion history. Requiring the story to match the observed surplus constrains the zero point length. Cosmology thus becomes a tool for testing quantum gravity ideas far beyond any collider. Sky based bounds reach scales no lab can touch. A tight sky bound on a small length is news worth the ink it gets.
arxiv-2512-03109:
AI agents act step by step, so each step needs a check. Shuvom Sadhuka and co-authors study verifiers for agent work in this 2025 work. Verifiers, such as model judges and process reward models, score how good each action is.

Weak scores can let bad steps pass or block good ones. The authors build a verifier method based on sequential hypothesis testing, which checks evidence step by step. Their tool is called E-valuator. More reliable checks could make agents safer to use in research and business tasks where errors compound fast. Sequential testing also lets a verifier stop early when evidence is already strong enough.
arxiv-2512-03209:
A star system with hot dust may hide a small companion star. T. A. Stuber and a large team report a detection in this 2025 work. The system, kappa Tuc A, sits inside a group of five stars and shows a changing infrared glow.

Using interferometry, which merges light from separate telescopes, the team found a subcomponent. They model its orbit and describe it as a low-mass star on an eccentric path. A companion could explain the hot dust near the main star. The finding sharpens the picture of this complex system. A companion on a wide, eccentric path can stir dust and gas around the main star over time.
arxiv-2512-03309:
Earth system models drift from reality over time. Aniruddha Bora and co-authors propose a way to correct them while they run in this 2025 work. Coarse grids, imperfect sub-models, and uncertain starting states all limit predictions.

Classic bias correction helps when data constrain the run, but less once models run freely. The authors train a neural operator that maps model states to correction tendencies. Those corrections apply online during integration, at a limited cadence. The approach could improve climate forecasts without rebuilding the whole model. Online corrections differ from after-the-fact fixes, since they steer the run while it unfolds.
arxiv-2512-03609:
Active proteins stir the membranes they sit in. Sneha Krishnan and Rickmoy Samanta model that stirring in this 2025 work. Membrane-bound motors exert force dipole flows along fluid interfaces and lipid bilayers.

The authors build a unified hydrodynamic and Hamiltonian framework. It covers pusher and puller dipoles in an incompressible two-dimensional membrane over a shallow viscous layer. Membranes govern how cells eat, signal, and move. A sound theory of active membranes helps explain those life processes. Pusher and puller dipoles stir flow in opposite senses, shaping patterns on the membrane that hosts them and their neighbors.
arxiv-2601-06609:
Anup Kushwaha and Om Prakash study symplectic hulls over an unusual ring in 2026. Their ring is non-unital, generated by two elements, kappa and tau. Its relations set twice each generator equal to zero.

Squares of the generators give a further set of relations. Each generator squared equals itself in this ring's arithmetic. Cross products between kappa and tau also collapse onto one generator. Symplectic hulls arise in coding theory for quantum and classical codes. Studying them over such rings extends where code constructions can live. Algebraists get the hull structure for this specific non-unital case. The results feed into constructing codes with controlled hull dimensions. Small rings like this often model error behavior surprisingly well.
arxiv-2601-06709:
Tiffanie Ng and Sara Clifton show how the bystander effect can grow from lone minds in 2026. Folks help a person in need less when more folks stand by. That group fact has long drawn a list of group-based accounts.

Past accounts cite doubt on what is wrong and cues copied from peers. Blame spread thin and joint denial also get named as causes of the effect. Their work starts one step down, with the odds as one mind sees them. Put many such minds in one place and the group effect shows up. If lone rules suffice, group causes may count for less than thought. The work gives a base model that tests can check against live trials. A known group effect is thus recast in lone, countable terms.
arxiv-2601-06809:
Hong-Bae Jeon and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with RIS-aided ISAC with k k -Rydberg atomic receivers. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors investigate a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) framework equipped with multiple Rydberg atomic receiver (RAR)-aided users.

By leveraging the reference-assisted reception mechanism of RARs. The authors develop a unified signal model that jointly captures downlink multi-user communication with RARs and monostatic radar sensing. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07009:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Shifa Sulaiman and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers sliding mode controller based on timoshenko beam theory developed for a Tendon-Driven robotic. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Development of dexterous robotic joints is essential for advancing manipulation capabilities in robotic systems.

The work presents a design and an implementation of a tendon-driven robotic wrist joint. Together with an efficient Sliding Mode Controller (SMC) for precise motion control. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07109:
A. J. Brizard and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers guiding-center dynamics in a screw-pinch magnetic field. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The guiding-center dynamics of charged particles moving in a doubly-symmetric screw-pinch magnetic field is investigated.

In particular, we verify that Kruskal’s adiabatic-invariant series expansion of the radial action integral associated with. The reduced full-orbit radial motion matches the perturbation expansion of the magnetic-moment gyroaction up to first order in magnetic-field non-uniformity. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07209:
Yu Guo and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to strip glare from a photo. Glass both lets light pass and throws light back. That mix makes a photo through glass hard to clean up. The task is called single-image reflection removal, or SIRR. It must clean one photo at a time, with no second shot to help.

Good training data for SIRR is hard to get. Fake data made by code tends to look less than real. Real shots are true to life but too few in count. Guo and the team built a new way to make training data. It traces light paths through 3D glass shapes set over real scene photos. The team can vary the glass, the camera, and the final look of each shot. The aim is a large set of training pairs that still act like real glass.
arxiv-2601-07309: Research by Zhuoka Feng and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with ARM. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Interactive large language model agents have advanced rapidly, but most remain specialized to a single environment and fail to adapt robustly to other environments. Model merging offers a training-free alternative by integrating multiple experts into a single model. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07509:
Feiyu Deng studies how a deformation changes boundary conformal field theories, in a 2026 theoretical physics preprint. The deformation is known as T T-bar, built from the theory's stress tensor. Deng also uses holography, which links such theories to gravity in a higher-dimensional space. The approach here stays intrinsic, working from field theory itself.

By restating the deformation as a change to the asymptotic variational principle in AdS space, Deng avoids a finite radial cutoff. From that setup he obtains an exact quadratic trace relation for the stress tensor. He takes that relation as the basic definition of the deformed theory. The paper then pursues a geometric realization of boundary flow. Specialists in holography and deformed field theories are the readers.
arxiv-2601-07609:
Marco Alfò and Roberto Rocci examine bias in regression models for data gathered over time. Longitudinal studies follow the same people across repeated measurements. Such studies can separate age effects from cohort effects, the differences present at the start. Models often add person-specific random effects to capture traits that stay constant. Those effects are also used to stand in for covariates the study never measured.

The authors focus on what happens when important covariates are omitted. They study finite mixtures of regression models for longitudinal responses. A mixture model assumes the population contains hidden groups, each with its own regression pattern. Understanding omitted covariate bias helps scholars avoid reading group effects wrongly. The paper serves statisticians who model repeated measures in medicine and social science.
arxiv-2601-07809:
S. Yu. Orevkov constructs plane curves that disprove a conjecture in algebraic geometry. He builds an irreducible rational curve of degree ten in the complex projective plane. The curve has twelve triple points, places where it crosses itself threefold. He also builds a union of three rational quartics with nineteen triple points. The 2026 preprint presents both constructions.

These examples counter a conjecture by Dimca, Harbourne, and Sticlaru. Conjectures about singular curves predict limits on how many singular points a curve can carry. A single explicit counterexample settles such a claim. Constructing curves with many triple points requires careful control of the defining equations. The paper serves algebraic geometers who study singular plane curves. It shows the true limits sit beyond what was guessed.
arxiv-2601-08109:
Sridhar Mahadevan describes Csql, a system that turns plain documents into a causal database. His 2026 arXiv paper, marked as a draft under revision, automates the conversion from unstructured text. The result can be queried with SQL, the standard database language.

A causal database differs from a normal one in its purpose. It is built to answer why questions through causal interventions and structured causal queries. Instead of only storing facts, it stores relations that support what-if reasoning. For data scientists, Csql points toward documents that can be asked direct causal questions, not just searched for keywords.
arxiv-2601-08409: Qin Ye, Fujun Zhou, and Weijun Wu prove a global compressible limit for a plasma kinetic system. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the ionic Vlasov-Poisson-Boltzmann system, a fundamental model of dilute collisional plasmas. The team derives the compressible ionic Euler-Poisson limit of that system. The result holds for the full range of cutoff potentials in a stated parameter interval. Rigorous hydrodynamic limits assure physicists that fluid equations faithfully capture kinetic plasma behavior, which supports fusion and space plasma modeling.
arxiv-2601-08509: Jinkwan Jang and co-authors present What If TSF, a benchmark for scenario-guided multimodal forecasting. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that time series forecasting drives real decisions, yet most methods stay unimodal. They extrapolate historical patterns without outside context. Language models suggest multimodal forecasting could use text as well, but benchmarks lag behind. Existing ones give retrospective or misaligned raw context, hiding whether models truly use text. The new benchmark reframes forecasting around what-if scenarios, testing if textual guidance changes predictions in the right way.
arxiv-2601-09109:
Samuel Everett links how hard a task is to how wild a motion is. He builds a bridge from code work to dynamics. To each motion of a set class, he ties a set of choice tasks. Those tasks ask if the motion can reach a zone in a set time, at a coarse scale. The tasks are called telic problems.

How hard the tasks are may tell how wild the motion is. A tame motion may yield easy tasks. A wild one may yield hard ones. This is part one of a plan to make that tie strict. A reader in either field gets a new joint tongue. It may let code tools probe motion, and motion tools grade code.
arxiv-2601-09709:
Sharim Khan, Paul Landes, Adam Cross, and Jimeng Sun extract social context from clinical notes. Their 2026 arXiv paper predicts social determinants of health tied to ICD-9 codes, using reasoning models. Factors like housing, work, and income shape patient outcomes but rarely sit in structured fields.

Recent work uses language models to pull these markers from sentences. The authors test reasoning models on the task. Adding social context to diagnostic systems can change risk scores and care plans. Reliable extraction would give clinicians a fuller picture without new forms for patients to fill.
arxiv-2601-09809:
Samar Abdelghani and Soumaya Cherkaoui design a federated learning system that mixes quantum and classical parts. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents QFed, a parameter-compact hybrid. Federated learning lets organizations train a shared model without pooling raw data, which suits healthcare, finance, and research under strict rules.

The obstacles are uneven data across sites, diverse hardware, and heavy models. A compact design lowers the burden placed on each participant site. Adding quantum components is the paper's distinctive bet. The aim is collective intelligence that fully respects privacy, regulation, and sovereignty at once.
arxiv-2601-09909:
Yoshiko Ogata writes a short note on states of matter with mixed states in two space dims. Such states can hold a kind of order that is not seen in local checks. To sort these states, one needs marks that do not grow when noise acts for a short depth.

Ogata looks at a state that meets a near duality rule. From it comes a braided tensor class tied to strong symmetry. She shows that two marks of that class, its S matrix and its twists, do not grow under short depth channels. That makes them fit tools for sorting these states.
arxiv-2601-10009:
Nathalie Rieger maps shapes where the metric can flip its type. On such a shape, the sign of length can change from place to place. The change can trace a line or a band. Rieger builds her cases from the Möbius strip, a band with one twist.

One set of cases joins two halves at a seam. The seam is where the type flips. A second set turns the strip itself into such a shape. These hand built cases show how a non turned shape can hold a type flip. They give clear forms for a field that has few such forms to study.
arxiv-2601-10109:
Lechen Zhang, Yunxiang Zhang, Wei Hu, and Lu Wang cut the data cost of teaching small models to reason. Large models can solve hard tasks step by step. Small models learn that skill from the large ones. But that teaching tends to need vast data sets. The cost in time and funds is high.

The team picks data by skill. They ask which skills a task needs. They then pick the cases that teach those skills best. With less data, fine tune runs can still yield strong skill. The work aims to make the teaching cheap and sharp at once.
arxiv-2601-10209:
S. Messelot and co authors test how long a shielded qubit can hold its state. The qubit is of cos two phi type. It is built from two Josephson parts in a loop. Their clash makes the state hard to disturb. That shield is its main draw.

A shield is of use only if the state lasts. The team probe what cuts the life of the state. Noise in phase, charge, or flux can each play a role. They map which noise bites most. The work helps judge if this qubit can scale to real chips.
arxiv-2601-10409:
Marcin Kotowski and Michał Oszmaniec bound how long a closed quantum rig takes to come back. An isolated rig moves in a set way. In time, it must near its start state once more. That return is named recurrence. Its scale was known in rough form, but a tight bound was lacked.

The team give tight bounds on that return time. Tight means the bounds can be met, not just claimed. The work rests on the size of the rig's state space. It also rests on how near the return must be. Such bounds are base facts for how quantum rigs act in time.
arxiv-2601-10509:
Richard Fitzpatrick replies to a note on his model of tokamak current ramps. A tokamak holds hot plasma in a ring with fields. Its current must rise at the start and fall at the end. Fitzpatrick gave a plain model of those ramps. It was set out in a past paper in Nuclear Fusion.

A. H. Boozer wrote a note on that model. This report is Fitzpatrick's reply. He takes up the points Boozer raised. He sets out where he holds his ground and where terms need care. Such swaps are how plain models get honed for real rig use.
arxiv-2601-10709:
The Euclid Collaboration reports groundwork for the Euclid space mission's galaxy surveys. Euclid aims to measure spectroscopic redshifts for about two million galaxies. It reads them from the H-alpha emission line in near-infrared slitless spectra from its Deep Fields. Both its red and blue grisms, the tools that spread light into spectra, play a role.

Redshifts give galaxy distances, and distances map the growth of cosmic structure. That map tests dark energy, the force speeding up cosmic expansion. Careful preparation papers like this one set out how the measurements will be made and checked. They are the base on which Euclid's dark universe claims will stand.
arxiv-2601-10809:
Young-Min Cho, Yuan Yuan, Sharath Chandra Guntuku, and Lyle Ungar study side effects of style prompts in conversational agents. Prompts often tell a model to be friendly, helpful, or concise. Such style features steer tone with ease. Yet their side effects on other traits are poorly understood. A nudge for one style may quietly bend others.

The authors present the first systematic study of cross-feature stylistic side effects. Their title gives the flavor: asking for a concise agent can make it seem less expert. Teams that tune agents by style need to know these trade-offs. The work helps designers pick prompts with eyes open about what else changes.
arxiv-2601-11009:
Xiaodong Jia and Xiaoyong Xi take up a question in domain theory raised by Matthew de Brecht. The question asks whether countable frames are continuous lattices. Frames are abstract versions of the open sets of a space, studied in pointfree topology. Countable ones are the test case: small enough to hope for a theorem, rich enough to resist one.

The authors prove that if a countable frame is continuous, its spectrum is quasicontinuous in the dual specialization order. They further show the answer is yes when the spectrum is a T1 space or a Scott space. Partial answers like these fence in where a counterexample could hide. The work serves logicians and topologists who study spaces through their algebra of opens.
arxiv-2601-11209:
Hans Buehler, Blanka Horvath, Anastasis Kratsios, Yannick Limmer, and Raeid Saqur price options. Their 2026 preprint is named SANOS, for smooth arbitrage-free surfaces. An option surface shows prices across time and strike at once. Traders need such surfaces to be smooth and free of free lunches.

Their method builds the surface with no set shape in mind. It is non-parametric, so the data picks the form. The build stays smooth across both time and strike price. It is also strict: no arbitrage is left in the surface. The team calls the method fast and flexible in use. A clean surface helps desks quote and hedge with less noise.
arxiv-2601-11309:
Katie Eggleton and seven coauthors grow quantum light sources in gallium nitride. Their 2026 preprint reports controlled epitaxy of the emitters. Quantum light made at room temperature is a prized goal. A mature chip platform would make such sources cheap and common.

The team grows gallium nitride on silicon wafers for the work. That pairing can use known skill and wafer-scale lines. Bright emitters in this material can sit in cavities. They can also sit in diodes and photonic circuits. Controlled growth means the emitters land where they are wanted. That control is what turns a lab effect into a device. The work is a step toward quantum tech on plain silicon.
arxiv-2601-12009:
W. Dong, V. Manea, R. Ferrer, and a team at the SPIRAL2 site in France present a gas cell design for work with radioactive nuclei. The cell will stop, pull out, and neutralize nuclei from the S3 separator. The work feeds laser studies of rare ion beams.

Their prototype aims to cut the time ions spend in the cell. It also adds a controlled way to neutralize them, which laser work needs. Sims test the design before build. Faster pull-out means more rare nuclei reach the tools alive.  The cell serves the low energy branch of the S3 line.
arxiv-2601-12109:
Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira, Rodrigo Moreira, and Leonardo Gabriel Ferreira Rodrigues grade coffee leaf disease with an eye on energy use. Fast, true diagnosis guards coffee yield. Field checks are hard, and AI vision models can be true yet heavy.

Heavy models fail on weak field devices with patchy links. Their ensemble method aims for high skill at low energy cost. That trade suits farms far from data centres. The work weighs which model mixes keep skill while using less power.  Low power use also suits off grid farms and co-ops.
arxiv-2601-12309:
Raz Halifa Levi and Yacov Kantor study large clusters in a correlated percolation model. They use a cubic lattice with side from 16 to 512. Sites are removed by a random walk whose step count scales with the lattice volume.

That removal rule makes the holes correlated, unlike classic random removal. Cluster size in such a system tests how correlation reshapes percolation. Percolation models guide work on flow, spread, and network failure. The team track the large cluster acts in this walk-led case.  Walk led holes give a new twist on an old model.
arxiv-2601-12409:
Sheng Tan studies the color code, a key model in quantum error correction. The color code is a topological code of the CSS type. It has a prized trait: the full Clifford group of gates can be applied transversally. That means gates act in a simple, spread out way that limits how errors spread.

Its strength against local noise comes from its topological excitations. Tan takes up those excitations on an infinite lattice. That limit is the thermodynamic limit, where bulk traits stand apart from edge effects. From the view of quantum phases of matter, this step is key. It shows which traits of the code are deep and which are mere finite size artifacts.
arxiv-2601-12509:
Yuhao Liu and ten co authors tackle a scheduling problem in quantum error correction. Error correction is key for scalable quantum computing. Its repeated syndrome measurement cycles eat most of the space and time cost. Stabilizers commute, so many valid orders exist for those measurements. The catch is that distinct orders send errors down distinct paths under real noise.

Those paths can change the logical error rate by a lot. Past work on scheduling has focused mostly on surface codes. The team present AlphaSyndrome for the broader scheduling problem across codes. Their paper was set for a major computer architecture venue in 2026. Better schedules could cut the hardware cost of fault tolerant machines.
arxiv-2601-12609:
Alberto Dominguez Corella and Jorge Rivera Noriega present a class of domains for parabolic equations. Parabolic equations, like the heat equation, model spread over time. Most theory assumes the domain is a cylinder, fixed in shape as time moves. Real problems often have domains that change shape, though, and those are far harder.

The pair define non cylindrical domains where Dirichlet type problems can still be posed and solved. The boundary of their domains obeys a mixed Lipschitz condition, spelled out in the work. Lipschitz rules bound how rough a boundary may be. A solvability result of this kind widens the range of heat problems with firm answers. It serves both pure analysis and applied models of moving fronts.
arxiv-2601-13209:
Haocheng Ju and Bin Dong map the rise of AI as a tool for maths. AI for maths has grown into its own field. It uses machine learning to roam maths ground that old logic tools could not cross. Mid last century logic tools could run formal proofs, but they hit a wall as search space blew up.

Fresh data led tools have brought new life to the hunt. Ju and Dong trace that arc. They set out where the field has gained, where it still stalls, and what may come next. For maths and AI staff, the map helps pick which open tasks are ripe for machine help and which need new ideas first.
arxiv-2601-13309:
J. Alfonso L. Aguerri and Stefano Zarattini map how the cosmic web reshapes galaxies near its threads. The web is the vast net of matter in space. It grew from small lumps in the early mix, pulled by gravity into walls, threads, and dense knots. Galaxies flow from thin voids to dense knots by those paths.

Threads, called filaments, are the main roads of that flow. The team marks the zone where a thread's pull starts to change a galaxy. That zone sets where a galaxy's form, hue, and star birth start to shift. For galaxy staff, a firm zone helps split web effects from crowd effects in dense knots.
arxiv-2601-13409:
Bo Ren, Ruchao Fan, and co-authors teach speech models to catch rare and trade words with a reward that favours them. Speech large language models have sped up end to end speech sense. They still trip on rare words and field terms, the words that oft count most in a call.

Their method is called RLBR, reward learning with biasing rewards. In reward sums, words on a bias list earn extra weight. That weight pushes the model to try hard on just those words in teach. As a result, rare word marks rise with no loss of plain speech skill. For call and meet tools, rare names and terms are where trust is won or lost.
arxiv-2601-13609:
Yoji Tomita and Tomohiko Yokoyama study fairness in apps that match people to each other in 2026. Dating apps and job boards both need two-sided matches. Each side must like the match for it to count. A system that boosts total matches can still treat some users in an unfair way.

The pair look at reciprocal recommender systems, tools that weigh the likes of both sides. They use Nash social welfare, a rule that values gains for all users in a balanced way. The aim is a high match rate that does not leave some groups behind. Their work frames the trade-off in clear math terms.
arxiv-2601-14209: Matthew Yang and co-authors improve how AI models learn from their own reasoning errors in 2026. Their method is called intervention training, or InT. It steps into a flawed reasoning trace at one step. That step is swapped for a correct one. The model then writes a new ending from that fixed step. These new endings can reach the right answer where the first try failed. The aim is better credit assignment for each step.
arxiv-2601-14409:
Thomas Tomlinson and a team of ten co-authors study the Milky Way's halo in this 2026 paper. The stellar halo holds remnants of past accretion events, smaller galaxies the Milky Way absorbed. Those remnants may show as substructures in integrals of motion space, using energy and angular momentum. The team uses a cosmological Milky Way analogue, a simulated twin of our galaxy.

Their question is in the title: what does a bar do to that picture? The Milky Way has a central bar of stars. The study asks how the bar stirs up halo substructures in the simulation. Readers get a test of how well real halo clumps can still be read after the bar has mixed them.
arxiv-2601-14509:
Michael F. Staddon, Natalie A. Dye, Marko Popović, and Frank Jülicher study growing tissue in this 2026 paper. Developing epithelial tissues coordinate cell proliferation and mechanical forces to reach proper size and shape. Epithelial cells adhere tightly to form a confluent sheet. In such a sheet, the distribution of cell areas shapes the possible packing patterns. It also shapes the mechanics of the whole epithelium.

The team's system is the growing fruit fly wing epithelium. Their title states the puzzle: cell proliferation maintains cell area polydispersity there. Polydispersity means cells keep a spread of sizes, rather than evening out. Readers get a study of how growth itself keeps that spread alive.
arxiv-2601-14609:
Ziwen Wang, Siqi Li, Marcus Eng Hock Ong, and Nan Liu work on privacy-preserving medical research in this 2026 paper. Model co-training across hospitals is often hindered by server-dependent architectures. Those designs clash with protected hospital data systems. Most work also focuses on relative effect measures, like hazard ratios. Such measures lack clinical interpretability for absolute survival risk assessment.

The team proposes FedRD, a communication-efficient framework for federated risk difference estimation in distributed survival data. Federated means the data stay in each hospital while the model travels. Risk difference gives survival gaps in plain absolute terms. A risk gap in plain points is a thing a team can act on at once. The data stay put. Each site keeps its files, and just the sums move. That is the point of the work. Readers get clinical estimates that are both private and readable.
arxiv-2601-14809:
Muhammad Adel Yusuf, Ali Nasir, and Zeashan Hameed Khan model human-robot teamwork in this 2026 paper. Collaborative robots, or cobots, are increasingly integrated into industrial and service settings. They work efficiently and safely alongside humans. For effective collaboration, though, robots must reason based on human factors. The authors name two: motivation level and aggression level.

The paper proposes a stochastic decision-making framework for human-robot collaborative environments. Stochastic modeling treats human states as uncertain and changing over time. The robot then picks actions that stay safe across that uncertainty. The frame is meant for real floors. It must hold up when a tired or cross worker is near the arm. Readers get a decision framework for factory cobots that plan around the person, not just the task.
arxiv-2601-15209:
Paige S. DeVries, Michaela Okosi, and a team of co-authors test whether smart assistants work for deaf users who speak. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with intelligent personal assistants. Many deaf and hard of hearing people use their voice in daily life.

Yet the assistants often fail to parse diverse accents, deaf speech among them. That leaves non-signing, speaking deaf users largely shut out. The authors compare voice-based options with a touch interface powered by a language model. The study weighs which route gives these users real, working, daily access in practice.
arxiv-2601-15309:
Jiaxin Xu, Chao Zhang, and co-authors review how social robots are used to nudge people toward healthier habits. Their 2026 arXiv paper is a systematic review of the field. Social robots are now common tools in health behavior change programs.

Yet designers lack clear, actionable guidance. The review pulls together two bodies of work. It sorts the behavior change strategies used in past robot studies. It also sorts the methods used to judge whether behavior truly changed. The result is a clear map of what has been tried and tested so far.
arxiv-2601-15709:
Asim Biswal and five co-authors give language models a memory for database work in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is AgentSM, a semantic memory for text-to-SQL agents. Text-to-SQL turns plain questions into database queries. Public benchmarks like BIRD and Spider show strong recent gains. Real enterprise settings are harder. Schemas are large and complex, dialects vary, and reasoning runs in costly steps.

A semantic memory can store what the agent learns across queries. Past schemas, joins, and fixes become reusable knowledge. That should cut repeated reasoning and steady the output. The work was done at Amazon Web Services, per a note in the record. For firms with sprawling data estates, an agent that remembers its own experience is the practical draw.
arxiv-2601-15809:
Silvia Casola and four co-authors improve how summary quality is judged across languages in a 2026 arXiv paper. Multilingual models now handle tasks like summarization in many languages. Progress stalls on a practical bottleneck. Accurate, robust evaluation metrics are scarce for many languages. Without good metrics, builders cannot tell if a summary is truly good. Their method is called SteerEval.

SteerEval uses inference-time interventions, per the title. Those interventions strengthen how a metric generalizes across languages. A metric that works only in English misleads multilingual work. Steering it at run time avoids retraining for each language. For low-resource languages, such shortcuts matter most. Their speakers deserve summaries judged by standards as sound as those in major languages.
arxiv-2601-16009:
Giovanna Broccia, Sira Vegas, and Alessio Ferrari study how requirements are read during inspection in a 2026 arXiv paper. Requirements inspection checks software needs before building starts. The representation of requirements shapes inspection accuracy. UML diagrams are widely used next to text requirements. Whether diagrams truly help inspection is still debated. The authors add a second factor: the inspector's cognitive abilities. Working memory and mental rotation skills may sway results.

Their objective, as the abstract begins, is to compare UML and textual forms with cognition in view. That design separates the format's effect from the reader's. Software teams choose formats by habit more than by evidence. Studies like this give them grounds. Catching requirement errors early is the cheapest quality step in software work.
arxiv-2601-16109:
Yashuai Yan and coauthors join a rule based walk plan with learned fixes for biped robots. Their 2026 preprint aims for firm walks in the real world. Real floors and pushes add doubt that a fixed plan can not meet. A pure learned plan can lack the firm base of a rule plan. The team starts with a rule plan for the walk path.

A learned part then adds small fixes on top of that plan. The plan uses the split part of motion to set each step. A whole body drive turns the plan into joint moves. Tests probe if the joined plan walks well through doubt. The work seeks walks that adapt but stay safe.
arxiv-2601-16309:
Dikshya Mohanty, Taisiia Sabadyn and Jelwin Rodrigues build a news set on the Russo-Ukrainian war. Their 2026 preprint sets out a set named dnipro. The set holds a large count of news texts on the war. Texts span from the start in 2022 to 2024. They come from out lets in five states and in three tongues.

A set that spans states and tongues lets teams track tale shifts. The same event can be told in far split ways by each press. Long span data shows how those tales moved in time. Such data serves study of press bias and war tales. The team built the set for open use in such work.
arxiv-2601-16409:
Yeasir Rayhan and Walid Aref set out seed agents that build and run data stores. Their 2026 preprint, named Gen-DBA, draws on a famed Go move. That move showed AI can find new plans past human skill. Data stores still need much hand work to tune and guard. Seed agents could learn store acts and find new ways to run them.

The team frames agents that grow skill from store task tries. Growth aims at plans a hand team may miss in set work. Such agents could cut cost and lift store speed. They could also raise hard calls on trust and check. The work is a seed frame for that path.
arxiv-2601-16509:
Jiaye Li and three coauthors build a graph that adapts for near mate search. Their 2026 preprint deals with the k near mate rule. That rule is a base tool for sorts in AI work. Big sets make its use slow, due to the cost of far counts. Each new point can need counts to all past points.

An adapt graph holds near links in a form that updates fast. New points join the graph with just a few link checks. Fast joins cut the cost of sorts on big data. The team tests the graph on large sort tasks. The work seeks near mate speed at big scale.
arxiv-2601-16609:
Mark Barnet sums gamma burst views from three small CubeSat craft. His 2026 preprint deals with GRBAlpha, VZLUSAT-2 and GRBBeta. Each craft is small and cheap next to big sky scopes. GRBAlpha flew in 2021 to a polar path at set height. It bore a CsI based burst probe for gamma rays.

Small craft fleets can watch the whole sky at low cost. Their burst lists test if small probes can do real sky work. Barnet sums what the three craft saw in their runs. Good lists would back more small craft for burst watch. The work is a fleet note for burst teams.
arxiv-2601-16709:
Nina Aguillon, Sophie Hörnschemeyer, and Jacques Sainte-Marie split sea flow into two speeds for fast math. Their 2026 preprint treats seas as stacks of thin layers. Layers trade water as waves pass through. One part of the flow is swift and near flat. That part sets the sea's top height. The rest is slow and stacked in depth.

The team splits the task in an exact way. The swift part runs on a one-layer plan. The slow part then trades flow among layers. Each part keeps the whole in fine balance. Such fast sea codes aid flood and tide work.
arxiv-2601-16809:
Musfiqur Rahman and Emad Shihab ask what lasts of code that AI writes. Coding bots now add code to open projects each day. A wide hunch says such code is tossed soon. It lands fast, then gets cut in later clean-ups. Their 2026 preprint tests that hunch on real project logs.

The team tracks bot-made code through months of change. They check how much stays, and what gets cut or reworked. If bot code fades fast, firms inherit a fix load. That load shifts cost from the write step to upkeep. The facts can guide how teams vet bot code at merge.
arxiv-2601-16909:
Lei You, Lele Cao, and Iryna Gurevych argue that peer review of science must change its aim. AI now helps check papers at many journals. Most AI tools ape how human judges write reviews. Their 2026 preprint says that aim is wrong. Tools should check claims first, not ape judge style.

They name truth-coupling as the right gauge for tools. It tracks how tight venue scores hug real truth. Two forces push scores off truth, by their frame. Claims grow past our power to check them. Real gains shrink till noise hides them. Their frame names when review tips to score games.
arxiv-2601-17009:
Yanhua Zhao tunes a small drone's flight traits while it flies. The drone is a Crazyflie, a palm-size quadcopter. Its mass, drag, and thrust traits set how it flies. Those traits drift with wear, load, and crashes. Her 2026 preprint gauges them live with an EM loop. The loop swaps twixt trait fits and path fits till both settle.

Live trait fits let drones adapt mid-flight. Quake zones show why such craft count. Rubble blocks roads, and drones reach spots folks can't. Sound flight there needs traits the drone can trust. This loop gives small drones a way to self-check.
arxiv-2601-17209:
Johannes Güttler, Karan Baker, Premjit Saha, James Warner, and Adrian Stein study how to keep machines steady when parts are not known for sure. They focus on input shapers. An input shaper times control signals so a system moves with less shake. Their tool is polynomial chaos expansion, a way to track doubt in math form.

The team puts special weight on doubt that changes over time. They use an intrusive form of the expansion, built right into the model. The goal is a shaper that stays robust as conditions drift. Such work helps engineers design controls that hold up in real use, not just on paper.
arxiv-2601-17309:
Anagha Sabu, Vidhya S, and Narayanan C Krishnan work on algorithmic recourse. Recourse tells a person what to change to flip a bad model call. A loan denial, for instance, should come with steps that can work. Steps must be real and within reach. The authors frame recourse as a constrained inference task under the accepted-class spread.

Their method, PAR, seeks counterfactual cases with high likelihood. It also respects the limits that make a plan sound. That plausibility check stops wild or unfair advice. Good recourse keeps automated choice honest and open to challenge. It gives people a path, not just a no. The frame can serve banks and other gatekeepers.
arxiv-2601-17409:
Seungwoo Lee studies solar cells built from stacked thin materials. Transition metal dichalcogenides and like materials can be transfer-printed in layers. No lattice match is needed between layers. That freedom allows many junctions in one cell. Lee asks what the true limit is for such stacks. He builds a detailed-balance frame with no cap on junction count.

The frame keeps real material and optical limits in view. It treats split-spectrum, multi-terminal designs. Past limits assumed few junctions and ideal parts. A fresh limit shows what thin stacks could reach in fact. Cell designers gain a target that fits their materials. It may steer work toward designs that beat old bounds.
arxiv-2601-17609:
Sara Rezaeimanesh and Mohammad M. Ghassemi draw hidden knowledge out of language models. In medicine and finance, labeled data is costly and scarce. Small training sets then fail on real populations. Language models hold vast prior knowledge from years of research text. The authors extract that knowledge without generation. Their non-generative prior extraction feeds small-data models.

A good prior can lift a weak dataset to useful skill. It avoids the risks of free text generation. Hospitals and banks could gain models they can afford. The method respects data limits that rule those fields. It treats the big model as a library, not an oracle. That stance may widen safe use.
arxiv-2601-17909:
Adriana Watson links three lines of work on privacy and fairness in data. Her 2026 preprint starts with differential privacy, now the gold standard for privacy-safe learning. Most work on it weighs privacy against utility alone. Fairness gets far less care. Watson argues that the trade-offs form a three-way knot, and she treats them as one problem in a systematic way.

One thread reaches back to Dalenius, an early thinker on statistical disclosure control. His dream of total safety from shared data ran into hard limits. Those limits still shape what private, fair AI can promise. The paper gives readers a map of where the goals clash and where they can be met together.
arxiv-2601-18009:
Ervin Dervishaj, Maria Maistro, Tuukka Ruotsalo, and Christina Lioma clean user profiles with the help of language models. Their 2026 preprint deals with recommender systems. These systems learn from implicit feedback, the clicks and views users leave behind. Such data is noisy by nature. Noise hurts how well recommendations work, and removing it has been shown to help. The preprint has not yet passed peer review, as its note states.

The team uses language models to denoise profiles after training data is built. Judging which clicks were mistakes is a language-like task in part. Cleaner profiles should yield picks that fit users better. The work targets a quiet but costly flaw in everyday recommendation.
arxiv-2601-18109:
Sergei Merenkov and Letian Shen prove a rigidity result about fractal sets from complex dynamics. Their 2026 preprint studies rational maps whose Julia sets are Sierpinski carpets. These carpets are fractals full of holes, built by the repeated action of the map. The maps in view are postcritically finite, a tame class. The authors consider a quasiregular map of the Riemann sphere that carries one carpet exactly onto another.

They prove strong limits on what such a map can do. Results of this kind say the fractal's shape holds deep information about the map that made it. They help classify dynamical systems by the sets they leave behind. The work sits in the core theory of complex dynamics.
arxiv-2601-18209:
Yu Meng and co-authors compute a background that could hide a dark matter signal. Their 2026 preprint studies the decay of the J/psi particle into a photon plus something invisible. Hunting dark matter is a primary goal of modern physics. Invisible decays of heavy quarkonia are a promising probe of light dark matter, with a sensitivity few other tests match. Experiments seek the radiative decay in which a photon flies out and the rest vanishes.

The catch is the neutrino background, a known process that looks the same. The team uses lattice methods to pin that background down. A firm background value tells experimenters what counts as a real excess. The work sharpens a delicate search.
arxiv-2601-18809:
Rui Xu, Zhan-Feng Mai, and Dicong Liang find a new solve for a spin black hole in a world view that adds a lone field to gravity. The view, called the bumblebee model, lets a field pick a set line in space and stay there. That pick breaks a deep rule of the plain view, in a small and set way. Black hole solves in such a view are hard to find in full form.

The pair of authors and their mate find a solve that looks just like the famed spin hole of the plain view. The new field rides with it, in a form that is not mere dress. They call it a stealth solve, since the hole's shape hides the field's hand. Such a solve gives a clean test bed: if the field is real, its marks must be sought in fine traits.
arxiv-2601-18909:
Ziyao Cui and Jian Pei study how doubt moves when a big model teaches a small one. In knowledge distillation, a student model learns to copy a teacher. Each step adds chance: the teacher output can vary, the training can vary, and the final answers can vary too.

Most work crushes all that doubt into one fixed number, which can warp what the student learns. Cui and Pei trace how the doubt flows from teacher to student at each stage. Their frame helps builders see where noise enters and how it shapes the small model they ship at the end.
arxiv-2601-19109:
An unnamed author makes music similarity scores that people can both trust and read. Systems that judge which songs sound alike help listeners find new music they will like. The best current systems learn from self supervision, but their scores are hard to explain and data to train them is scarce.

The author instead builds on embeddings from models that are already trained. The aim is a score that matches human ears while staying open to inspection. A readable score lets curators and listeners see why two tracks count as close, not just that a black box said so.
arxiv-2601-19209:
Zhen Yang and six co-authors tune superconducting qubits to sit at their calmest working points. A qubit run at a dynamical sweet spot shrugs off the low frequency flux noise that scrambles quantum states. How long that calm can last, and what hard limits cap it, stayed open questions.

The team frames the search as a multi objective trade, using a fully parameterized scheme that wiggles the flux in a repeating pattern. Their Pareto front view shows the best swaps between calm and other needs. Longer calm times mean quantum machines that can run deeper computations before errors win.
arxiv-2601-19409:
Abylaikhan Tlemissov and three co-authors study black holes that carry a small charge of a heavy photon. The Proca idea gives the electromagnetic field a mass, which changes the classic Einstein-Maxwell picture. No exact solutions are known for that mixed theory, so the team works by perturbation, treating both the Proca mass and the charge as small.

They map how such weakly charged holes behave and what signs an observer might see. Even small changes to black hole physics matter, since real holes now get weighed and imaged with fine precision. The work gives theorists a worked case where the new physics stays calculable.
arxiv-2601-19809:
Lorenzo Clemente studies products of formal power series whose variables do not commute. Such series underlie the theory of automata, machines that recognise patterns. A product operation combines two series into one. Different product rules define different classes of automata.

Clemente considers a large family of products defined by polynomial rules. A P-product is defined coinductively: the rule builds the product recursively from the series and their derivatives. For each family he examines the automata classes that arise and their equivalence problems. Deciding whether two automata agree is a basic question with practical weight. The work unifies many product constructions under one recursive recipe.
arxiv-2601-19909:
Kathi Lakshmi Mani Thirdhana speeds up a classic algorithm: the sieve that finds prime numbers. Prime generation underpins cryptography, number theory, and randomised algorithms. The Sieve of Eratosthenes is simple and efficient in theory. On modern processors its speed is throttled by memory access, not arithmetic.

Her cache-aware hybrid sieve combines three tricks. Segmentation processes the range in blocks. Bit-packing stores flags densely. Block boundaries align with cache lines to use the fastest memory well. Together these raise memory bandwidth use and keep data in the small, fast caches. Faster sieves mean quicker key generation and number theory searches. The work is a lesson in designing algorithms for real hardware.
arxiv-2601-20009:
J. Ben Tamo and colleagues ask which layers of a language model handle which language. Despite multilingual pretraining, models often stumble on non-English tasks. The authors separate two failure modes. In the transfer bottleneck, the model replies in the right language but gets the task wrong. In the consistency bottleneck, the answer is right but in the wrong language.

Their study, LinguaMap, characterises where each failure lives in the network. Knowing the responsible layers tells practitioners how to tune them. Targeted tuning could fix language control without retraining everything. Most users of these models do not work in English. Work on language control is therefore central, not peripheral, to the field.
arxiv-2601-20109:
Shamse Tasnim Cynthia, Al Muttakin, and Banani Roy examine what happens after AI-written code is merged. AI coding agents now produce pull requests that are merged with little or no human review. The productivity promise is clear. Their post-merge code quality, though, is largely unexplored, since prior studies used benchmarks and controlled tasks.

The authors run an empirical investigation of post-merge quality issues in agent-generated pull requests. Real repositories reveal problems that benchmarks cannot: issues that surface in review threads, fixes, and later maintenance. Knowing the failure modes tells teams where human oversight still pays. The work grounds a heated debate in evidence from production code.
arxiv-2601-21509:
Enrico Le Donne, Sebastiano Nicolussi Golo, and Andrea Tettamanti measure how fast certain geometric spaces settle toward their limit shapes. Some Lie groups with distance structure look, at large scales, like simpler nilpotent models. Two classic theorems describe those limits but say little about the speed.

The authors give quantitative estimates of the gap between the true metric and its limit. They treat both the broad-scale limit and the tangent, small-scale limit. Rates matter when a theorem is used for computation rather than pure theory. Their estimates tell users how large a scale must be before the simple model can be trusted.
arxiv-2601-21609:
Bingqian Li, Xiaolei Wang, Junyi Li, Weitao Li, Long Zhang, Sheng Chen, Wayne Xin Zhao, and Ji-Rong Wen build a recommender that lets user tastes spread and evolve. Agent-based recommenders use language models to read complex behavior. Most model taste changes from direct user-item history alone.

That history is sparse and noisy, and it misses how users and items sway each other in real time. Their system propagates preferences through the network and lets the pattern evolve on its own. Richer taste dynamics should mean suggestions that track what people want now, not what they clicked months ago.
arxiv-2601-21709:
Qingyue Yang and eight co-authors seek one explanation for the attention patterns seen inside language models. Past work catalogued patterns one by one: heads that fetch earlier text, heads that park on the first token, and diagonal traces. The catalogue lacked a unifying account.

The authors take a temporal view, asking how attention evolves over the life of a sequence and of training. A single frame that predicts which patterns appear would turn folklore into engineering. Builders could then design attention on purpose instead of discovering its habits after the fact. The work aims at that unified picture.
arxiv-2601-21909:
Shaojie Wang and Liang Zhang argue that language models are trained to reason in a way humans do not. Standard post-training fine-tunes whole reasoning traces, then applies reinforcement learning based on final outcomes. It works, but it skips how people actually solve problems.

Human problem solving splits into two stages: first gaining abstract strategies, then applying them to the case at hand. The authors' 2026 preprint proposes cognitively aligned post-training that mirrors that split, moving from meta-thought to execution. Aligning training with human reasoning could help models generalize. Their skills would transfer to new problems. They would not just memorize the shape of old ones. Their failures would also be easier to predict and repair.
arxiv-2601-22209:
Xinyuan Song and Liang Zhao recommend teams of agents, not just single tools. Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by orchestrating agents and tools picked from fast-growing marketplaces. As those marketplaces expand, many candidates overlap in function, and selection becomes more than a retrieval problem.

An orchestrator must filter for relevance, then choose options that are reliable and compatible with the other picks. The authors learn to recommend whole subgraphs of agents from calling trees, the records of which agents called which. Their 2026 preprint treats agent selection as a structured recommendation task. Better selection could make multi-agent systems dependable enough for real business processes.
arxiv-2601-22409:
Puyu Wang, Junyu Zhou, Philipp Liznerski, and Marius Kloft derive training, error, and privacy bounds for a new kind of network. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks swap fixed activation curves for learned ones, a bid for leaner models. Their 2026 preprint notes that sound theory for their training has lagged the hype.

The team study plain gradient descent on a two-layer form of the network. They bound how fast it learns, how well it generalizes, and what privacy it can claim. Firm bounds tell users when to trust the new design. They also show where it may fail. The work is a reality check.
arxiv-2601-22609:
Anastasiia Tkachenko and Haitao Wang find dominating sets fast in disk graphs whose centers sit in convex position. A disk graph links points whose disks overlap. Their 2026 preprint studies the placed case, where centers form a convex shape, like points on a ring.

A dominating set is a small crew that touches every node or its neighbor. Such crews serve sensor nets and network guards. The convex layout lets the team beat the general case's cost. The work is algorithm design with a clean setup. It shows how shape can make a hard task tractable.
