bateson-mendel-principles-1909:
William Bateson was a Cambridge biologist who became the loudest English champion of Gregor Mendel's newly rediscovered laws of inheritance. His 1909 book Mendel's Principles of Heredity gathers his lectures and papers for a wide scientific audience. Bateson even coined the word genetics for the new science.

He shows how traits in peas, poultry, and other bred stock split and recombine in fixed ratios across generations. He defends Mendel's rules against older ideas of blending inheritance with case after case. The book sold Mendelism to the English-speaking world and trained its first geneticists. He writes as a missionary for a science still fighting for a hearing.
berkeley-new-theory-vision-1709:
George Berkeley, a young Irish scholar, published An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision in 1709. It was his first major work, written when he was only twenty-four. The question sounds simple: how do we see distance, size, and place? Berkeley's answer upset the settled teaching of his day.

He argues that distance, magnitude, and situation are not seen at all, in the strict sense. The eye gives us light and color; touch and habit teach us what those signs mean. Sight, for Berkeley, works like a language learned in childhood. The essay opened his path to immaterialism, the claim that being means being perceived. Its clarity still startles.
bernard-sermons-advent-christmas-1909:
John Hedley translated Bernard's sermons for Advent and Christmas into English in 1909. Bernard preached these sermons to his monks at Clairvaux in the twelfth century, marking the opening weeks of the church year. Advent, the season of waiting for Christ's coming, drew some of his most tender preaching.

The sermons treat Christ's coming in three ways: in history at Bethlehem, in the soul by grace, and in glory at the end. Bernard moves between close reading of Scripture and warm address to his hearers. His honeyed style, which earned him the name mellifluous doctor, is at its gentlest here. Hedley's translation gave English readers the devotional Bernard, the preacher of longing and joy, rather than the controversialist of the letters.
bogoras-chukchee-1904-1909:
Waldemar Bogoras spent years among the Chukchi people of far northeast Siberia, and this large study came out in 1909. His work formed part of the Jesup work in the North Pacific. The texts were set down word for word as they were told to him. He lived with the people he wrote about and learned their tongue. He also made long trips by sled and boat along the coast.

The pages cover daily life, kin ties, tales, and rites in close detail. A long share deals with shamans, spirits, and the cures and songs they used. It stays a key firsthand source for the folk ways of the Chukchi.
carrington-eusapia-palladino-1909:
Hereward Carrington tests a famed seer at close range in Eusapia Palladino and Her Phenomena, out in 1909. Palladino was a stout dame from Naples whose sittings shook the age. Tables rose, hands grasped guests, and strange stuff seemed to flow from her frame. Carrington sat through long runs of tests in Naples with peers from the chief band for such study.

He grants fraud in part, yet holds a strange rest stands. His tale is tense, fair, and full of night by night notes. The book is the best close tale of the most fought seer.
chinesische-alchimie-separatabdruck-1909: Chinesische Alchimie, Separatabdruck, 1909. The Chinese alchemy. This book preserves that offprint. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
cia-0000008009:
South Vietnam had existed for barely a year when CIA analysts weighed its possible course in March 1955. Ngo Dinh Diem led the new state after Vietnam split at Geneva in 1954. Armed religious sects, refugees from the north, and communist cadres all tested his rule.

The paper asks whether Diem's government could survive and what might bring it down. Washington was beginning its long bet on South Vietnam, and judgments like this one guided that choice. Reading it now shows how much uncertainty attended the first step. The estimate stands at the head of a twenty-year American commitment.
cia-0000009709:
Near Muong Ngoi, in Luang Prabang province, stood a Pathet Lao prison, a June 1969 item reports. Muong Ngoi is a river town in northern Laos, reached more easily by boat than by road. Prisons in such country were hidden by distance itself.

Northern Lao camps held a mix of Lao, Thai, and some American prisoners, far from any observer. A located prison gave the map one more fixed point in the uplands. It also told families of the northern missing where to focus hope. The file records that point as reported, in the secret war's quietest corner.
cia-0000009809:
Possible cooperation between American prisoners of war and the Viet Cong, in a Quang district the title cuts short, is weighed in an October 1971 paper. Quang could begin several province names in central Vietnam. The subject itself was among the war's most delicate.

Captivity broke men unevenly, and the line between survival and collaboration was hard to draw from afar. Analysts had to judge reports of cooperation without knowing the pressure behind them. Such papers affected men's reputations and their welcome home. The file preserves that judgment being made carefully, on partial evidence, in the middle of the war.
cia-0000009909:
Forty-two American prisoners were detained by the Viet Cong in the South Vietnam-Cambodia border region, a November 1966 report states. A count of forty-two made the southern prison system look larger than many assumed that early. Border camps held the men beyond easy reach.

Large counts forced officials to rethink the south's place in the captivity story. Hanoi's prisons drew the cameras, but the numbers said the jungle camps mattered greatly. Verifying a count like this took years of cross-checking names. The report preserves the claim at its first filing, when it challenged the accepted picture.
cia-0000012409:
Meeting number twenty-three, July 28, 1961, nears the end of the summer phase's London run. The season's harvest was nearly gathered by then. Weeks of answers on Soviet forces, weapons, and plans stood taken down in numbered order. Soon the colonel would return to Moscow again. Contact would thin to signals and drops until his next trip west gave the handlers another season.

The twenty-third session's record closes July's account of the case. Handlers could tally the summer in sessions, and the tally was remarkable. For readers, the page shows a great operation at its steady, productive peak.
cia-0000013209:
The Viet Cong captured an American near Da Lat, and a CIA report from September 1971 records the incident. Da Lat, in the southern highlands, was a resort town turned garrison in a hard-fought region. Every capture began in chaos: a fight, a flight, a man taken. The reports that followed tried to impose order on that chaos, fixing who, where, and when while the trail was warm.

The report preserves the moment of taking in the file's plain form. Such notes opened the long files that some families waited years to close. For readers, it is the capture report as the war produced them, one by one.
cia-0000013609:
Panama gets a country survey of its own in a CIA paper from April 1967, titled with the country's name alone. The brief gives the republic's Cold War profile in compact form. It covers the canal and the Zone that split the country in two. It also covers the oligarchy that ruled the republic and the National Guard that guarded, and finally replaced, its rulers.

Such one-word briefs were the file's shorthand for a standing watch. This one catches Panama a year before the Guard's coup remade its politics. For readers, it is the isthmus in brief: the waterway, the families, and the soldiers.
cia-0000013909: American prisoners were observed at Hang Co Railroad Station in Hanoi, in a CIA note dated November 1, 1967. A rail station sighting placed prisoners inside the capital itself. Men seen there were being moved through the heart of the north. The note adds the capital's main station to the list of known transit points.
cia-0000014709: Propaganda aspects of the Rosenberg atomic spy trial fill a CIA paper dated June 4, 1952. The paper weighed how the trial played as a public message, at home and abroad. The Rosenbergs' fate had become a worldwide argument by 1952. A paper on its propaganda side shows the agency cared as much about the story as the secrets.
cia-0000015409: Staff comments on letters about unidentified flying objects fill a CIA record dated March 5, 1958. One exchange asked whether the Air Force objected to sending letter writers a copy of the panel report. Major Tacker replied that the Air Force would rather answer the letters itself. The note shows two agencies sorting out who should reply to writers like Major Keyhoe and Mr. Davidson.
cia-0000022309: Gary Powers was awarded the Intelligence Medal, a CIA record dated in 1970 notes. Powers had flown the U-2 shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960, then faced prison and a swap. A medal a decade later was a quiet act of repair. The entry marks his old service honoring a pilot once left to carry blame alone.
cia-0000044009:
A jurist assured a fair trial for the Jesuits' murderers, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. A fair trial was exactly what the case's critics doubted was possible. Salvadoran courts worked under pressure from every armed side.

Inside, the judge's pledge of fairness is preserved as given. Such pledges mattered to the foreign governments watching the case. Aid and standing turned, in part, on the trial's good faith. The file keeps the promise at its making, leaving readers to set it beside the verdicts and appeals that the courts produced in the years that followed.
cia-0000049109: An allegation in 1985 tied ARENA, El Salvador's hard-right party, to the assassination of Archbishop Romero. A CIA item from that year preserves the charge, filed with the Truth Commission records. The claim had circulated since the murder itself; putting it in an official file gave it a different weight.
cia-0000049209: A country commentary from 1991 gauges the Salvadoran armed forces' attitude toward the Jesuit case, in a partly blacked-out CIA item. Country commentaries were the station's considered take, written for readers who set policy. This one measures an army's mood toward the case that was remaking its future, month by month.
cia-0000049309: From September 2, 1991, declassified CIA document 0000049309 reports that a five-man jury in El Salvador found Salvadoran Army Colonel Guillermo Benavides guilty. The heading names the verdict and the officer at its center. The short file preserves how the agency noted a court outcome in the Salvadoran case, without adding background beyond the jury's finding itself.
cia-0000049409: Government performance and problems in El Salvador are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049409, dated June 3, 1982. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper grades the government in general terms. It is a short declassified item whose heading pairs performance with problems, preserved as a broad agency judgment rather than a study of one policy.
cia-0000104909:
Statement to the Court on Behalf of the Victims of Harold J. Nicholson's Espionage is declassified CIA document 0000104909, dated May 1, 1997 in the catalog. The sample is a letter dated June 2, 1997, to Judge James Cacheris in Alexandria, Virginia. The writer signs as Acting Director of Central Intelligence.

The letter says Nicholson betrayed his friends and colleagues and put their lives in danger. He revealed, or planned to reveal, the names and posts of many CIA officers working in secret. Some could no longer do the assignments they were trained for. Officers under the deepest cover were withdrawn, their missions and lives at risk.
cia-0000112809: List and Information Regarding Individuals Conn is the heading, cut off mid-word and with its date an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000112809, dated January 1, 1945. The catalog marks the file untitled, then gives this list label. What the individuals were connected with breaks off at Conn in the heading. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the break.
cia-0000117909: Recent Developments in Southeastern Europe is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000117909, dated June 6, 1950. The heading promises fresh events in one region, southeastern Europe, in plain survey words. Recent is the title's own word for how new the events were. The brief record is a regional survey item from the summer of 1950 in the files.
cia-0000119209:
This March 1984 CIA document reports Vietnam's assessment of American policy in its region. The heading adds that Hanoi kept a continuing hope for something from the United States, then breaks off before naming it. Nearly a decade after the war ended, the two countries still had no normal relations.

Hearing the other side's view was the point of such reporting. The document sets out how Vietnamese leaders read Washington's moves and what they still wanted from America. It captures a frozen relationship beginning, very slowly, to thaw, and it shows the agency listening to a former enemy whose choices still shaped Southeast Asia.
cia-0000119709:
A February 1954 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Argentina. President Peron's second term was running into economic trouble, and his grip on the country was weakening. Eighteen months later the military would drive him from power.

The paper weighs the forces pressing on Peron's government and the paths the country might take. Argentina mattered to Washington as South America's second great power and as a test of populist rule. Reading the forecast now, one can judge how clearly the agency saw the fall coming. It is a period piece from the years when Peronism first rose, broke, and began its long afterlife.
cia-0000124309: Dated April 1951, this CIA document carries two items: the arrival of American prisoners of war in Canton, and their transfer onward, the heading breaking off. The paired items trace the men's movement step by step through Chinese hands during the Korean War. Paired items of arrival and transfer sketch the route men took into the interior, the same route later tracing work would follow in reverse for decades.
cia-0000132209: Situation report 526, from January 1991, notes the European Community boosting aid to frontline states. Those states bore heavy costs from the war on their borders, and European money helped hold the coalition's Arab members steady. The report records the aid decision. Aid to frontline states was coalition maintenance in cash form, paying the neighbors of Iraq and Kuwait to bear refugee, trade, and military burdens without wavering.
cia-0000132409: The situation in Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 1, 1959. It was filed just one month after Castro's victory, which makes it one of the earliest Cuba files in the set. The revolution was only weeks old at that point. Washington was still deciding what the change of power meant, and the document gives the situation as analysts first found it.
cia-0000132509: Chile treating Cuba as a bilateral problem for the United States fills a CIA document dated February 2, 1961. Santiago wanted no part of a joint campaign against Havana. Chile's stance pointed ahead to the split that would open inside the Organization of American States over Cuba. The short document notes the position and what it meant for Washington's hopes of regional unity.
cia-0000135709: Brigade 2506's Spanish archive holds this document, dated 6 February 1961. By February the exile force was in its final training phase, weeks from embarkation. The catalog gives the item no subject heading, so none is invented here. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release. For students of the Bay of Pigs operation, such dated records mark the brigade's pace in its last full month of preparation.
cia-0000135909: A meeting record in the declassified CIA files, dated 4 May 1954, covers points covered in talks held on the first and second of June, the speaker's name deleted. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136209: The open CIA files hold a press file dated 1 May 1954 that deals with the Guatemala press file for the eighth through the eleventh of June. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136309: Operational Situation Report No. 12, dated late June 1954, tracks PBSUCCESS rebel teams across eastern Guatemala. It reports the combined Johnny-Danny force capturing Chiquimula except the enemy barracks, after a requested air strike failed when both F-47s had mechanical trouble. Other teams report no change, request mortars and 20-mm guns, or stay silent without radios. A resupply flight could not locate its team near Gualan. The report shows an invasion running on patchy information.
cia-0000136609: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 1 January 1961 and flags the date as estimated. Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained force of Cuban exiles, was in its final training winter. Estimated dates recur at the New Year in this series. The record names no subject for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, as part of the brigade's archive from the months before the Bay of Pigs.
cia-0000136709: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 3 February 1961, marked as estimated. An earlier summary filled this item with London, Washington, and an alliance against Hitler; that is Second World War material with no place in a 1961 brigade record, and it is removed. What the record supports is a Spanish document of the exile brigade, then in final training, released in the CIA's declassified files.
cia-0000137009: Communists in embassies are violating asylum, the themes in this June 1954 cable charge. Asyleed communists pass arms and money in and out by radio. They conduct propaganda from inside. Carlos Manuel Pellecer sits in the Mexican embassy. He is said to be making tape recordings. The tapes aid subversive propaganda by party remnants. Themes to push are listed. The government is as democratic and just as possible. There are no blood baths. Asyleed communists and common criminals grossly violate asylum's privilege.
cia-0000137109: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents, dated only to 1960 in the catalog record. The papers are in Spanish, the language of the brigade's Cuban members, who were training that year under CIA direction for the landing that came in 1961. The record states no month or subject for this item. It survives as released through the CIA Reading Room, part of the exile force's early paperwork.
cia-0000137309: NSC Briefing — Cuba, dated 1960, is a declassified CIA briefing paper prepared for the National Security Council, the president's senior advisory body on security policy. Its subject, per the title, is Cuba, in the year when Castro's government broke openly with the United States and Washington began planning against it. Several such Cuba briefings survive in these files. The catalog gives no finer breakdown of this one's contents, so it is described at that level: a dated council briefing, released through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-03190609: September 15, 1957: the daily bulletin circulated. The intelligence roundup went to senior readers. The Cold War's September note. Writers of history may cite it later. This declassified paper is saved. The text is preserved. The record is kept.
conceptions-of-matter-ancient-and-modern: Conceptions of Matter, Ancient and Modern, microform, 1909. The matter conceptions. The files keep it safe. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
constitution-bolivia-2009: Bolivia's 2009 Constitution, backed by referendum, refounded its state. It honors indigenous nations. The Tower library holds the full text. It rewrote a republic. Andes voted. Natives rose. Law renewed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-luxembourg-2009: Luxembourg's 1868 Constitution, amended through 2009, frames its grand duchy. The Grand Duke reigns. The Tower library holds the full text. It kept a small crown. Fortunes grew. Duke reigned. People thrived. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-poland-2009: Poland's 1997 Constitution, amended through 2009, frames its republic. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It buried communism. Shipworkers struck. Priests blessed. Freedom won. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-venezuela-2009: Venezuela's 1999 Constitution, amended 2009, built Chavez's republic. It lifted term limits. The Tower library holds the full text. It rode oil boom. Caudillo rose. Votes lifted. Crisis followed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
corneille-polyeucte-constable-1909:
An Armenian Christian faces a pagan court in Corneille's Polyeucte, given here in Thomas Constable's Harvard Classics translation. Polyeuctus embraces the faith and smashes the idols, knowing the price is death. His wife Pauline, torn between her father, her old love, and her husband's God, carries the play's heart.

French classical tragedy reaches its religious summit in this drama of conversion and sacrifice. Duty and grace argue in high, ordered verse, as Corneille loved to stage them. The translation joins the library's Le Cid, letting English readers meet both faces of France's first great tragedian.
croce-aesthetic-1909:
Aesthetic as Science of Expression and General Linguistic, published in English in 1909 in Douglas Ainslie's translation, is Croce's foundational work on art. It opens his Philosophy of Spirit, the system that made him Italy's leading philosopher.

Art, Croce argues, is intuition given expression: not copying nature, not decoration, but the mind's first form of knowledge. From that claim he rebuilds the history and theory of aesthetics, treating language and art as one activity. The book's learning is vast and its tone magisterial. It set the terms of Italian criticism for a generation and traveled worldwide.
croce-philosophy-practical-1909:
Philosophy of the Practical, published in English in 1909, is the second volume of Croce's Philosophy of Spirit. After art and expression comes action: this book treats the economic and the ethical as the two practical forms of the spirit.

Croce distinguishes useful action, aimed at single ends, from moral action, aimed at the universal good, and shows how each corrupts the other when confused. Politics, law, and history are drawn into the scheme. The argument is abstract, but its stakes are conduct itself. With this volume, Croce's system covered both knowing and doing in one design.
crowley-777-1909:
Aleister Crowley built a master key to his magic in 1909 and called it 777. The book sets out tables that match gods, planets, signs, and symbols to the thirty-two paths of the Tree of Life. Crowley was then shaping the system he would teach for life.

Row by row, the tables let a student pass from a god to a scent, a stone, a plant, or a verse. The scheme rests on the Jewish Kabbalah as the Golden Dawn had taught it. Workers in the Thelemic line treat 777 as their standard desk book. Few tables of symbols have been thumbed so hard for so long.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-09:
Number nine of The Equinox came out in March 1913, the journal's fifth year of life. Crowley's twice-yearly numbers had built a shelf of white volumes by now. The spring issue carries the work of the order into its next phase.

First printings of rites and teachings fill the number, as in each issue before it. The pages show Crowley's school at work in rite, song, and argument. Each number locks one season of that work into the lasting record. Number nine locks the spring of 1913 in its place. One more number would close the great first volume.
davies-mythology-british-druids-1809:
Edward Davies, a Welsh cleric, set out his grand scheme of British druid lore in this book of 1809. He wrote in the Romantic age, when old British roots drew much public zeal. His aim was to trace the druids back to the dawn of faith.

Davies tied the druids to Noah, the flood, and the ark of the Bible. He read old Welsh verse and stone works as proof of one vast rite scheme. Grand and flawed, the book fixed what druidism meant for a whole age of readers. Few books show the age's hunger for old roots so well.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-09: Volume nine continues Montaigne's lifelong conversation with himself. He weighs his faults, his habits, and his ever-changing mind with total candor. No thinker is more honest about being human. The essays at their most personal and most enduring.
eucken-life-spirit-1909:
Philosophy itself is the problem at the heart of Rudolf Eucken's introduction, first printed in German and Englished by F. L. Pogson in 1909. Eucken refuses to treat philosophy as a fixed set of facts to hand over. Instead he presents it as work the human spirit must keep doing.

Across a few clear leading lines, he traces how that work went on through the centuries. Doubt and conflict mark the path, since spiritual life rests on no safe, given base. The book asks readers to take part in the search themselves. It served many newcomers as their first door into Eucken's thought.
eucken-problem-human-life-1909:
Great thinkers from Plato onward have each formed a view of what human life is and should be. Rudolf Eucken gathered those views in Lebensanschauungen grosser Denker, a German survey of life views held by major minds. W. S. Hough and W. R. Boyce Gibson translated the work into English in 1909.

Eucken walks through the answers given across the ages, from Greek thought to his own century. He compares each view, notes what it grasps and what it misses, and builds toward his own position. The survey shows how one deep question kept changing shape. It also gives readers a guided tour of Western thought.
europmc-pmc10154209:
Therriault and colleagues model Alzheimer's disease stages from brain scans in a 2023 study, using a staging system first built from autopsy tissue. The Braak system ranks how far tau tangles have spread through the brain. The team applied it to living patients using PET scans with a tau tracer, in a group of more than three hundred people.

They then modeled how blood and scan markers change across those stages. The model links marker shifts to disease progress in life, not just after death. That link helps trials pick patients and track whether drugs work.
europmc-pmc10329209:
Aiken led a large 2023 survey of doctors and nurses who work in US hospitals. The US Clinician Wellbeing Study Consortium backed the work. The team asked 15,738 nurses and 5,312 doctors about stress, burnout, and plans to quit. Burnout means deep work fatigue that harms health and care.

Aiken found that burnout was high and spread across hospital staff. It linked to staff quitting and to worries about patient safety. Staff had low trust that bosses would fix care problems. They ranked more staff and a better work setting above wellness classes for their own health. The team urges bosses to act on staffing and work design first.
europmc-pmc10406609:
Ashuach and colleagues built MultiVI in 2023, a model that joins two kinds of single-cell data. One kind reads which genes a cell has switched on. The other reads which parts of its DNA lie open for use. Each view alone gives a partial picture of the cell.

MultiVI merges both views into one shared profile for each cell. It can even fill that profile for cells where one view is missing. Ashuach built it as a chance-based model that learns from the data. Users can then group cells, spot subtypes, and chart how cells differ. The tool is free through the scvi-tools site. It aims to sharpen work on cheaper, single-view data sets too.
europmc-pmc10501909:
Lu led a vast team in 2023 to build ageing clocks that work across all mammals. The clocks read methylation, small tags on DNA that shift with age. Past clocks fit one species or a few tissues. The team pooled 11,754 samples from 185 mammal species and 59 tissue types.

Their clocks guessed tissue age with very high accuracy, a score above 0.96. Lu found that gaps from true age track death risk in humans. The same gaps shift with calorie limits and with growth gene faults in mice. Age-linked tag sites cluster near genes for growth, cancer, weight, and long life. The work hints that ageing is an old, shared program tied to development.
europmc-pmc10767809:
Rauluseviciute and co-authors marked 20 years of JASPAR in 2024, a free data bank of transcription factor binding profiles. A profile sums up where a factor, a protein that switches genes, grips DNA. JASPAR staff curate each profile by hand and keep the set free of repeats. This is the tenth release of the bank.

The CORE set gained 329 new profiles, a 20% rise. Three old profiles were updated, and 72 past drafts gained firm backing. Rauluseviciute adds a trim step that cuts low-value edges from profiles. Binding site tracks were rebuilt for eight organisms. A new tool lets users pull predicted sites that cross their own genome zones.
europmc-pmc10837209:
Wu, Wu, Chen, and Li review two signal families that build and maintain bone and cartilage in this 2024 paper. Cartilage is the smooth tissue that caps joints. The TGF-beta and BMP families send growth signals that guide bone-forming and cartilage-forming cells. Their signals pass through relay proteins inside the cell, and small shifts in those relays change the outcome.

BMP signals promote bone and cartilage growth at all stages, the review says. TGF-beta signals act in a more stage-dependent way and help keep the bone cell network intact. The two families pull in opposite directions for joint cartilage balance. The authors map the many control layers that tune these signals. They also list human diseases and mouse models tied to faulty signalling, in hopes of guiding bone drugs.
europmc-pmc11111409:
Zuntini and hundreds of co-authors rebuild the family tree of flowering plants from nuclear genes in this 2024 study. Flowering plants, called angiosperms, anchor most land ecosystems and human livelihoods. Past trees rested mainly on the plastid genome, the small genome of the cell's food-making parts. Sampling of species and genes was limited and biased, weakening trust in those trees.

The team built the tree for almost 8,000 genera, about 60 percent of all such groups, using 353 nuclear genes. That is a 15-fold jump in genus sampling over prior nuclear studies. Many older relationships held, but key groups, above all rosids, changed. Dated with 200 fossils, the tree shows explosive early branching that produced over 80 percent of living orders. Bursts returned in the most recent era.
europmc-pmc11180609:
Roohani, Huang, and Leskovec present an AI method that predicts how cells respond to gene tweaks never tried before in this 2024 paper. Testing gene perturbations, meaning switching genes up or down, is central to cancer and regenerative medicine work. The number of possible multi-gene combos explodes far past what labs can test. The team built a predictor to cover that gap.

Their method, GEARS, fuses deep learning with a knowledge graph of gene relationships. It trains on single-cell data from perturbation screens. It can predict outcomes for combos of genes that were never perturbed in any experiment. On a combinatorial screen it scored 40 percent higher precision than prior methods at sorting four interaction types. It also flagged the strongest interactions twice as well. The authors offer it as a guide for designing perturbation experiments.
europmc-pmc11742009:
Jomova, Alomar, Nepovimova, Kuca, and Valko review heavy metal toxicity and human health effects in this 2025 paper. Heavy metals occur naturally in the Earth's crust and persist as pollutants in the environment. People take them in by breathing air and dust, and by eating or drinking tainted food, water, or soil. Their build-up in the body can damage many tissues and organ systems.

Toxicity depends on the metal's properties, dose, route, and duration of exposure, the authors explain. The main harm route is interference with antioxidant defences. Metals bind glutathione and the sulfur groups of defence enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase, disabling them. Arsenic is thought to bind thiols directly at critical sites, the sulfur sites on proteins. Alternative routes that generate hydrogen peroxide are also postulated. The review maps effects organ by organ.
europmc-pmc1270009:
Haycraft and co-authors studied two gene switches and cell antenna proteins in 2005. Cilia are tiny hair-like structures built by transport proteins. Those proteins also serve the Sonic hedgehog signal pathway. Gli2 and Gli3 are the switches that pathway controls.

Both switches were found located at cilia themselves. A transport protein called Polaris proved needed for their processing. Without Polaris, Gli3 processing went wrong in mouse limb buds. That failure lifted repression on a target gene, Gli1. Yet Gli1 activity itself stayed intact at molecule level. Haycraft shows transport proteins tune specific switch steps.
europmc-pmc1797809:
Salazar and colleagues tracked in 2007 how dengue virus type 2 moves through the mosquito Aedes aegypti after an infected blood meal. To reach a new human host, the virus must infect the gut, spread through the body, and enter the saliva glands. The wait between meal and possible spread is the extrinsic incubation period.

They used a newly colonized mosquito strain from Chetumal, Mexico. Gut virus levels peaked between seven and ten days after infection, then viral protein and live virus fell while viral RNA stayed stable. Spread from the gut tracked with virus appearing in the trachea, the insect breathing tubes. Virus showed in saliva glands of over a third of mosquitoes by day four, and it built up in nerve tissue throughout the wait.
europmc-pmc1878509:
Aid, Timmusk and co-authors redrew the map in 2007 of a key brain growth gene in mice and rats. The gene makes BDNF, a factor that supports neuron development and the plasticity behind memory, learning, and addiction. Rodent versions of the gene were heavily studied, yet their structure stayed incompletely known.

The team found several new transcript forms with previously unknown starting sections. Both the mouse and rat genes hold eight alternative first exons, meaning start pieces, plus one shared protein-coding final exon. Each transcript splices one of the eight starts onto that coding end. Each start version also shows its own pattern across brain regions and body tissues. Seizures induced by kainic acid, plus shifts in cell calcium and gene-tag removal, tuned the starts differently, showing fine-grained control.
europmc-pmc1892109:
Stahlhut, Swan and co-authors asked in 2007 whether everyday plastic chemicals track with obesity and insulin resistance in American men. Phthalates, used to soften plastics, can block male hormones in rodents and lower testosterone in men. Low testosterone in turn goes with more belly fat and diabetes risk.

The team used a national survey of adult men from 1999 to 2002, measuring six phthalate breakdown products in urine. They modeled those levels against waist size and a standard index of insulin resistance, adjusting for age, race, diet, activity, smoking markers, and kidney and liver function. The abstract frames the study as the first population test of this chain. Its title reports the direction found: higher metabolite levels went with larger waists and stronger insulin resistance in these men.
europmc-pmc1994709:
Caicedo and co-workers mapped DNA variation in domesticated rice in 2007. Rice, Oryza sativa, is among the oldest crops and feeds more people than any other plant. The team compared rice with its wild ancestor, Oryza rufipogon. They sequenced 111 randomly chosen gene fragments across varieties. Their aim was to infer how domestication shaped the rice genome.

They found, genome-wide, an excess of high-frequency derived variants, a pattern not reported in other crops. A simple bottleneck model, where numbers crash during domestication, could not explain the pattern. Models adding selective sweeps, where favoured genes spread fast, fitted better. So did models with population subdivision and gene flow. Strong selection may thus mark variation across the whole genome.
europmc-pmc2065909:
Hoshida and co-workers introduced SubMap in 2007, a method for matching disease subtypes across separate gene studies. Gene expression profiling can reveal molecular subtypes of a disease. But subtypes found in one data set often fail to match those in another, especially across platforms. Supervised models trained on one set can miss real structure in a new set. SubMap instead compares both data sets in both directions.

The method defines a score for how well subtypes correspond, and tests whether that match is significant. It builds on the team's earlier gene set enrichment work. Applied to cancer data sets, SubMap found shared breast cancer subtypes tied to estrogen receptor status. It also found a lymphoma subgroup with similar survival patterns. That match improved the accuracy of a clinical outcome predictor.

europmc-pmc2265709:
Bello, Izergina, Caussinus and Reichert found in 2008 a new mode of brain cell production in the fruit fly Drosophila. In mammalian brains, neural stem cells amplify their output through intermediate progenitor cells that keep dividing. Whether fly brain neuroblasts, the stem-like cells there, do the same was unknown. Using lineage tracing and genetic markers, the team examined remarkably large neuroblast lineages in the dorsomedial larval brain.

These neuroblasts divide asymmetrically to renew themselves, but unlike others they do not pass the differentiation factor Prospero to their smaller daughters. Those daughters keep neuroblast markers and divide repeatedly, acting as intermediate progenitors. Their divisions look symmetrical but are molecularly asymmetrical, segregating fate determinants into one daughter only. This amplification mirrors mammalian neurogenesis, suggesting deep conservation of neural stem cell biology between insects and mammals.
europmc-pmc2289809:
Rafailidis, Mourtzoukou, Varbobitis and Falagas systematically reviewed severe cytomegalovirus infection in 2008 in people with apparently normal immunity. This virus is well known for harming transplant recipients, HIV patients and unborn babies. Its toll on immunocompetent adults had received little attention. Searching major databases for 1950 to 2007, the team gathered reports of severe infection in such patients and examined where it struck and whether antivirals were used.

They found 89 articles covering 290 immunocompetent adults with severe disease. The gut, mainly colitis, and the central nervous system, including meningitis and encephalitis, were the commonest sites. Other manifestations included blood disorders, vessel clots, eye inflammation and pneumonia. Reported practice reserved antiviral treatment for the most severe brain, eye and lung involvement. The authors conclude severe complications in healthy hosts may be less rare than assumed.
europmc-pmc2323709:
The START Trialists' Group reported Trial A in 2008, a UK trial of radiation treatment after surgery for early breast cancer. The standard plan gave 50 gray of radiation in 25 small daily doses. Gray is the unit for absorbed radiation dose. The trial tested whether 13 larger doses could work as well.

Over 2,236 women at 17 centres took part between 1998 and 2002, split among three dose plans. After about five years, cancer returned near the treated site in 3.6% of the standard group. The higher of the two new plans gave 3.5%, a difference the data showed was tiny. The lower new plan, 39 gray, caused fewer late changes in breast appearance. The authors concluded breast tumors respond to dose size much like normal tissue does.
europmc-pmc2360509:
Lloyd and colleagues measured how the UK public values life with metastatic breast cancer in 2006. Metastatic means the cancer has spread beyond the breast. Health economists use utility scores, where 1 is full health and 0 is death, to compare treatments fairly.

The team wrote plain descriptions of disease states, from stable cancer on treatment to cancer growing again, plus six side effects. One hundred members of the public rated each state using the standard gamble, a choice task that reveals how much risk people accept to avoid a state. Stable disease scored 0.72 on the utility scale, and a good response added 0.07 to that value, while progression cut 0.27 from it. Side effects cost between 0.10 and 0.15, with fever from low white cells the worst.
europmc-pmc2397409:
Perez-Iratxeta and Andrade-Navarro built a web tool to read protein shape from light in 2008. The lab method is circular dichroism spectroscopy, which shines twisted light through a protein solution. The way the protein absorbs that light betrays how much of it is coiled into helices or folded into flat strands.

Their method, K2D2, learns from spectra of proteins whose shapes are already known. It arranges those spectra on a self-organised map, a grid where similar spectra sit together, and ties each spot to known shape contents. A new spectrum is placed on the map, and its spot gives the estimate. The free web server returns the shares of alpha-helix and beta-strand, the two main shape elements, plus an error estimate for the prediction.
europmc-pmc2515109:
Rosa and Everaers used computer simulations in 2008 to explain why chromosomes keep to their own territories inside the cell nucleus. When a cell is not dividing, its chromosomes loosen, yet microscope images show each one still occupies a distinct region. Many had assumed some scaffold or protein anchors must hold them apart.

The simulations show no scaffold is needed. A plain model of loosening chromosomes, built only from polymer physics with no fitted values, reproduced the territory shapes seen in human, fruit fly, and yeast cells. The territories persist because long chain molecules stay tangled with themselves and cannot pass through each other. Confined random motion plus these topological limits, meaning the chains cannot cross, is enough to keep chromosomes apart.
europmc-pmc2612009:
Arvidsson, Kwasniewski, Riaño-Pachón, and Mueller-Roeber presented a tool called QuantPrime in 2008 for designing PCR primer pairs automatically at scale. Quantitative PCR measures gene activity, but each assay needs a specific primer pair, and designing hundreds by hand is slow and error-prone. QuantPrime automates the choices, checking specificity against ready-made transcriptomes.

The tool ships with data for 295 species, from model organisms to crop plants, and uses gene structure information such as exon borders and splice variants to place primers well. Parameters are highly customisable, and it runs online or locally. Tests in the model plant Arabidopsis, in barley, and in a green alga gave success rates above 96 percent for designed primer pairs. The framework also extends to probe design for related techniques.
europmc-pmc2631809:
Dowell proposed in 2001 a fresh explanation for the seasonal cycles of infectious diseases: the susceptibility of the host population itself may rise and fall with the seasons. Standard explanations blame weather, how common or strong the pathogen is, or human behaviour. Dowell lists observations those ideas struggle to fit, including outbreaks igniting simultaneously across wide regions at the same latitude.

Pathogens can also be detected during the off-season, yet no epidemic follows. Seasonal timing stays consistent despite wide variation in weather and behaviour. Dowell points instead to the annual light-dark cycle. It acts through the hormone melatonin, whose release pattern tracks day length. Light-driven body change is well documented in mammals. Some is documented in humans too. If such change governs resistance for much of the year, finding and shifting it could prevent and treat a great deal of illness.
europmc-pmc2657209:
Brownlie and co-authors reported in 2009 a hidden benefit that a common insect bacterium, Wolbachia, may give its hosts. Wolbachia lives inside many insects and spreads by bending their reproduction in its favor. Some strains cannot do that trick, yet still spread, which hinted they must pay their hosts something in return.

Fruit flies carrying Wolbachia laid more eggs when their food held too little iron, or too much. Iron is a nutrient both flies and bacteria need, and the bacterium's genes suggest it can handle iron for the host. The team also measured iron in wild-caught flies. Wild levels matched the low-iron lab diets, so the benefit likely matters outside the lab too. A supposed parasite, the authors argue, may often act as a quiet nutritional partner.
europmc-pmc2659709:
Brooks and colleagues warned in 2009 that the flushed face many East Asians get after drinking alcohol marks a hidden cancer risk. About 36 percent of Japanese, Chinese, and Korean people inherit a weak form of an enzyme, ALDH2, that clears a toxic alcohol byproduct. Their faces redden, and they may feel sick and race in the chest.

Because the byproduct lingers, these drinkers face a far higher risk of cancer of the esophagus. That is the tube carrying food to the stomach. Drinkers with the normal enzyme face no such added risk. This cancer is among the deadliest, with low survival rates on every continent. The authors aim their warning at doctors: a flushing patient shows a sign of the flaw. Asking about flushing, they argue, is a cheap way to spot patients who should be urged to drink far less.
europmc-pmc2728709:
Thring, Hili, and Naughton tested in 2009 extracts from twenty-one plants for anti-aging effects on skin enzymes and for antioxidant power. Elastase and collagenase are enzymes that break down elastin and collagen, proteins that keep skin firm, and their activity rises with skin aging. Plant extracts are widely sold for skin care, but few are tested side by side.

White tea topped both enzyme tests, blocking each by close to nine tenths, and also held by far the most phenolic compounds, plant chemicals tied to antioxidant effects. Sixteen extracts blocked collagenase and nine blocked elastase, with green tea, cleavers, and burdock root among the stronger ones. All extracts showed antioxidant activity in at least one assay.
europmc-pmc2790509:
Somm and colleagues tested whether contact with bisphenol A before birth and during nursing changes how rat pups store fat. Bisphenol A, or BPA, is a chemical used in plastics that can disturb hormones. Pregnant rats drank water with a low dose from early pregnancy through the end of nursing in the 2009 study.

At weaning, female pups exposed to BPA carried about three times more fat around their reproductive organs than unexposed pups. Their fat cells were larger, and genes that build fat ran at higher levels in both fat and liver tissue. Later weight gain depended on sex and diet, while food intake stayed the same across groups.
europmc-pmc2820409:
Balsitis and colleagues built the first mouse model in 2010 of dengue disease made worse by antibodies from a prior infection. Dengue comes in four types, and catching a second type after the first can turn deadly, because cross-reactive antibodies help the virus enter immune cells instead of stopping it. No animal model had captured that worsening before.

Giving mice dengue antibodies before infection reproduced the human danger signs: low platelets, leaking blood vessels, high cytokine levels, and heavy virus loads. High doses of type-matched antibodies protected, but lower or cross-reactive doses worsened disease. One rebuilt antibody that cannot grip cell receptors both prevented and treated the lethal course, pointing to a safer antibody design.
europmc-pmc2838909:
Bayoh and colleagues traced a forty-year shift in 2010 in which malaria mosquito dominates western Kenya, following the spread of insecticide-treated bed nets. Two close mosquito species share the region: Anopheles gambiae, which prefers human blood and rests indoors, and Anopheles arabiensis, which feeds more on cattle. Records from 1970 onward plus new sampling along a transect gave the long view.

The indoor species made up about eighty-five percent of house catches until the late nineteen nineties. As net ownership rose after 2004, its share crashed to about one percent by 2009, while its sibling took over almost completely. Infection and breeding rates also fell where nets were common, a population-level effect of the nets.
europmc-pmc2846909:
Aulchenko, Struchalin, and van Duijn introduced ProbABEL in 2010, a software package for genome-wide association studies built on imputed genetic data. Imputation fills in unmeasured genetic variants with probabilities rather than certainties, and simply treating the likeliest guess as fact biases results. Ordinary tools built for directly measured variants cope badly with such guesswork.

ProbABEL folds the uncertainty straight into its tests, covering measured traits, yes-or-no outcomes, and time-to-event outcomes under the matching models. A fast two-step score test handles related samples, such as families and isolated populations, without crushing computing time. The authors offer it as a usable way to hunt complex-trait genes across the whole genome from imputed data.
europmc-pmc2857309:
Deaths tied to a gut germ were rising fast in the United States, and Redelings, Sorvillo, and Mascola measured the trend for 1999 to 2004 in this 2007 study. The germ is Clostridium difficile, a spore-forming bacterium that often strikes older patients after antibiotic treatment. It can cause severe diarrhea, colon inflammation, and blood infection.

Using national death records, the team found the death rate rose more than fourfold across the six years. It climbed from under six deaths per million people to nearly twenty-four per million, and the rise held through the whole period. Rates ran higher in white patients than in other groups. The authors link the surge in part to a newer, stronger strain then spreading in hospitals.
europmc-pmc2858209:
Repeated miscarriage may reflect a womb lining that fails to screen embryos, Salker and colleagues propose in this 2010 study. Recurrent pregnancy loss means three or more miscarriages in a row. The lining cells must change into a state called decidual each cycle, and that change should let the lining sense embryo quality.

Biopsies from women with repeated loss showed too little prolactin, a marker of the decidual state, and too much of a signal that invites implantation. Cells grown in the lab repeated the same faulty pattern and ignored signals from the embryo. Paradoxically, the women conceived again very quickly, which fits a lining that accepts embryos too easily, including weak ones it should reject.
europmc-pmc2948509:
Yao and colleagues tested a short stretch of ribosomal DNA called ITS2 as a universal barcode for telling species apart, in a 2010 study. A good barcode needs standard primers, easy copying, and enough variation to separate close relatives.

They downloaded tens of thousands of plant and animal ITS2 sequences from a public bank and measured length, base makeup, and variation within versus between species. Between-species gaps generally beat within-species spread. Naming success at species level ran from roughly two thirds in conifers to over nine tenths in animals, varying by family. The folded shape of the segment added extra clues.
europmc-pmc2988709:
Simarro and colleagues built an atlas of human African trypanosomiasis, sleeping sickness, in a 2010 mapping effort led with world health bodies. Charting where cases occur guides the push to end its standing as a public health threat.

The atlas covers twenty-three of twenty-five affected countries for the decade to 2009, with two still being processed. Records combine active screening of over two million people with cases found at clinics, totalling tens of thousands of cases across thousands of localities. Village coordinates anchor the maps. The database gives control programmes a shared, detailed picture for targeting.
europmc-pmc3037909:
Woodruff and colleagues reviewed in 2011 the causes, models, and treatment attempts for ischemic stroke, where a blocked vessel starves part of the brain. Stroke kills more people worldwide than almost any other condition and leaves many survivors badly disabled. Few treatments exist to limit tissue death after onset, so better models and targets are urgently needed.

The review walks through how brain tissue dies, then details animal and cell models used to copy the injury in the lab. It judges the strengths and flaws of the best mouse models and the lab practices they demand. Past single target drugs protected brains in animals yet failed in every human trial so far. The authors urge work on targets with broad, multi sided effects instead. They frame the review as a guide for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc3053509:
Jain, Gautam, and Naseem reviewed in 2011 the proteins the body floods into the blood within hours of infection, injury, or trauma. These acute phase proteins are made mainly by the liver after alarm signals arrive from the damage site. They help trap microbes, clear cell debris, neutralize harmful enzymes, and tune the immune response while repair gets under way.

Because their levels rise and fall with illness in predictable ways, the proteins double as diagnostic tools. The review lists veterinary and medical uses, from cattle lung infections and pig diseases to prostate cancer and blood cancers in people. In farm practice, a blood test for these proteins can flag sick animals before clear symptoms show. The authors present them as a cheap, early window on animal health that complements hands on examination.
europmc-pmc3237409:
Patrick Schloss, Dirk Gevers, and Sarah Westcott worked out how to clean up errors in gene-based surveys of microbial communities, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Studies that read the 16S ribosomal gene to profile microbes were plagued by sequencing mistakes and by chimeras, hybrid sequences created during amplification, which invent species that do not exist.

The team sequenced ninety identical mock communities built from twenty-one known species, so every error could be spotted against the truth. They tested ways to flag bad reads, trim poor-quality regions, and correct bases, cutting the error rate sharply; one established algorithm gave the best balance of accuracy, length, and yield. Chimeras made up a notable share of raw reads and drove most fake diversity, but filtering plus a detection program reduced them to about one percent. The pipeline still left batch effects to watch for.
europmc-pmc3278109:
Gunther Eysenbach asked whether tweets can predict which papers will be heavily cited, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Citations are the standard measure of scientific impact but accumulate slowly. Eysenbach mined every tweet linking to articles in his own journal over more than three years and built metrics of social attention, then compared them with later citation counts.

Most tweets arrived on publication day or the day after, then decayed fast. Tweet volume correlated moderately with later citations, and a combined model using timing and tweets explained a meaningful share of citation variation. Articles in the most-tweeted group were about eleven times more likely to end up highly cited than the least-tweeted. Top-cited papers could also be flagged from tweet data with high specificity. He proposes a twimpact factor to capture social impact alongside citations.
europmc-pmc3315009:
Moore and Fletcher reviewed how people come to feel that they caused their own actions, in a 2012 article. This feeling, called the sense of agency, helps people learn from outcomes and take responsibility for what they do. Older theories split over whether the feeling comes mainly from inside signals tied to movement, or from outside clues in the situation.

The authors argue that both kinds of clues matter and are weighed together, much as the senses combine sight and sound. They adapt a statistical framework from perception research to explain how the brain merges these cues. The review then applies that lens to disorders where the feeling of control breaks down. Delusions of being controlled by outside forces are one example. The authors also note where the framework still falls short.
europmc-pmc3320609:
Smith and co-authors revisited the classic mathematical theory of mosquito borne disease, in a 2012 article. The framework is usually credited to Ronald Ross and George Macdonald, two pioneers who modeled malaria spread. Tracing publications across seventy years, the authors show that many scientists added pieces, and that Ross built two models while Macdonald built a third.

What textbooks call the Ross Macdonald model is really a family of models sharing a core set of assumptions. Around the math grew a wider theory covering how transmission is measured and how mosquito control cuts it. Its key measure, vectorial capacity, and the main field methods were all settled before the nineteen sixties ended, as the worldwide malaria eradication campaign wound down. The authors argue the theory still anchors research and control strategy for mosquito borne diseases.
europmc-pmc3374609:
Abubucker and a large team introduced HUMAnN in 2012, a method to read what a microbial community can do from its DNA. Shotgun sequencing of mixed samples yields short reads from hundreds of species at once. Piecing those reads into whole genomes is slow and often impossible.

HUMAnN instead counts gene families and pathways directly from the short reads, along with their abundances. Tests on fake communities recovered both big pathways and small modules with high accuracy. Applied to hundreds of Human Microbiome Project samples from seven body sites, it found a core set of modules present nearly everywhere. Other pathways marked single niches, such as sugar breakdown in the gut.
europmc-pmc3378609:
Basu and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2012 whether private or public health care serves poorer countries better. The debate had grown heated as tight budgets pushed governments toward private provision. Both camps accused the other of cherry-picking friendly case reports, so a full evidence check was overdue.

Reviewing the comparative studies, the team found the evidence mixed and often thin. Private services tended to cater to wealthier patients with fewer medical needs, an unfair pattern seen across many settings. Claims that private care is simply more efficient or effective did not hold up consistently. The review urges policy built on measured performance rather than ideology.
europmc-pmc3394709:
Kueider, Parisi, Gross, and Rebok systematically reviewed in 2012 whether computerized training sharpens the minds of healthy older adults. Their net caught studies of people averaging at least fifty-five, free of dementia and mild impairment. Of more than one hundred fifty reports found, thirty-eight met the bar.

Programs fell into three families: classic training tasks, therapy-style software, and video games. Nearly all reported gains after training, with effect sizes ranging from tiny to very large. Most studies also found that seniors did not need prior computer skill to finish or benefit. The gains matched or beat paper-and-pencil training, at far less labor, making the digital route attractive.
europmc-pmc3444709:
Bady and colleagues built a prediction model in 2012 for glioblastoma. It reads the methylation status of the MGMT gene from chip data, a status that forecasts benefit from certain chemotherapy. Whether the gene is silenced by methylation depends on exactly which spots in its promoter carry the tags, which makes classification tricky. The team mined a chip reading well over a hundred spots in and around the gene.

Two promoter regions carried nearly all the signal for silencing and for patient outcome. A two-probe model built on them classified tumors about as well as the standard lab test in a training set, and held up in an independent patient group. Methylation patterns also shifted with tumor grade and a broader methylator state. The model lets researchers mine existing chip datasets for treatment-resistance clues.
europmc-pmc3474909:
Barrett, Fletcher, and Wilton reviewed how the non-coding parts of genes control gene activity, in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2012. Sections of a gene that never become protein were once dismissed as junk. The review argues the opposite: those regions hold much of the control system that lets complex organisms time and place gene activity with great precision.

The authors walk through the regions before and after each gene's coding part, the stretches cut out of messages, and the many non-coding RNAs copied across the genome. Together these elements fine-tune output through many layered interactions. Barrett's team ties the growth of such control regions to the rise of complex body plans. Variation in them, they note, helps explain differences between people and species.

europmc-pmc9671809: A fresh look at the influence of the microbiome (microbes living in the body), diet and genetics on inter-individual variation in the human plasma metabolome arrived with this 2022 research paper. europmc-pmc9816309: A fresh look at neoantigens: promising aims at for cancer therapy arrived with this 2023 research paper. Recent advances (new steps forward) in neoantigen research have accelerated the growth and regulatory approval of tumor immunotherapies, including cancer.
