Mice bred to make too much of it in muscle grew a wasting myopathy. In human samples of one such ill, the enzyme was also off its normal level. Those twin facts make a strong case for its role. They also mark it as a target for care in wasting muscle ills.
plos-pone-0001709:
Feng Ding and co-authors deleted a small RNA gene in mice to probe an obesity syndrome, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Prader-Willi syndrome is the leading genetic cause of obesity. Children with it start weak and floppy, then develop extreme hunger and severe obesity if food is not controlled. They also tend to be short, with hormone and learning problems.

The deleted piece is the snoRNA Snord116, also called Pwcr1 or MBII-85, from the syndrome's chromosome region. Mice without it showed growth deficiency and overeating, per the paper's title. The full text gives the mouse growth and feeding data. A single small RNA driving core features of the syndrome narrows the search for its causes sharply.
plos-pone-0001809:
Getnet Yimer, Getachew Aderaye, Wondwossen Amogne, and their co-authors studied liver damage from tuberculosis drugs in Ethiopia in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Anti-tuberculosis therapy can injure the liver, a side effect called hepatotoxicity. The team set out to assess and compare its prevalence, severity, and prognosis in TB patients with and without HIV.

They enrolled 103 HIV-positive and 94 HIV-negative TB patients and evaluated all of them during treatment. The full text gives the liver injury rates and outcomes in each group. Co-infected patients take many drugs at once, so knowing whether HIV raises liver risk helps clinics schedule monitoring where it counts most.
plos-pone-0001909:
Cathy Helgason and Thomas Jobe wrote a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on judging one patient against trial results. Large trials report how the average patient fares on a drug, but a doctor treats one person at a time. The authors note that one patient's state can be set out as a set of measured values, each a point in a fuzzy set.

From that view, they set out a way to compare a single patient with the average patient in big double-blind trials. The comparison is meant to be precise and measurable. If the match can be scored, trial proof could be weighed for the person in the room, not just the group.
plos-pone-0002009:
Xuan Fu and co-authors traced how a cancer drug prompts cells to build more power units, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Breaks in both strands of DNA had been shown to spur mitochondrial biogenesis, the making of new mitochondria. The steps behind that response were poorly known, though a key sensor of such breaks is a protein called ATM.

The team used etoposide, a drug that breaks DNA, in their tests. As the title states, the drug induced ATM-dependent growth of mitochondria through activation of AMPK, an energy sensor. The chain links DNA harm to energy supply, a link that may shape how cancer cells survive treatment.
plos-pone-0002109:
Izumi Mori and co-authors found an early blood sign that tracks recovery in a nerve illness, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Guillain-Barre syndrome is a sudden paralysis caused by the immune system attacking nerves. High doses of pooled antibodies, called intravenous immunoglobulin, are commonly used to treat it and many autoimmune diseases. Yet how they work is only partly explained, and no early marker predicted their efficacy.

The team report that prominent plasmacytosis, a surge of antibody-making cells in blood after the treatment, correlates with clinical improvement. An early marker lets doctors switch tactics sooner when a costly therapy is failing.
plos-pone-0002209:
Jarosław Bryk and co-authors tested whether one gene variant was favored by evolution in East Asians, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Genome scans had produced long lists of regions that might have undergone positive selection in humans, meaning helpful variants spread fast. Few candidates had been checked in depth.

The team focused on a variant of the EDAR gene in East Asian populations. They report evidence that selection favored this allele, which boosts the activity of a signal pathway called NF-kappaB. Confirmed cases like this one show how recent human evolution can be read directly from DNA.
plos-pone-0002309:
Pedro Miura, Meghan Andrews, and Martin Holcik studied how steroid drugs raise levels of a backup muscle protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Glucocorticoids are the only drug treatment known to benefit Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a fatal muscle disease of boys. Why they help is not fully known, but a rise in utrophin, a protein akin to the missing dystrophin, is one suspect.

The team showed that glucocorticoid treatment enhances translation of utrophin A in muscle cells. The boost runs through an internal ribosome entry site, a special start point in its message. Raising utrophin is a leading drug strategy for Duchenne, and this pinpoints one route steroids may take.
plos-pone-0002409:
Kuhn, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Irene Kuhn, Paul Harden, Maxine Bauzon, among others. Its subject is directed Evolution Generates a Novel Oncolytic Virus for the Treatment of Colon Cancer. Viral-mediated oncolysis is a novel cancer therapeutic approach with the potential to be more effective.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002509:
Paterson and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Steve Paterson, Clare Wilkes, Colin Bleay, among others. Its subject is immunological Responses Elicited by Different Infection Regimes with Strongyloides ratti. Nematode infections are a ubiquitous feature of vertebrate life.

In nature, such nematode infections are acquired by continued exposure to infective stages over a prolonged period of time. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002609:
Wilson and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Kitchener D. Wilson, Zongjin Li, Roger Wagner, among others. Its subject is transcriptome Alteration in the Diabetic Heart by Rosiglitazone: Implications for Cardiovascular Mortality. Recently, the type 2 diabetes medication, rosiglitazone, has come under scrutiny for possibly increasing the risk of cardiac disease and death.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002709:
In 2008, Kurt I. Kamrud and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about analysis of venezuelan equine encephalitis replicon particles packaged in different coats. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Kurt I. Kamrud, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The Venezuelan equine encephalitis (VEE) virus replicon system was used to produce virus-like replicon particles (VRP) packaged with a number of different VEE-derived glycoprotein. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002809:
In 2008, Hyunjeong Yang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was transmembrane and Ubiquitin-Like Domain-Containing protein 1 (Tmub1/HOPS) facilitates surface expression of GluR2-Containing AMPA receptors. The catalog record names Hyunjeong Yang first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Some ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain-containing proteins are known to play roles in receptor trafficking. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002909:
Yunhe Li, Michael Meissle and Jörg Romeis fed Bt maize pollen to adult green lacewings in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Lacewings are common pollen eaters in maize fields, so they meet the insect-killing proteins made by engineered maize. The two proteins tested were Cry1Ab and Cry3Bb1.

Adult Chrysoperla carnea lacewings ate the pollen under test conditions so harm could be checked directly. The title reports that eating either pollen did not harm the adults. Results like this feed into safety reviews of insect-resistant crops, where effects on helpful insects weigh heavily. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003009:
Daniel Catron and Mohamed Noor compared gene expression in fruit fly hybrids in 2008. Hybrid problems such as sterility may stem partly from disrupted regulation of gene expression. Studies in the Drosophila simulans group had found genes expressed above or below both parent species in hybrids.

Here the contrast is organism versus organ: whole-body patterns set against single-organ patterns in species hybrids. That distinction matters, since a disruption in one organ can vanish in a whole-body average. Published in PLOS ONE, the work refines how hybrid dysfunction is measured in speciation research. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003109:
Bob Uttl, Peter Graf and Amy Siegenthaler tested how relative size affects memory for object photos in 2008. Participants saw color photos of pairs of common objects shown at either appropriate or inappropriate relative sizes, a large object shrunk or a small one enlarged. Implicit memory was assessed by priming, explicit memory by direct recall tests.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team investigated both memory types side by side. Size realism is a neat test of whether memory stores scenes faithfully or reconstructs them. Results bear on eyewitness work and on how displays should present objects.
plos-pone-0003209:
Howard Chia-Hao Chang, Douglas N. Dimlich, Takakazu Yokokura and colleagues model spinal muscular atrophy in fruit flies in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Spinal muscular atrophy is a recessive inherited neurodegenerative disease in humans, linked to mutations in the survival motor neuron, or SMN, gene. Patients show early onset lethality with motor neuron loss and skeletal muscle wasting. The team used Drosophila as their system.

Readers get a fly model for a human disease that is hard to study directly. Flies allow fast genetic tests of which other genes worsen or ease SMN loss. Such screens can nominate drug targets for later testing in mammals.
plos-pone-0003309:
Werner Baumgartner, Florian Fidler, Agnes Weth and colleagues image a sand-swimming lizard in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The sandfish, Scincus scincus, is a lizard with the remarkable ability to move through desert sand for significant distances. It is well adapted to living in loose sand by a combination of morphological and behavioural specializations. The team investigated the body form and locomotion involved.

Using NMR imaging, they observe the sandfish moving within desert sand without digging it up. Readers see an animal swim through a solid-looking medium. Its mechanics interest biologists and engineers who design robots for sand and rubble.
plos-pone-0003409:
Katy Milne and colleagues looked at immune attack in ovarian cancer for this 2008 paper. Tumors filled with CD8 T cells tend to grow more slowly. Many patients also make antibodies against tumor proteins on their own. The team asked how those two responses relate in epithelial ovarian cancer.

They focused on antibodies against one tumor protein, NY-ESO-1. Patients with those antibodies also had strong T cell presence in tumors. The two arms of immunity seemed to answer the same tumor flag. That link supports efforts to treat this cancer through the immune system.
plos-pone-0003509:
Francisco J. Quintana, Aderet Solomon, and Irun R. Cohen studied how B cells switch antibody types in 2008. B cells weigh antigen signals from their own receptor plus help signals. Help can come from cytokines or from other cells. Toll-like receptors add another form of co-stimulation.

The team examined antibody IgG3 made against LPS, a bacterial surface molecule. Toll-like receptor 4 supplied a needed co-signal for that production. Two keys together license a specific antibody response. The finding shows how danger signals shape antibody choice. Antibody class choice decides how well a response clears each kind of germ.
plos-pone-0003609:
Yi-Hsiu Chen and co-authors studied gene control in a gut parasite in this 2008 paper. Giardia lamblia forms a cyst wall to survive outside its host. Three cyst wall protein genes switch on strongly during encystation. How those genes are governed was little known.

A factor called UPF1 regulates the cyst wall protein transcripts. UPF1 is conserved across life as part of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. That system normally destroys faulty messages. Here it helps time the parasite's infectious transformation into a cyst. Giardia is a common cause of diarrhea in travelers and children worldwide.
plos-pone-0003709:
Yuko Seko, Noriyuki Azuma, Yoriko Takahashi, and colleagues published this eye study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The sclera is the tough white coat that holds and protects the eyeball. It does not itself take part in seeing, yet its diseases are hard to cure. The team studied its makeup across species.

They found the human sclera keeps traits in common with cartilage throughout evolution. That kinship reframes the white of the eye as a cartilage-like tissue. It also hints at new angles for treating scleritis, perforation, and the extreme nearsightedness tied to scleral change.
plos-pone-0003809:
Thomas G. Paulson, Patricia C. Galipeau, Lianjun Xu, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The tumor suppressor gene p16 is altered in many human cancers. Barrett's esophagus is a premalignant change in the food pipe, often from chronic reflux. How often p16 mutates there was much less known.

The team charted the spectrum of p16 mutations in Barrett's tissue. They set those point changes beside other p16 damage known from cancers. The pattern helps mark the genetic road from a reflux-damaged esophagus toward cancer, and where checks might catch it early.
plos-pone-0003909:
Henrick Horita, Arthur E. Frankel, and Andrew Thorburn studied a targeted toxin against leukemia in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer. The disease brings about 13,410 new U.S. cases and 8,990 deaths a year, they note. A lab-built toxin, DT-GMCSF, had shown it can kill leukemia stem cells.

The authors asked how that toxin kills the cells it targets. They found it switches on two death paths, apoptosis and necroptosis. A toxin that kills by two routes may be harder for cancer to dodge. The result guides how such toxins might be paired with other drugs.
plos-pone-0004009:
Yunzhao R. Ren, Fan Pan, Suhel Parvez, and co-authors tested an old drug on an immune channel in 2008. The Kv1.3 potassium channel matters in memory T cells. It is implicated in multiple sclerosis, psoriasis, and type 1 diabetes. Many groups have built blockers for that channel.

Their PLOS ONE article reports clofazimine blocks Kv1.3 in T lymphocytes. It does so by disturbing calcium oscillations inside the cells. Clofazimine is a known drug long used against leprosy. A second use in immune disease could speed new treatments. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004109:
Kira Foygel, Bokyung Choi, Sunny Jun, and co-authors studied a stem cell factor in early embryos in 2008. Oct4 is a master regulator of embryonic stem cell pluripotency. It is also highly expressed at the one- to two-cell embryo stage. The early embryo's gene network was far less known than the stem cell one.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a novel, critical role for Oct4. It regulates the maternal-to-embryonic transition in development. That handover switches control from mother's RNA to the embryo's genome. Oct4 thus bridges the stem cell and embryo gene programs. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004209:
Nathalie Mandairon and colleagues published this smell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In humans, how pleasant an odor seems shapes social relations and food intake. Smells attract or repel according to their hedonic value, and these preferences shift with experience and learning.

The team asked whether mice share human olfactory preferences, judging the same odors as pleasant or unpleasant. A match between species would mean preferences are built into the nose, not just learned. The comparison matters for using mice to study a sense that, in humans, is deeply emotional.
plos-pone-0004309:
Andrzej Slominski and colleagues published this steroid study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme P450scc transforms 7-dehydrocholesterol, the skin's vitamin D precursor, into 7-dehydropregnenolone in the test tube. Whether living tissue performs the same chemistry was the open question.

The team studied adrenal glands from rats, pigs, rabbits, and dogs outside the body. They report rapid, time- and dose-dependent metabolism of 7-dehydrocholesterol into steroidal 5,7-dienes. They also discuss what this pathway implies for the skin, where the starting compound is plentiful and sunlight adds energy. The work was done on glands from four species, which makes the shared result stronger.
plos-pone-0004409:
Vitamin C at high doses may slow cell growth. Sophie Belin, Ferdinand Kaya, Ghislaine Duisit, and co-authors study that effect in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. Ascorbic acid is best known as a nutritional supplement with antioxidant properties.

The team had shown high concentrations affect a gene tied to a nerve disease in mice. Here they link the antiproliferative effect to inhibition of genes needed for cell cycle progression. Blocking those genes could stall dividing cells. The work adds a mechanism to debates on vitamin C in cancer. Cell cycle genes are core growth drivers, so their inhibition links dose to effect.
plos-pone-0004509:
Four human chemokine receptors, hard to study because they sit in cell membranes, were made in bulk by Hui Ren, Daoyong Yu, Baosheng Ge, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The receptors are CCR5, CCR3, CXCR4, and CX3CR1. They belong to the GPCR family, proteins that pass signals from outside the cell to inside.

How these receptors change shape when they bind their signals was still unclear, mainly because pure receptor protein is scarce. The team reports high-level production of synthetic versions, then solubilizing and purifying them. CCR5 and CXCR4 are famous as doors HIV uses to enter cells. A supply of pure receptors opens the way to structural studies and to drugs designed against exact shapes.
plos-pone-0004609:
Sleep's role in strengthening memory may not be the same across all mammals, test Isabella Capellini, Patrick McNamara, Brian Preston, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sleep is a pervasive characteristic of mammalian species, yet its purpose remains obscure. It is often proposed that sleep is for the brain, supported by studies showing sleep improves memory consolidation.

The authors take a comparative approach: if sleep evolved to consolidate memory, species' sleep patterns should track their memory needs in predictable ways. Comparing many species is a strong test that single-species lab studies cannot give. The paper asks an old question with a wide lens. Its answer bears on why we sleep at all, a puzzle that touches every human life.
plos-pone-0004709:
Diana Stauch and colleagues asked how two T cell clearing drugs affect natural killer cells, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Drugs that deplete T cells are a core part of care after transplants and blood treatments. One widely used drug is made from rabbit antibodies, yet its full effects were not well mapped.

Little was known about what it does to natural killer cells, a fast acting immune cell type. The team compared its effects with a second clearing drug. They found like effects despite unlike targets. The work helps doctors predict infection and cancer risks after treatment.
plos-pone-0004809:
Charles Ansong led a team that mapped how two RNA binding proteins shape Salmonella for PLOS ONE in 2009. In bacteria, a small set of such proteins can tune many genes after their messages are made. Two of the best known are Hfq and SmpB. Both help the cell control which proteins it builds, and both can affect how sick the bacteria make a host.

The team deleted each gene and then read both messages and proteins across the whole cell. Loss of either protein reshaped that picture in broad ways. The maps show how one small protein can steer growth and virulence at once. That makes these proteins good targets for new drugs against Salmonella.
plos-pone-0004909:
Martin Graziano and Mariano Sigman studied spatial and temporal construction of confidence in the visual scene, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human subjects can report many items of a cluttered field a few hundred milliseconds after presentation. Memory decays rapidly and after a second only three or four items remain in working memory. Dynamics of objective performance were compared with confidence measures across locations and delays.

Confidence builds unevenly across space and time. People know less about what they misjudge. Metacognition dissociates from accuracy measurably. Visual awareness research gains quantitative tools. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0005009:
Vesicles are tiny sacs bounded by a fatty membrane. Researchers use them for drug delivery and origin-of-life studies. Small uniform vesicles are easy to make. Large uniform ones were not. Ting Zhu and Jack Szostak presented a solution in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their method prepares large monodisperse vesicles. Monodisperse means the vesicles share nearly one size.

Extrusion through tiny pores works well for small vesicles. For larger sizes it gives very uneven batches. The new preparation method overcomes that limit. It gives researchers reliable large bubbles for experiments. Such vesicles can model early cells. They can also carry drugs in a controlled way.
plos-pone-0005109:
Small proteins called thymosins appear in human saliva. Their levels change during development. Sonia Nemolato and colleagues measured them in pre-term newborns. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They studied thymosin beta 4 and beta 10. Samples came from babies' mouths and fetal salivary glands. Sensitive mass spectrometry did the measuring.

Despite wide variation between babies, a pattern showed. The secretion of these thymosins switches during fetal development. The switch marks a changing of the guard before birth. Saliva chemistry carries developmental information. Such markers might one day track fetal maturation. Noninvasive saliva tests are attractive for fragile pre-term babies. This study maps what is there to measure.
plos-pone-0005209:
Brain tumors in children look like adult gliomas under the microscope, yet they behave in distinct ways. Drug developers have been hampered by a lack of cell lines grown from children's tumors. Bax and colleagues filled part of that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team characterized pediatric glioma cell lines at both the molecular level and in their visible traits. Well-described lines give labs faithful stand-ins for testing new targeted drugs before any child is treated. The work lays groundwork for therapies designed for children, not borrowed from adult care.
plos-pone-0005309:
Vaccines built on single antigens are being pursued for many diseases. Two recipes can raise similar total antibody levels yet produce very different antibody mixes. Denisova and colleagues profiled those mixes in PLOS ONE in 2009 using affinity-selected mimotopes.

Mimotopes are small molecules that mimic parts of an antigen and fish out matching antibodies. Profiling complex antibody mixtures this way reveals what immunization actually produced. Vaccine makers can use that detail to compare recipes by quality of response, not just by quantity. Two shots may look the same in a crude count of total response yet protect in quite different ways. A fine map of the mix can show why one works and one fails in the field, and how to fix the weak one before the next big trial.
plos-pone-0005409:
Vaccines that work at mucosal surfaces, the body's entry points, need strong cell-mediated immunity without excess inflammation. Champion and colleagues used a recombinant nanoparticle called a vault as a delivery platform, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Vaults are natural barrel-shaped particles found in cells, rebuilt here to carry vaccine cargo. The vault nanoparticle vaccine induced protective mucosal immunity in their tests. A platform that guards the gut, lung, and genital surfaces could serve against many mucosal infections. The nose, gut, and lung are where most germs first meet us. So a shield raised right at those gates could stop a disease days before it would take hold deep in the body.
plos-pone-0005509:
Virginia Le Verche and co-authors studied a receptor in the developing brain for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Somatostatin is a small signal that affects growth, movement, and thought in adults. It was also thought to shape the brain before birth.

The team found one of its receptors in large amounts on young moving nerve cells. That held in both rats and humans. The signal helped those cells move and grow fibres. That helps explain how the brain wires itself in an orderly way before birth. Faults in this migration help cause some birth defects of the brain, which is why each guiding signal matters.
plos-pone-0005609:
Xiaohui Yuan and co-authors identified a natural partner for a lonely receptor in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Some receptors in the cell nucleus had no known natural trigger and were called orphans. Finding their triggers has revealed new signalling paths and drug targets.

Most searches screened random compounds, which can mislead. The team instead pulled the trigger molecule straight from the native receptor itself and identified it. A receptor's true partner explains what the receptor does in the body and what a drug should mimic or block. The direct method can be reused for other orphan receptors whose triggers are still unknown.
plos-pone-0005709:
Rachel Williams and co-authors studied in 2009 how an HIV protein teams with immune signals to raise a distress chemical in brain support cells. Brain disorders linked to HIV affect a large share of infected people. Astrocytes, the brain's support cells, sit at the center of that damage.

The HIV protein Tat worked together with two immune signals, IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha. Together they drove up CXCL10, a chemical that calls in more immune cells. That call can harm neurons over time. Knowing the partnership behind CXCL10 may help design ways to calm the brain during HIV infection.
plos-pone-0005809:
Takuro Horii and co-authors hunted in 2009 for genes whose chemical tagging changes as fat cells form. DNA methylation, a tag that quiets genes, shapes many cell-fate decisions. Whether it steers fat cell development was an open question.

Scanning the genome during insulin-driven fat formation, the team found a factor called WGEF whose tagging shifts. WGEF belongs to a family that switches on Rho signals inside cells. Its epigenetic control links surface signals to the fat cell program. Such links help explain how diet and hormones can leave lasting marks on body composition.
plos-pone-0005909:
Ulrich Weidenbacher and Heiko Neumann modeled in 2009 how the visual brain pulls surfaces out of flat images. We segment objects effortlessly, yet a two-dimensional retinal image loses depth whenever one surface hides another. Somehow the brain rebuilds the hidden wholes.

Their recurrent model links the first two visual areas, V1 and V2, in loops that extract surface-related features. Feedback between the areas helps resolve occlusions, borders, and partly hidden edges in the scene. Such models guide both neuroscience experiments and computer vision design. The work turns a perceptual gift into explicit, testable circuitry.
plos-pone-0006009:
Prostate cancer is common in some lands and rare in others, a gap diet may help explain. Kimberly Henderson, Salvatore Stella, Sarah Kobylewski and colleagues studied boric acid, a boron compound found in foods, in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tests its effect on calcium signals inside prostate cancer cells, since calcium steers cell growth.

When a receptor tells the cell to release its stored calcium, boric acid blocks that release, the title reports. A brake on calcium signals could slow the growth signals a tumor depends on. The study gives the diet-cancer link a concrete test in cells and names a simple compound for further checks.
plos-pone-0006109:
Boundary proteins can guard a gene, and sometimes they also switch it on. Wendy Gombert and Anton Krumm tested that double role at the MYC gene in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper deletes several CTCF-binding elements in the human C-MYC gene, building on earlier work with the MYC insulator element in transgenes, and measures what happens to MYC expression.

CTCF turns out to be required for MYC expression, not merely a fence around it. Since MYC is one of the most powerful cancer genes, a required partner is a notable find. The result reframes insulator biology: the guards of the genome can also be keepers of a gene's voice.
plos-pone-0006209:
Lung macrophages are immune cells that swallow germs landing in the airways. Glen DeLoid and colleagues measured how evenly they swallow Staphylococcus aureus, a common staph germ, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The cells can grab germs even without antibody coating, using scavenger receptors on their surface.

Using fast scanning cytometry, the team found wide differences in uptake between staph strains. What happens after swallowing likely shapes whether the germ lives or dies. Uneven eating may explain why some strains cause worse lung infections. The high-speed method lets labs compare many strains quickly and fairly.
plos-pone-0006309:
Tiny RNA molecules that tune genes may mark the course of multiple sclerosis. David Otaegui and colleagues compared micro RNA profiles in blood immune cells from patients and healthy people in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Gene expression differences were already documented between patients and controls, and during relapses.

Micro RNAs added a new layer of difference between the groups. These small regulators can shift many genes at once. Their profiles could become markers for tracking disease activity. They may also reveal which gene networks drive attacks on the nervous system.
plos-pone-0006409:
Sepsis is a grave state in which the body fails to clear germs that invade it. Balazs Csoka and his team studied two kinds of germs at once in mice for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Sepsis strikes about three quarters of a million people a year in the United States alone.

A cell sensor known as CB2, part of the system that responds to cannabis-like signals in the body, made things worse. With the sensor at work, germs broke in more easily and more mice died. Blocking that sensor may be a new way to help the body win. The work names a clear target for the next round of tests.
plos-pone-0006509:
Baibaswata Nayak and co-authors tested a poultry vaccine strategy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus and Newcastle disease virus are the two most important poultry viruses in the world. Both can devastate flocks. Natural low-virulence Newcastle disease strains are already used as live vaccines.

The team immunized chickens with a Newcastle disease virus engineered to express the H5 hemagglutinin, a surface protein of bird flu. Their title reports protection against highly pathogenic avian influenza. One vaccine tackling two diseases would simplify flock protection. The approach is an example of using a safe virus as a delivery vehicle.
plos-pone-0006609:
I-Ching Wang and co-authors deleted a transcription factor from lung cells in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Forkhead Box M1 protein is induced in a majority of human non-small cell lung cancers. Its expression is associated with poor prognosis. However, specific requirements for it in lung tumors were untested.

Deleting FoxM1 from respiratory epithelial cells inhibited pulmonary tumorigenesis, as their title reports. The factor is not merely a marker; tumors need it. That requirement makes FoxM1 a candidate drug target in lung cancer. The mouse genetics give strong causal evidence.
plos-pone-0006709:
Sally Metsuyanim and colleagues searched for stem cell markers in the human fetal kidney in PLOS ONE in 2009. The developing kidney holds self-renewing stem cells in a tissue layer. Those cells are induced to form every cell type of the nephron. They keep working until late in pregnancy. Clear markers are crucial for finding and isolating these rare cells.

The team recorded which stem cell markers the fetal kidney expresses. Expression patterns point to where the true stem cells sit. Marked cells can then be separated for closer study. That step matters for understanding how kidneys build themselves. It also matters for future attempts to repair or regrow kidney tissue.
plos-pone-0006809:
Rakesh S. Birjmohun and colleagues tested whether an HDL enzyme predicts heart disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme is paraoxonase-1, an antioxidant riding on HDL particles. A common variant, Q192R, strongly influences its activity. The enzyme was thought to protect against atherosclerosis. Whether that protection is independent was unclear.

The EPIC-Norfolk prospective study followed a general population over time. Neither genotype nor enzyme activity predicted future coronary artery disease. The title reports that null result directly. Null results matter because they prune false leads in prevention research. This one argues against using paraoxonase-1 as a risk marker.
plos-pone-0006909:
Akiko Hirao and colleagues fed mice different diets to test food's grip on the liver clock in PLOS ONE in 2009. Peripheral clocks can be entrained by feeding schedules, not just light. Rising glucose after meals was suggested as one entraining signal. Applying feeding-based entrainment needs diet details right. The liver clock is central to metabolism timing.

A balanced diet proved necessary for proper entrainment signals. Unbalanced feeding failed to set the liver clock correctly. Composition matters, not only meal timing. The result guides studies hoping to reset body clocks with food. It may also inform dietary advice for shift workers.
plos-pone-0007009:
Silvia González, Martín Fló, Mariana Margenat, and colleagues catalogued parasite defense proteins in PLOS ONE in 2009. Echinococcus granulosus is a tapeworm that causes hydatid disease. Its larvae settle remarkably well in the gut of dogs, their final host. How they survive that first contact was largely unknown.

The team described a family of Kunitz inhibitors made by the parasite. These proteins can block enzymes, including the host's digestive ones. They may mediate cross-talk between parasite and host. Blocking them could leave young worms exposed at their most vulnerable moment.
plos-pone-0007109:
Daniela Paccagnini, Lee Sieswerda, Valentina Rosu, and colleagues probed type 1 diabetes triggers in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cause of this autoimmune disease is still unknown. Environment likely helps trigger it in susceptible people. SLC11A1 is a transporter in the cells that present antigens to the immune system.

The team linked a chronic bacterial infection with variants in that gene. The bacterium was Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis. Infection plus gene variant may jointly raise diabetes risk. Testing such gene-environment pairs is a promising route into a disease with many false leads.
plos-pone-0007209:
Wei Wei, Jian Huang, Yu-Jun Hao, and colleagues studied stress tolerance genes from soybean in PLOS ONE in 2009. Soybean is a major world crop for oil and protein. Improving how soybean plants handle stress would help protect seed production under drought, salt, and cold.

The authors identify six soybean genes called GmPHD genes. These genes make regulators that switch other genes on or off. They test the regulators in transgenic Arabidopsis plants, a common lab plant. They report improved stress tolerance, suggesting routes toward hardier soybean lines in future breeding work.
plos-pone-0007309:
Sarah Lambert-Langlais, Jean-Christophe Pointud, Anne-Marie Lefrançois-Martinez, and colleagues studied hormone control in the adrenal gland in 2009. A lipid signal called prostaglandin F represses ovarian hormone production and helps initiate birth in mammals. Its impact on the adrenal gland, which makes stress and salt hormones, was unknown.

Prostaglandin production depends on a chain of enzymes. No dedicated synthase for this prostaglandin had been placed in the adrenal story. The authors identify an enzyme, aldo keto reductase 1B7, alongside the prostaglandin. They report both act as regulators of adrenal endocrine functions.
plos-pone-0007409:
Haider A. Naqvi, Sajjad Hussain, Muhammad Zaman, and colleagues measured delays before psychosis treatment in Karachi, Pakistan in 2009. Substantial time is lost before treatment starts in schizophrenia. That delay is called duration of untreated psychosis, and longer delays predict worse outcomes for patients and their families.

Most estimates came from western countries with better developed health systems. Data from Pakistan were scarce. The authors study pathways to care in Karachi. Their PLOS ONE paper documents how long untreated psychosis lasts there and which routes families take. Such maps help design services that shorten delays.
plos-pone-0007509:
Yao Xu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on KaiC, the central clock protein of cyanobacteria. KaiC cycles daily between lightly and heavily phosphorylated forms, in living cells and even in a test tube. That tagging rhythm is the heartbeat of the bacterial clock. Crystal studies had pinpointed the exact residues where tags attach. The team asked how KaiC regulates its own tagging state.

They found the control is intramolecular: KaiC manages its phosphorylation from within itself. Different parts of the same protein push the cycle forward and back. Self-regulation explains how one molecule keeps such reliable time. Few clocks are this simple, which is why KaiC draws attention. Understanding its internal logic informs the study of clocks in all organisms, including our own daily rhythms.
plos-pone-0007609:
Mathieu Darsigny and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a gut regulator called HNF4 alpha. This transcription factor runs gene programs in the intestinal lining. Its levels fall in inflammatory bowel disease, and it protects mice against chemically induced colitis. What it does to keep the healthy gut calm was unclear. The team removed it from the mouse intestine and watched the consequences.

Without HNF4 alpha, the colon's ion transport faltered. The mice developed chronic inflammation resembling inflammatory bowel disease. So a gene regulator's loss shows up first as faulty salt and water handling, then as disease. That sequence links basic plumbing to immune flare-ups. It also explains why the factor's decline in patients matters. The study gives bowel disease research a mechanism chain from gene to symptom.
plos-pone-0007709:
Peter Geuking and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses the fruit fly Drosophila to study a stress pathway called JNK. The pathway helps control growth and responses to damage. Two enzymes, Mkk4 and Mkk7, switch it on.

In flies, Mkk7 has a gene partner named Hemipterous. The authors show that Mkk4 and Hemipterous each play a distinct, non-redundant role. Both are needed when a signal protein called TAK1 activates JNK. Sorting out who does what in this pathway helps explain similar stress circuits in human cells.
plos-pone-0007809:
Pablo Aranda and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It maps chemical marks on DNA in human stem cells. Stem cells differ in how many cell types they can become. That differentiation potential varies between cell populations. The differences likely stem from their epigenetic profiles.

Epigenetic marks do not change the DNA code itself. They change how genes are read. The authors compared signatures across cells of differing potential. Distinct signatures matched each level of flexibility. Such signatures could let labs judge a stem cell batch's promise before using it in therapy.
plos-pone-0007909:
Hiroko Morimoto and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It challenges the idea that sperm-making stem cells have a fixed identity. Spermatogonial stem cells divide for life to support sperm production. Transplant experiments had let scientists isolate and describe them.

They were thought to hold a set phenotype. The authors show these mouse stem cells display phenotypic plasticity instead. Their traits shift with conditions more than expected. Plasticity changes how biologists think about male fertility and its loss. It may also open new ways to grow these cells in the lab for research.
plos-pone-0008009:
Matt Craddock and Rebecca Lawson tested how people know objects by eye and by hand in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sight and touch feel unlike, yet people match an object seen with one felt in the dark with ease. The question was whether the two senses share one inner picture of the object.

Tests showed the shared picture keeps size, not just shape. People carried the true size of an object across from one sense to the other. That detail suggests the brain holds a rich, size-true model it can reach by more than one road, rather than thin notes for each sense apart.
plos-pone-0008109:
Kian Peng Koh and colleagues worked out how the tolerance master FOXP3 grips DNA in PLOS ONE in 2009. FOXP3 runs the regulatory T cells that stop the immune system from attacking the body. When it fails, severe autoimmunity follows in mice and people alike.

The team defined which parts of the protein must be whole for binding and which DNA sequences it prefers. Those rules explain how one protein can hold the leash on many immune genes at once. They also clarify why certain faults in the gene cause disease while others do not.
plos-pone-0008209:
Stéphane Chevaliez and colleagues addressed hepatitis C testing in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. New drugs target specific hepatitis C virus enzymes and functions. Response and resistance to those drugs may differ by viral subtype. So trials must identify genotype 1 subtypes correctly from the start. Clinical practice will need the same accuracy later.

The authors examined how well subtype identification can be done. Getting the subtype right affects who joins a trial and how results are read. It also affects treatment choices for patients. The paper supports standards for testing as new hepatitis C drugs arrive.
plos-pone-0008309:
Seiichi Sakatani and colleagues studied mice lacking a receptor gene in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. RAGE is a cell surface receptor that binds many partners. Its activation speeds disease progression in diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. How RAGE influences normal brain function was less clear. The team deleted the RAGE gene in mice to find out.

Mice without RAGE showed hyperactivity. They were also more sensitive to auditory stimuli. A receptor known for harming diseased brains also shapes everyday behavior. The findings may help separate RAGE's normal roles from its harmful ones.
plos-pone-0008409:
Richard W. Steketee and Thomas P. Eisele asked whether malaria control is fair in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria in Africa hits young children and pregnant women hardest. Rural and poor households bear the greatest burden. Intervention coverage has increased in many countries as programs scale up. Rising averages may mask limited coverage in the highest-risk groups.

The authors examined whether scale-up is also achieving equity. If nets and treatment bypass the poor, impact will fall short. Their analysis presses programs to track who is actually reached. Equity data can redirect resources to those most at risk.
plos-pone-0008509:
Mounira Abiola and co-authors link a signaling path to insulin action in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Fat buildup inside muscle cells is strongly tied to insulin resistance. High glucose can drive fat making and resistance in mouse muscle cells. Wnt signaling affects the balance between muscle growth and fat storage. The team activate the Wnt and beta-catenin path in those cells. They track two genes, Wnt10b and SREBP-1c.

Activating the path raises insulin sensitivity in the cells. It does so through reciprocal control of the two genes. One rises while the other falls in a coordinated way. The mechanism suggests Wnt activation could counter insulin resistance in muscle.
plos-pone-0008609:
Roanna London and co-authors present an automated microbe counter in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Visual colony counting has been the mainstay of microbiology for over one hundred thirty years. Its power and simplicity are unmatched for many tasks. Its disadvantage is the long time needed for visible colonies to grow. New rapid tests often sacrifice that simplicity or accuracy. The team build an automated system for rapid, non-destructive enumeration of growing microbes.

Their system detects colonies far earlier than the human eye can. It counts them without destroying the sample. Earlier results speed clinical and food safety decisions. The method preserves the classic plate approach while removing its delay.
plos-pone-0008709:
D. Priyadarshini, Rajesh Gadia, Anuradha Tripathy, and colleagues profiled dengue illness in western India. Their facility-based study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most knowledge about how dengue harms the body came from South-east Asia and the Americas. India, despite many cases, was poorly covered. The team enrolled hundreds of patients in Pune during 2005.

They recorded symptoms and measured pro-inflammatory cytokines, the blood signals of immune activity. The patterns show how Indian cases compare with reports from elsewhere. Local data like this helps doctors spot severe cases sooner. It also guides where future dengue research in India should focus.
plos-pone-0008809:
Rolf Knoth, Ilyas Singec, Margarethe Ditter, and colleagues counted newborn brain cells across the human lifespan. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The hippocampus, a memory center, keeps making neurons into adulthood in animals. Human evidence rested largely on one famous 1998 study. How human production compares with mouse patterns across ages was unknown. Their samples spanned donors from infancy to age one hundred.

Markers of young neurons appeared in human tissue with mouse-like features. The census shows production continuing across much of life. Lifelong neurogenesis may support memory and mood in old age. The data anchor debates about human brain renewal.
plos-pone-0008909:
Viviana Cremasco, Elisa Benasciutti, Marina Cella, and colleagues tied one enzyme to the way key immune cells move in sore joints. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cells at issue pick up bits of germs in the skin and gut. They then haul those bits to the lymph nodes. There they meet T cells and wake them up. Both the trip and the meet-up need a soft, bendy inner frame. That frame is made of actin, and it must shift shape all the time to let the cell crawl.

When mice lacked the enzyme, the cells could not shift their actin well. The sore-joint disease in those mice then took a new course. A flaw in how one cell type moves can thus change a whole disease. The enzyme may be a good drug target for sore joints.
plos-pone-0009009:
Shahram Lavasani and co-authors fed friendly bacteria to mice with an MS-like illness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Multiple sclerosis is a chronic disease where the immune system attacks the nervous system. One treatment idea is to grow regulatory cells that calm that attack. Probiotics, including lactobacilli, are known to nudge the immune system toward tolerance.

The team gave a new probiotic mixture to mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. The treated mice fared better than untreated ones. Protection ran through regulatory T cells that release IL-10, a calming signal. The result supports testing gut-based approaches for calming autoimmunity.
plos-pone-0009109:
Jian-Shen Zhao and co-authors read the genomes of cold-loving sea bacteria that eat explosives, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two Shewanella species live and thrive in cold marine water. They were among the first bacteria found to break down RDX without any oxygen. RDX is a military explosive that pollutes soil and groundwater at many sites.

Comparing their genomes with warmer-living relatives revealed their cold adaptations. Gene gains and losses had fitted them for a chilly marine lifestyle. The same toolkit happens to dismantle explosive molecules step by step. Such bacteria could one day help clean up contaminated training ranges naturally.
plos-pone-0009209:
Donna Douglas and co-authors published this liver study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It tests whether transplanted human liver cells can take over a failing liver. The test hosts were special mice whose own livers fail over time. Donor cells must outcompete the mouse's remaining liver cells to rebuild the organ.

These SCID/uPA mice lack a working immune system, so human cells are not rejected. The team transplanted human hepatocytes and measured how well the treatment worked. Success in this model is a key step toward cell therapy for severe liver disease. The study reports how effective the transplants were in mice with inducible liver disease.
plos-pone-0009309:
Christian Roussilhon and co-authors published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Staying safe from malaria leans on antibodies that team up with monocytes, white cells that swallow germs. As people gain that safety, their antibodies shift toward kinds that work best with monocytes. Field work hinted that worm infections get in the way of that shift.

The team looked at how human defense against the malaria germ Plasmodium falciparum acts when worms are also present. Their work found a role for the worms in shaping that defense. Worms seem to sway the antibody mix that safety from malaria rests on. That counts most where the two infections meet, which is much of the tropics.
plos-pone-0009409:
Katrin Wenzel and co-authors published this rat heart study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some patients with hard-to-treat high blood pressure carry unusual antibodies. Those antibodies attack a receptor called alpha 1A-adrenergic, and they switch it on. Whether the antibodies actually cause harm was uncertain.

The team immunized Lewis rats with pieces of the human receptor to mimic the condition. The rats developed damage in the left ventricle, the heart's main pumping chamber. Their hearts also relaxed poorly between beats, a fault called diastolic dysfunction. The experiment supports the idea that these autoantibodies are culprits, not bystanders.
plos-pone-0009509:
Robert McDonald, Richard Forman, and Peter Kareiva mapped land change across United States cities in PLOS ONE in 2010. City growth paves over fields, woods, and other open space. That loss hurts wildlife and the services nature gives people. The team used land cover and census data for 274 metro areas. They covered the decade from 1990 to 2000.

Open space fell across the country in that decade, but not evenly. Some communities lost far more green land per person than others. The authors call this gap land inequality. Naming it matters, because growth plans can then aim for fairer outcomes, not just slower loss.
plos-pone-0009609:
Jos Barlow and co-authors weighed how to value untouched tropical forest in PLOS ONE in 2010. Planners must rank land uses by their worth for wildlife. Counts of common species are easy to gather. Rare species that show up only now and then are often left out of those counts. The team asked whether those occasional species change the rank of primary forest.

When occasional species are included, primary forest looks still more distinct from other land uses. Leaving them out can understate what old forest holds. The study refines a basic tool of conservation planning. Better counts send protection to the places that truly hold the most life.
plos-pone-0009709:
Big objects feel lighter than small ones of the same weight, a trick called the size-weight illusion. Gavin Buckingham and Melvyn Goodale asked what role vision plays in that illusion. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The work points to lifting without seeing, where vision is removed from the task. Comparing lifts with and without sight separates what people feel from how they act. The illusion shows that perception and action can follow different rules. Studies like this reveal how the brain handles objects it cannot fully trust.
plos-pone-0009909:
The airway's lining decides which viruses get in by where it places its doors. Katherine Excoffon and colleagues studied one such door and its variant forms in human airway tissue. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The door is the Coxsackie and adenovirus receptor, used by two virus families to enter cells. Isoform-specific regulation means each variant form of the receptor follows its own rules. Localization adds where in the airway epithelia each form sits. Epithelia are the sheet-like tissues that line organs and airways. Placement decides how exposed the airway is to infection.
plos-pone-0010009:
Chang-Yi Cui, Makoto Kunisada, Yulan Piao, and co-workers wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about how mice grow two kinds of hair. Guard hairs protect the coat, while finer hairs help hold body heat. A signal protein called Eda is needed for the first kind, yet mice lacking it still grow the second kind.

The team reported that a second protein, Dkk4, which blocks Wnt signals, helps control that second hair type. Together, Eda and Dkk4 run distinct programs for distinct hairs. The work clarifies hair development and may inform care for people born with faults in these pathways.
plos-pone-0010209:
Jenna Morgan, Aaron Darling, and Jonathan Eisen sequenced a made-to-order microbe mix in 2010. Microbes dominate life on Earth, yet many cannot be grown in a lab at all. Metagenomics reads DNA straight from the environment to catalog them. Their PLOS ONE study built a simulated community in vitro to test how well that approach performs.

A mock community with known members gives sequencing a fair test. Errors and biases show up clearly when the right answer is already known. Benchmarks like this help scientists trust metagenomic surveys of soil, oceans, and the human body.
plos-pone-0010309:
Jochen Schulze and co-workers reported a brake on bone building in a 2010 paper. The other authors were Sebastian Seitz and Hiroaki Saito. Wnt signaling is a key pathway that controls bone formation in mice and humans. One regulator, Dkk1, blocks Wnt by forming a complex with membrane receptors, including a protein called Kremen-2.

The team showed Kremen-2 itself negatively regulates bone formation in their study. That makes the receptor more than a passive docking point for blockers. Their PLOS ONE findings add detail to pathways targeted by bone-building drugs for osteoporosis.
plos-pone-0010409:
Bing Wang, Shiyun Ling and Weei-Chin Lin connected a helper protein to the cell's recycling system in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells eat their own worn parts in a process called autophagy. A protein named Beclin 1 is essential for starting that cleanup. How Beclin 1 itself is controlled was largely unknown. Clues pointed to a gene switch called E2F and a partner protein family named 14-3-3.

The team showed one family member, 14-3-3tau, steadies that gene switch. Through it, the helper controls how much Beclin 1 gets made. Without the helper, autophagy falters. Cleanup failure is tied to cancer and brain disease, so its controls matter. This study names one control that had been missing from the map.
plos-pone-0010509:
Juan Soler and Jesús Avilés compared nestling mouth displays across bird species in PLOS ONE in 2010. Baby birds that cannot leave the nest beg with wide, colorful gapes. The bright mouth tells parents about need, strength, or health. Parents use that signal to divide food among chicks. Siblings thus compete partly through display. The authors asked how gape showiness varies with competition across species.

Comparative studies test whether a trait evolves where it is needed most. If fiercer sibling rivalry matches brighter gapes, the signaling story gains support. Such work connects family conflict to evolution of animal signals. It also shows how much information a simple mouth can carry. Parents reading gapes are reading a health and hunger report.
plos-pone-0010609:
C. William Birky and colleagues tackled a basic question in PLOS ONE in 2010: what counts as a species when an organism never mates? Asexual microbes and fungi reproduce by copying themselves. The usual species test, based on interbreeding, cannot apply.

The authors used population genetics and DNA sequences to draw species borders. Groups whose sequences formed tight, separate clusters counted as distinct species. The method worked on real asexual eukaryotes. A clear rule for naming these organisms matters for ecology, medicine, and tracking harmful microbes that spread without sex. The rule rests on sequence data alone.
plos-pone-0010709:
Marc Jung and colleagues mapped the gene network run by OCT4, in PLOS ONE in 2010. OCT4 is a master switch that keeps embryonic stem cells able to become any tissue. Embryonal carcinoma cells, a cancer counterpart, lean on the same switch. Knowing its full network is key to using stem cells safely.

By merging several large datasets, the team charted which genes OCT4 controls in both cell types. The shared core was smaller than the parts unique to each. Cancer cells had rewired parts of the healthy program. The map helps separate the self-renewal doctors want from the growth they must avoid.
plos-pone-0010809:
Jennifer Yokoyama, Carolyn Erdman, and Steven Hamilton tested dog DNA taken from saliva, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dog genetics studies need DNA from thousands of animals for genome-wide scans. Blood draws are the standard source, but owners and vets find them costly and stressful for the dog. Saliva collection is cheap and gentle, if the DNA is good enough.

Array scans run on saliva DNA produced high-quality results. Call rates and accuracy matched what blood-based studies expect. A spit sample owners can collect at home opens the door to much larger dog studies. Larger studies find the genes behind inherited diseases that dogs and people share.
plos-pone-0010909:
Zongzhi Liu, Ao Li, Vincent Schulz and co-authors published this cancer genomics method in PLOS ONE in 2010. SNP arrays can reveal where a tumor's genome has gained or lost DNA, and which parental copy survived. Real tumor samples, though, are mixtures: cancer cells are diluted with normal supporting cells, which blurs every signal.

Their tool, MixHMM, is a statistical model whose hidden states stand for the structural changes a chromosome can undergo, designed to read through that mixture. It infers both copy number changes and allelic imbalance, including cases where one parental copy is lost without changing total DNA amount. Liu and colleagues built the method for the messy samples clinics actually produce. Cleaner readings of tumor genomes lead to better classification of cancers and, eventually, better matched treatments.
plos-pone-0011009:
Monica Ferreira, Kurt Berndt, Johan Nilsson and co-authors published this yeast genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fission yeast carries two similar gene-silencing proteins, Tup11 and Tup12, yet they are not interchangeable: certain target genes and stress conditions need one specifically. The authors hunted for the part of each protein that creates that difference.

The obvious suspect, a fast-changing region that touches histones, turned out not to explain the specificity in general. Instead, the more conserved tail region built from WD40 repeats carried the distinguishing features, including surface residues that differ between the two proteins. Ferreira and colleagues redirect attention to a domain usually assumed to be generic scaffolding. Their result shows how near-identical repressors divide labor through subtle surface changes.
plos-pone-0011109:
Smith, Treadwell, Zhang and colleagues charted brain growth in PLOS ONE in 2010. They measured tiny RNA pieces, called microRNAs, across stages of human brain development. These small pieces help turn genes up or down as the brain is built.

The large survey found that each stage carries its own distinct pattern of these RNAs. That changing code helps direct the orderly growth of the brain before birth. A clear map of normal stages gives a baseline for spotting what goes wrong in brain disorders. It also shows when each control piece is likely to matter most.
plos-pone-0011209:
Evangelista, Rao, Filo and colleagues measured muscle motor control in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nitric oxide is a gas the body makes to send quick signals. The team tested whether it and related natural compounds act directly on myosins, the motor proteins that power heart and skeletal muscle contraction.

They found these compounds do directly regulate the motors. That creates a fast path to adjust contraction in real time, without waiting for slower signals. Fine control of the heart's motors matters in health and disease. The finding adds a direct chemical dial to how physiologists explain muscle strength.
plos-pone-0011309:
Guan, Jiang, Guo and colleagues mutated a fungal transporter in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fungi resist drugs partly by pumping them out through transporter proteins. The team changed one important pump gene in a fungal pathogen and measured sensitivity to several antifungal drugs afterward.

Mutations shifted drug sensitivity in opposing directions: resistance to one drug rose while sensitivity to another grew. That trade off is useful, because it gives therapy a lever. Doctors could rotate drugs to exploit the weakness each resistance step creates. The finding informs smarter antifungal schedules for hard to treat infections.
plos-pone-0011409:
Jeroen van Kampen and colleagues presented in 2010 a much faster way to measure HIV drugs in children. Children on HIV treatment take protease inhibitors, and the right dose depends on how much drug reaches the blood and the inside of cells. Slow lab methods made that checking rare, so doses were often guessed from adult data.

Their method uses a fast form of mass spectrometry that reads drug levels in plasma and in cells from small samples in a fraction of the usual time. Speed matters in a busy clinic, where a result that arrives next week cannot fix today's dose. With quick, precise readings, doctors can tune each child's dose to that child's body. The study shows a lab advance becoming a direct clinical benefit for young patients.
plos-pone-0011509:
Nora Volkow and co-authors tested in 2010 whether a familiar ADHD drug calms the brain's overreaction to cocaine cues in people addicted to cocaine. Sights and sounds tied to the drug can hijack attention and trigger craving, and imaging shows the limbic system, the brain's emotion core, responding abnormally to them. The team gave methylphenidate and scanned users as cues were shown.

The drug attenuated the abnormal limbic inhibition that followed cue exposure, moving the response toward a steadier pattern. A stimulant steadying the circuits that cues throw off balance sounds paradoxical, but controlled dosing differs from abuse. The result hints that methylphenidate, or drugs like it, might support addiction treatment by blunting cue power. It also gives researchers a brain measure against which to test other anti-craving candidates.
plos-pone-0011609:
Luca Giliberto and co-authors tested a suspect piece of a brain protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cutting the amyloid precursor protein releases amyloid-beta, which forms the plaques seen in Alzheimer's disease. The same cutting also frees the protein's inner tail piece, which lab studies had linked to cell death.

The team made mice that produce only that tail piece in their brains. The mice did not develop Alzheimer's-like traits. Clearing this piece of suspicion helps focus the search for the disease's drivers on other products of the same protein, saving effort on a likely dead end.
plos-pone-0011709:
Qingxian Zhang and co-authors tested a gene-silencing treatment for diabetic kidney disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diabetic nephropathy is complex and poorly understood, and current treatments are limited. A developmental protein called gremlin, which blocks helpful bone morphogenetic proteins, had emerged as a suspect driver of the damage.

The team delivered RNA designed to silence gremlin into living animals. Silencing it restored levels of the protective protein BMP-7 and eased the kidney disease. The result in a living system marks gremlin as a promising treatment target for a condition with few options.
plos-pone-0011809:
Nathan Moore and Joseph Messina built a predictive map of tsetse flies in Kenya, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tsetse flies transmit Trypanosoma parasites that cause high illness and death among humans, cattle and wildlife in Africa. Fly distributions shift rapidly with environmental change, so yesterday's map can mislead control efforts.

Their logistic model combines landscape and climate data to estimate where tsetse occur. The resulting distribution map identifies the conditions the flies favour. Health and veterinary teams can aim control at the flies' likely haunts and update the aim as conditions change.
plos-pone-0011909:
Philippe Marguet and colleagues built in 2010 tiny genetic circuits that make bacteria kill themselves on a schedule, then watched them pulse. Synthetic biology aims to program cell behavior with engineered circuits, but those circuits run inside host cells full of their own machinery. The two systems interact in ways designers cannot fully predict.

The suicide circuits did not simply run steadily; they oscillated, switching behavior over time. Those pulses exposed hidden features of how the host cell and the added circuit affect each other. Using a dramatic circuit, programmed death, as a probe turns a design problem into a measuring tool for the physiology engineers must work with.
plos-pone-0012009:
Ryan O'Connell and co-workers used in 2010 a virus-based delivery system to supply human interleukin-7 to mice carrying human immune tissue. These human immune system mice are valuable models, but human cells inside a mouse face compatibility problems. One gap is that the mice do not provide enough of the signals human T cells need to thrive.

Delivering the gene for human interleukin-7, a T cell growth signal, by lentiviral vector expanded the T lymphocyte populations in the mice. A fuller human T cell compartment makes these models far more useful for testing vaccines and immune therapies. The work removes one specific bottleneck rather than merely noting that the models are imperfect.
plos-pone-0012109:
Dong Woo Kang and Do Sik Min reported in PLOS ONE in 2010 on two signals that boost each other inside colon cancer cells. One is a growth pathway that runs out of control in nearly all colon cancers, driving growth, spread, and survival. The other is an enzyme long tied to the advance of this cancer, though how the two connect was not clear.

The authors show each signal raises the other, forming a loop that keeps cancer cells growing even without the anchors normal cells need. A loop is harder for a tumor to lose than a single switch, which makes it a tempting drug target. Breaking the loop at either point might slow growth that single-target drugs miss.
plos-pone-0012209:
Esther Conde, Bárbara Angulo, Pilar Redondo, and co-authors tested a stain for telling apart two lung cancers, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lung tumors divide mainly into adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, and the split now decides treatment: some drugs are unsafe or useless in one type but preferred in the other. A protein called P63 had stood out in gene studies as far more active in the squamous type.

The team checked whether staining tumors for P63 cleanly identifies squamous cases in everyday pathology work. A reliable stain means smaller hospitals can make the same call as big centers, from a sliver of tissue. Getting the type right is the gate through which every later treatment choice must pass.
plos-pone-0012309:
David Tyssen, Scott Henderson, Adam Johnson, and co-authors mapped the structure of tree-shaped antiviral molecules, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Women urgently need protective gels they control themselves against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. Dendrimers, tiny particles branched like trees, are candidates, able to block viruses on several fronts at once, but which features of their structure do the blocking was not mapped.

By varying the structure piece by piece and testing against both HIV and herpes virus, they charted which shapes work best. A structure-activity map turns molecule design from guesswork into engineering. The dual action matters: one product guarding against two common infections is far more likely to be used consistently.
plos-pone-0012409:
Liuh Ling Goh and Ed Manser studied how a cell shape switch is kept in check, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The switch, RhoA, drives the cell's inner skeleton, and its activator Syx turns it on. A relative called Rnd3 stays always on and was known to influence this system, but the mechanism was murky.

The authors show that Rnd3 targets Syx and controls it through a domain that resembles a piece of the Raf1 protein. That control tunes how strongly RhoA fires. Since RhoA shapes cell movement and division, and its miscontrol aids cancer spread, each regulator mapped adds a possible point for drug intervention.
plos-pone-0012509:
John Hodsoll, Kimberly Quinn and Sara Hodsoll tested whose baby faces grab adult attention, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Infant faces normally capture attention automatically, which helps ensure babies get care. The authors asked whether that pull is equal for infants of all races, or biased toward the viewer's own race.

Adults prioritized own-race infant faces over other-race ones in their tests. An own-race bias in basic attention could ripple into caregiving and adoption settings in ways worth knowing about. The finding also feeds the wider science of how face experience in infancy tunes the adult brain.
plos-pone-0012609:
Leskinen and co-authors used identical twins to separate exercise habits from shared genes. Some twin pairs in their 2010 study differed sharply in how active they had been for years. One twin trained often, the other stayed inactive, yet both shared the same genes and early home.

The team read gene activity in muscle and fat and compared it with heart and metabolic risk markers. Long-term activity left clear marks on gene use in both tissues. Because genes were held constant, those marks point to habit itself. The work supports exercise as a direct lever on health.
plos-pone-0012709:
Yoneda, Guillaume, Sato and co-authors showed that the side proteins of Nipah virus drive much of its harm. Nipah is a dangerous virus that can inflame the brain and lungs. Its P gene makes the main P protein plus three side proteins, V, C and W, each known to blunt immune defences in cell tests.

Their 2010 animal infections tested whether those side proteins matter in a living host, not just a dish. They did, marking them as key to the disease itself. That makes them targets for future vaccines and drugs.
plos-pone-0012809:
Schillaci, Waitzkin, Carson and co-authors compared pregnancy care among mothers in poor and richer parts of New Mexico. Care during pregnancy is a core part of basic health services. Their 2010 study covered the years 1989 to 1999, tracking how much care mothers used and how their births turned out.

They set low-income areas against higher-income ones in the same state and era. Gaps found this way point to where outreach and clinic access fail mothers most. The long window also shows whether those gaps narrowed over a decade of policy.
plos-pone-0326009:
Jin Liu and Tian Li surveyed and interviewed students, parents, and teachers in Guangdong, China, about young people's attitudes toward traditional Chinese music. The music carries cultural identity, yet pop dominates young ears and schools struggle to keep tradition alive. The study sorted influences into the student's own traits, family forces, and school forces to see which levers move engagement.

Girls held warmer attitudes and joined in more than boys. Enthusiasm ran highest in younger students and faded as exam pressure grew. Parental involvement helped strongly, but, surprisingly, parents' own artistic ability worked against engagement, a hint that skilled parents may push or judge in ways that cool a child's interest. The authors argue for policies fitted to these realities, with special attention to poorer regions where resources and exposure lag.
plos-pone-0326409:
Tiffany Choi and colleagues adapt in 2026 a World Health Organization schedule for rating disability into a Hong Kong version of traditional Chinese. Existing Chinese versions did not fit local language and culture well. Adults with disabilities who used community rehabilitation services completed the new version alongside two trusted life quality measures, and some repeated it later.

Scores were consistent within each area and fairly stable over time. Links with the other measures supported the idea that the schedule tracks real disability and life quality. A check of its six area structure fit only in part, so the authors call the structure early and ask for larger, wider samples.
plos-pone-0332009:
Yujia Yang, David J Evans, and Suzanne M J Fleiszig led a mouse study with a surprise twist. Mice wore a contact lens on one eye for a few days. Lens wear stirs mild swelling on the eye's surface. Then both eyes got a light scratch and a dose of germs. The team asked if the worn eye would fare worse. It fared better.

Germs stuck to the lens-worn eyes about half as much. This held for a mild eyelid germ and a harsh eye germ alike. Immune cells had also moved into the worn eyes in force. The team reads the lens stir as a kind of drill. It primes the eye to fight off germs after small harm.
plos-pone-0334209:
Erin V. Satterthwaite and her team asked a bold question. Can the tiniest life in the sea tell us where the biggest animals feed? They used survey data from the seas off Southern California, from 2014 to 2020. Ship crews counted blue, fin, and humpback whales. At the same spots, the team took water samples full of microbes and tiny drifting life.

Some of these small sea life forms matched whale numbers with great skill. They beat the plain methods used before by a wide margin. A few may live on the whales or feed their prey. If this holds up, a jug of sea water could help map whale habitat at low cost.
plos-pone-0339109:
Kunle Apanisile and three colleagues mine a huge transplant registry for the drug combinations that protect kidneys longest. Their 2026 study covers nearly two hundred twenty-nine thousand deceased-donor kidney recipients in the United States, transplanted between 2000 and 2024. Every recipient takes immune-suppressing drugs to stop rejection. Regimens vary, and their long-term trade-offs are contested. Classic survival models handled the clinical comparisons. Four machine learning survival models separately tested how well outcomes can be predicted.

One backbone combination stood out. Regimens built on calcineurin inhibitors plus mycophenolate carried lower hazards of graft failure. They also carried lower hazards of patient death. Adding steroids helped less than the simpler pairing. The scale of the data makes these differences hard to dismiss as noise. Transplant teams choosing maintenance therapy balance rejection against infection and cancer risk over decades. Registry evidence this large gives those lifelong choices a firmer empirical floor.
plos-pone-0344409: Babazadeh Shareh and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on modeling COVID-19 spread in Thuringia, Germany. Their software searches on its own for a model that fits the recorded case data well. Automatic model building can speed up how experts test ideas during an outbreak. The approach may also suit other diseases where data arrive fast and models must keep up.
plos-pone-0344709:
Jianxiong Wu, Shaoke Lu, Hui Yao, and Zhaoyuan Fang re-benchmarked the twelve most-used computer methods for finding genes whose activity differs between conditions, the everyday first step of transcriptome research. Their 2026 study ran all twelve across eighty simulated and real datasets and graded them on six dimensions, from accuracy and false alarms to stability and toughness against outliers and noise.

No method won everywhere. With the tiny samples common in practice, one older method led overall; at slightly larger samples two famous tools gained sensitivity while one predecessor kept false alarms lowest. Simple rank-based testing proved hardiest against noise. The authors package the results as a selection map, so researchers can pick a method fitting their data instead of following habit.
plos-pone-0345009:
Jason Weatherald and colleagues used health records from Alberta, Canada to see how the COVID-19 pandemic changed care for people with cystic fibrosis, a genetic disease that damages the lungs. Their 2026 study compares the eighteen months before March 2020 with the eighteen months after, paying special attention to whether men and women were affected differently.

Emergency visits and hospital stays fell during the pandemic, while clinic visits, including virtual ones, edged upward. Death rates barely changed. Women showed a sharper drop in emergency visits than men despite similar hospitalisation rates. The authors worry women may have faced bigger barriers to urgent care, even as routine care adapted.
plos-pone-0345209:
Sayesta Mehejaveen Begum and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies the developmental biology of the mango pulp weevil, Sternochetus frigidus, a quarantine pest that grows hidden inside mango fruit. The work was done under laboratory conditions and also covers substrate preference, what materials the insect chooses.

A quarantine pest triggers trade bans when found, so mango exporters fear it greatly. Knowing its life stages and preferences under controlled conditions guides inspection and treatment of fruit. Plant protection officers and mango growers in Asia are the readers who must keep this weevil out of shipments.
