plos-pone-0346509:
Qi Chwen Ong and colleagues describe the design of a Singapore trial tackling a quiet problem: many people prescribed cholesterol-lowering statins simply stop taking them. The 2026 paper is a trial protocol. It lays out a study of at least three hundred seventy-six adults who are not taking their statins as directed, recruited from primary care clinics.

Half will use a phone app acting as a personal health assistant, backed by a human coach; half receive usual care. After six months the team will compare pill-taking behaviour, cholesterol levels, motivation, quality of life, and costs. The trial tests whether digital help with a human touch can keep patients on preventive medicine.
plos-pone-0347209:
Qing Zhang and colleagues studied a gene control protein called EP300 that is often faulty in bladder cancer and may help cancers spread. Spread requires cancer cells to loosen and move, a shift tied to a driver gene called SNAI2. Patient tissue checks, cell tests, tiny organ like cultures, and mouse work all tested a drug that blocks EP300.

Blocking the protein slowed cell movement in dishes, broke linking tubes between mini tumours, and trended toward less invasion in mice. Gene reading showed the blocker turned down SNAI2 linked pathways, and SNAI2 levels fell. Restoring SNAI2 boosted movement again. The chain from blocker to driver gene gives drug makers a clear target path.
plos-pone-0348109: Varughese and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how common certain gene changes are in the general population. The genes are tied to a disorder that causes cysts in the liver, and some also affect the kidneys. The team counted changes that computer tools predict to be harmful. Knowing how often such changes occur helps doctors judge whether a change found in a patient is truly the cause.
plos-pone-0348209:
Takuma Watanabe and colleagues reviewed a decade of jaw surgery cases to pin down when patients lose feeling in the lower lip and chin. The operation, which splits and repositions the lower jaw, passes close to a nerve that supplies those areas. Among four hundred sixty-three patients treated between 2014 and 2024, about five percent suffered lasting sensory disturbance, the 2026 study reports.

The yearly rate fell steadily, which the authors credit to growing experience and better instruments. One warning sign dominated: when pre-surgery scans showed the nerve canal touching the outer bone layer, the risk of disturbance rose roughly fivefold. Careful, gentle cutting in those cases is the paper's practical message.
plos-pone-0348509:
Qingyu Qi and three colleagues engineer a cheaper route to a blockbuster diabetes drug's core piece. Their 2026 study concerns semaglutide, the long-acting hormone mimic behind modern diabetes and obesity treatment. Making it industrially is expensive and low-yielding. The team targeted its main chain, a fragment called P29. They grew it inside cells as part of a larger fusion protein. The fusion carries a tag and a cutting site designed for a two-step release.

First, a nickel-assisted chemical cut trims the construct. Then the enzyme enterokinase snips the fragment free. The helical fusion partners were derived from semaglutide's own sequence, helping the chain fold and accumulate. High expression was the reported payoff. Semaglutide demand keeps straining global supply. A fermentation route that yields its core intermediate cheaply could lower manufacturing cost for a medicine millions now depend on weekly.
plos-pone-0348609:
Nahed Yehia and co-workers track bird flu viruses in Egyptian chicken flocks during twenty twenty-four, watching for dangerous mixing between strains. Two flu types were circulating together, which raises the chance they swap gene parts and spawn new forms. Their 2026 study tests fifty sick flocks across seven regions and fully sequences the flu viruses from seven of them.

Sequencing found exactly the feared mixing. One new virus combined surface genes from the severe strain with inner genes from the milder one, and two others showed the reverse blend. Some carried fresh changes not seen in local viruses before. The authors press for constant farm surveillance, since such hybrids can shift how widely a virus spreads.
plos-pone-0348709:
Yunchuan Long leads a team of six weighing the risk in the droppings of migratory birds at a plateau wetland, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Caohai, in China, hosts wintering cranes, coots, and ducks, whose feces fertilize the marsh. The team sampled seven species across three seasons and assayed the phosphorus forms, the genes that shrug off drugs, and the germs the droppings carry, using chemical extraction and genetic sequencing.

The material was rich and risky. Most sat in a form plants and algae can use at once, a strong threat of choking the water. Sequencing found over two hundred germs, led by names such as Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella. Twenty-one classes of such genes appeared. Most shrugged off many drugs. Heavy metals in the feces seemed to encourage the mobile elements that shuttle resistance between bacteria. Protecting the birds and policing their pollution are the same job.
plos-pone-0349009:
Ibrahim Nafisah and Mohamed Kayid present this 2026 PLOS One statistics paper on detecting whether things wear out with age. In reliability work, the baseline assumption is that failures strike at a constant random rate; the question is whether data show risk creeping upward over time instead. The authors build a test that measures departure from that baseline in a way users can interpret directly.

Unusually, their test yields exact answers for small samples rather than relying on large-sample approximations, and a scale-free version removes the need to know unknown parameters. Computer simulations against several lifetime patterns showed strong detection power compared with existing tests. The authors also apply it to real datasets, arguing it gives engineers and medical researchers a trustworthy way to judge aging behavior.
plos-pone-0349109:
Kerry-Lee Rosenberg and colleagues used a British dialysis trial cohort of four hundred and thirty five new patients to test whether losing remaining kidney function faster harms thinking. Earlier work hinted at such a link. Thinking was scored with a standard test at start and over two years, alongside dialysis settings like fluid temperature and weight gain between sessions.

Speed of remaining function loss showed no link with new thinking impairment or with yearly score change. Warmer dialysis fluid linked with a modest yearly thinking gain. Large fluid weight gain helped thinking scores in patients without heart failure but harmed scores in those with it. Fluid management, not residual loss speed, deserves focus.
plos-pone-0349209:
Thomas Seth Davis and colleagues watered Engelmann spruce trees unevenly on purpose to learn how drought rewires the defences of this widespread western North American forest tree. Drought often precedes bark beetle outbreaks, and the team suspected the trees' own chemistry helps explain why. They tracked water stress, a defence hormone called salicylic acid, scent chemicals, and the growth of resin ducts that trap attacking insects.

Dry trees built up the hormone in needles and inner bark, and certain scent chemicals rose alongside it. Worse, chronically dry trees largely failed to grow new resin ducts when given a chemical that normally triggers them. The authors conclude that drought does not merely weaken spruce growth; it scrambles the defence system itself, trading one kind of protection for another and leaving trees open to insects.
plos-pone-0349409:
Jinpeng Cong and colleagues examined whether vitamin D levels track with early aging of the arteries in adults still in their younger and middle years. Early vascular aging, arteries stiffer than they should be for a person's age, predicts heart disease. More than two thousand healthy adults at a Chinese hospital health center had their vitamin D measured and their artery stiffness gauged by pulse wave speed.

About a third fell into the early-aging group. The analysis tested how the vitamin D relationship bent across its range, including whether a threshold exists below which risk climbs. It also checked whether the pattern differed by age, sex, smoking, or season of blood draw. Vitamin D is cheap to measure and correct, so a firm link would be an easy screening addition.
plos-pone-0350109:
Xiaoying Zhang and colleagues ran two studies on how watching peers suffer changes whether people share their own distress. Sharing pain can bring support, yet shame often seals lips. The first study modelled stress, self esteem, and hostility. The second used a staged scenario to test a chain of effects across groups who saw adversity versus prosperity in others.

Stress directly cut sharing and also cut it by lowering self esteem, with hostility shaping that path. Under adversity, a full chain ran from seeing hardship to finding meaning to sharing. Willingness to join helped sharing after adversity but hurt it after prosperity. Framing peer hardship well can turn defence into honest disclosure.
plos-pone-0350209:
Self-driving cars sometimes must change lanes, ready or not, and the car behind in the target lane may not cooperate. Zhe Wang and colleagues framed that standoff as a staged game, in this 2026 PLOS One study of mandatory lane changes.

Payoff scores for the merging car and its new followers update as the move unfolds, letting each side adjust its plan in steps. A controller then steers the car along the chosen path, keeping combined position and heading errors inside a preset band. Traffic simulations plus sessions with three human drivers of different temperaments gave first evidence the approach handles real interaction styles.
plos-pone-0350509:
Charlotte Williams, Prithwish Banerjee, and co-authors interviewed heart patients about what it actually felt like to train with short, hard exercise bursts versus steady moderate exercise in rehabilitation. The parent trial had already found the interval approach safe and good value, but numbers say little about lived experience. Their 2026 study spoke with nineteen patients from two rehabilitation centers, most of them men around sixty years old.

Both groups described gains in mood, confidence, purpose, fitness, and weight. Interval trainers enjoyed feeling pushed but sometimes found sessions monotonous, while steady trainers gained more social contact. Everyone wanted ways to keep exercising after the program ended. The authors suggest building more social time into interval training and planning support beyond discharge.
plos-pone-0350609:
Florence Perquier and co-authors surveyed teenagers in Matiari, a mostly rural district of Pakistan, about depression and anxiety. Their 2026 PLOS One study reached about fourteen hundred boys and girls aged nine to sixteen, in a country where teen mental health data from the countryside are scarce.

Roughly one in ten showed strong signs of depression. Anxiety varied by type, with fear of separation from parents most common, especially among girls. Symptoms ran higher in homes where mothers faced partner violence or where food was short, and lower when mothers stayed home full time. A mother's own mental health softened the harm of hunger for girls.
plos-pone-0351109:
Min Shen and colleagues built an explainable model to predict air use by helper nozzles on air jet looms, machines that weave with blasts of air. Helper nozzles burn nearly four fifths of a looms air, yet data to train models are scarce. Their hybrid joins image style networks, attention, and a classic regressor, tuned by an improved search algorithm.

The hybrid beat all simpler rivals, explaining over ninety nine percent of variation in air use on tests. Explanation plots ranked which nozzle shape traits drive air use most. Loom makers can cut energy bills at the drawing board by reshaping the greediest traits first, with the model showing its reasoning.
plos-pone-0351209:
Hana Rohan and colleagues interviewed the senior officials who built COVID-19 alert level systems. Those systems were the color-coded ladders that told whole nations their risk level and the rules that came with it. Eight places took part, from New Zealand to California to South Africa. The informants had run the ladders during the pandemic itself. The study distills their lessons for the next emergency.

The officials rated the ladders useful on the whole. A simple scale spoke clearly and steadied public cooperation as measures changed. The interviews also exposed the strains: consistency, trust, and the politics of moving between levels. These witnesses are the designers themselves. Their lessons carry the kind of detail no outside audit could reach.
plos-pone-0351309:
Sally Lindsay, Gozde Oncil, and Sarah Leo gathered research on unfair treatment in housing for people with disabilities. Safe, affordable housing is a basic right, yet disabled people more often face homes they cannot enter, cannot afford, or cannot keep. Their review searched six databases and kept fifty two studies from thirteen countries over nearly five decades.

Unfairness showed up when hunting for a home, viewing it, renting, and buying. Poor supply, high cost, and blocked access recurred. Landlord ignorance, low income, kind of disability, and weak policy rules deepened the harm. Effects spilled into neighbourhood life and safety. Naming the pattern as ableism, the authors argue, helps law and housing practice target it directly.
plos-pone-0351409:
Julia Döge and colleagues drew on a large German health cohort to ask how hearing loss relates to one specific thinking skill: planning ahead. Over four thousand adults aged forty to eighty took hearing tests, a speech-in-noise test, and a tower puzzle that scores planning. General links between hearing and cognition are known; the team wanted the finer grain of a single executive skill.

People with hearing loss in both ears scored lower on planning, though they were not clearly more likely to fall into the clinically poor range. The relationship also ran the other way: stronger planners were less likely to have hearing loss and coped better with speech in noise. The authors read this as hearing loss taxing the attention and working memory that planning borrows, while admitting only follow-up over time can sort cause from effect.
plos-pone-0351509:
Jinxing Dai and six colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study on telling two childhood lung conditions apart using ordinary blood tests. Bronchopneumonia and simple upper respiratory infections look alike at a first visit, which leads to unneeded antibiotics and scans. The team studied more than five hundred children with mild breathing symptoms and trained seven machine learning models on routine laboratory results.

A support vector machine model performed best, separating the two conditions with high accuracy on held-out cases, and its risk estimates were well calibrated. An explanation method then showed which lab values drove each prediction and at what levels they mattered most. The authors propose the tool as a cheap, noninvasive triage aid for busy clinics deciding which children need closer attention.
plos-pone-0352209:
Jonathon Weakley and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One sports science study measuring how bar speed changes with load in seven Olympic weightlifting movements. Coaches often prescribe training using generic speed bands tied to qualities like starting strength or absolute strength. Fourteen competitive weightlifters completed maximal strength tests and then profiling sessions for movements including the power snatch, hang power clean, and clean pull.

Bar speed fell steadily as load rose in every lift, but each exercise had its own speed profile that clashed with the standard bands. Most strikingly, the speeds recorded at the heaviest loads were far above the speed commonly labeled as the starting-strength threshold. The authors supply exercise-specific zones and argue coaches should build profiles per lift rather than borrow universal bands.
plos-pone-0352309:
CORRECTION: Molly Plovanich and colleagues correct an error in a figure of their earlier article on MICU2, a protein that helps mitochondria control calcium. In one panel of the figure, the wrong blot image had been placed: the panel labeled for one protein actually duplicated the panel for another. This notice replaces the figure with the correct material.

Alongside the swapped panel, the corrected figure presents two related panels in their original blot form as a single panel. The authors explain the mix-up likely happened while preparing final files, and they supply the underlying blot images, including both short and long exposures, as a supporting file. An editorial board member was consulted about the fix. Readers should use the corrected figure rather than the original.
plos-pone-0352509:
Sundh and colleagues, in a 2026 review, gather everything known about testing hamstring strength in sport. Hamstring strains are among the most common and most repeated injuries in athletics, so teams test strength to judge readiness and risk. More than one hundred sixty studies were gathered, and over one hundred were pooled statistically.

Machine-based testing was the most used method, followed by force platforms and Nordic exercise devices, with field-friendly tests rising since 2010. Several methods proved reliable and sensitive to fatigue. Strength stayed depressed for one to three days after hard activity, a danger window when schedules crowd games together. Small differences between legs, around a few percent, turned out to be normal and meaningless alone. The authors urge teams to set each athlete's own baseline and judge change against it, not against a universal line.
plos-pone-0352609:
Behnoush Khasheii led a team of six authors on this 2026 study of tiny regulatory molecules in the milk of cows with mastitis, a painful udder infection. Milk from healthy cows and from cows with obvious or hidden infections caused by two kinds of bacteria was tested for nine inflammation-related microRNAs using sensitive gene counting.

Several microRNAs surged in obvious infections, and two stood out as strongest at separating sick from healthy cows, with one raised in hidden cases too. Khasheii proposes milk microRNAs as painless early warning markers for dairy herds.
plos-pone-0352809:
He and An built a multi-task learning system for online trade data in a 2026 study. Cross-border sellers must forecast demand, judge running risk, and spot anomalies at once. Their model shares one feature reader across tasks, with focused attention shaped in a pyramid, then splits into task-specific heads.

Tests on a global trade data set and a network traffic set split data into training, checking, and test parts. The system cut forecasting error and raised anomaly detection scores versus a strong video-style baseline. Sharing one reader across tasks mirrors how trade signals overlap, and it lowers computing cost for sellers watching many markets.
plos-pone-0353109:
Punyanuch Chayanopparat and four co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One heart study from Thailand. It looks at silent heart attacks in patients with obesity. The team used detailed heart MRI scans. They searched for scar signs of heart attacks that patients never knew they had. The scans covered more than a thousand people from 2014 to 2016. None had a prior heart attack diagnosis.

About one in ten patients carried such a silent scar. Over roughly nine years of follow-up, those patients had major heart events at nearly three times the rate of others. The scar added warning power beyond standard risk factors. The pattern held across age, sex, and diabetes subgroups. The authors argue that finding silent damage on scans could sharpen prevention for this high-risk group.
plos-pone-0353309:
Mo Zhou, Yue Zhou, and Kai Song built a detection system that finds objects such as bridges, vehicles, and storage tanks in satellite and aerial images. Their 2026 paper, presenting a method called DAAF, fuses two kinds of neural network: one strong on fine local detail, one strong on wide context. Naive fusion wastes that pairing because the two produce mismatched feature patterns.

DAAF first calibrates the two streams so their features align, then selects the most useful channels from each, and finally gates the blend pixel by pixel. On three public benchmarks it beat simple fusion by about two points of average precision, with large gains on hard categories like bridges, at almost no extra computing cost. Cleaner aerial detection feeds mapping, disaster checks, and land monitoring.
plos-pone-0353609:
Neiva and colleagues tested a model of leadership and teamwork in British health care in a 2026 study. Answers from national staff surveys over two years fed the analysis. The model asked how good leadership shapes teamwork, and how teamwork in turn shapes engagement, well-being, and stress.

Good leadership lifted teamwork, which raised engagement and well-being. Yet teamwork also raised role confusion and cut autonomy, which fed stress. Leadership quality decided whether teamwork's benefits outweighed those costs. The authors advise pairing team building with clear roles, real say in decisions, and leadership training, so teamwork helps staff instead of quietly burdening them.
plos-pone-0353909:
Keyvan Sarebanzadeh and Mahboubeh Es'haghi simulate gas explosions. They want to know what decides how far a blast reaches. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. They used industrial hazard software. More than three hundred leak scenarios were modelled. All involved one large pressurised tank at a refinery. The team varied hole size and gas mix. They also varied leak position, weather, season, and time of day.

Blast distances ranged enormously. The worst ruptures threw dangerous pressure beyond two kilometres. A machine-learning check ranked the factors. Hole size dominated the outcome. Gas mix came second. Weather and operations barely mattered. For engineers drawing safety setbacks, the ranking is gold. It shows where precision counts, and where rough estimates suffice.
plos-pone-0354309:
Subrata Koiry and co-authors measure in 2026 energy hardship among tea estate workers in the Moulvibazar area of Bangladesh. Household data came from several hundred workers chosen through staged random sampling. A combined index counted gaps across cooking, lighting, and other basic energy needs, and a statistical model searched for what drove high scores.

About half of households counted as energy poor on the combined measure, with cooking the largest contributor. Schooling, job type, family size, land, housing quality, and earnings all mattered. The authors favour better housing, wider schooling, and cleaner cooking options as practical ways to cut the hardship they found.
plos-pone-0354509:
Baratta and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, measure what adults in north-western Italy know about oral cancer. Caught early, mouth cancer has a far better outlook, yet late diagnosis is common, partly because the public knows little about it. Pharmacies, which people visit often and trust, were the survey setting.

More than nine hundred pharmacy customers answered questions from trained interviewers. About seven in ten had heard of oral cancer, most often from family, friends, or the media. Nearly everyone knew smoking is a risk, but far fewer knew alcohol plays a role, and very few knew sun exposure can drive lip cancer. Awareness rose with education and differed by sex, age, and smoking habits. Almost all respondents wanted more information, and two thirds named the pharmacy as their preferred source. The authors propose pharmacies as a front line for awareness campaigns.
plos-pone-0354709:
Shaye Kivity led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of heat camera checks for inflamed joints. Two hundred and thirty-nine people, including arthritis patients and healthy controls, had knees, ankles, wrists, and finger joints imaged with consumer-grade thermal cameras. Instead of temperature alone, the team measured texture patterns in the heat images and compared sides and front-to-back views.

Texture features separated inflamed joints from quiet ones, with effects running in opposite directions at the wrist and finger joints. Kivity sees cheap heat imaging as a possible screen for hidden inflammation where scanners are scarce.
plos-pone-0354809:
Abuşka and colleagues, in a 2026 study, look back at emergency patients with confirmed COVID-19 from the first months of the pandemic, before vaccines were in use. They ask whether simple scores built from a routine blood count could predict who would die within thirty days. Three such scores, all based on blood cell counts tied to inflammation, were tested.

Records covered close to three thousand patients at a large hospital in spring 2020. Overall, about six in every hundred patients died within a month. The three scores predicted death only modestly in the whole group. In patients under sixty-five, one score did clearly better. In older patients, all three did worse. The age gap was strongest for that leading score. The authors caution that these cheap scores help less in older patients, the group at highest risk, so age must shape how they are used.
plos-pone-0355109:
Venu Allapakam and Yepuganti Karuna build an automated system for outlining a rare digestive tract tumor in medical scans, in this 2026 paper. These tumors, called GISTs, blur into surrounding intestine on CT images, and doctors currently trace them by hand, a slow and subjective task. The authors' two-stage model first fuses CT and PET scans into a single richer image. It then segments the tumor using a vision transformer architecture designed to capture both fine detail and broad context.

Across a battery of standard scores for both fusion quality and segmentation accuracy, the combined system beat existing models. The authors argue that better fused images make the transformer's job easier, and that the pairing could give clinicians faster, more consistent tumor maps for diagnosis and treatment planning. The work is a methods demonstration on scan data rather than a clinical trial.
plos-pone-0355209:
Lynn Fenton leads an international team publishing the protocol for a scoping review on what a mother's imprisonment does to mothers and their children. Most imprisoned women worldwide are mothers, and separation can scar both sides for years, yet the evidence is scattered across many fields that rarely talk. Their plan searches six databases across disciplines, with independent reviewers screening studies and charting what each reports about harm, support, and outcomes.

No findings appear in this entry; its job is to fix the question and method in public before the review runs. Fenton and colleagues aim to hand charities and policymakers, who often fund support on thin budgets, a single map of what is known and where the gaps yawn widest.
plos-pone-0355409:
Shiyi Zhu and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE on a small natural peptide called AcSDKP and its effects in chronic kidney disease. Using a mouse model of kidney injury plus cultured mouse and human cells, they asked how the peptide acts on the support cells that wrap tiny kidney blood vessels. They also asked how it acts on the tubule cells that filter waste.

The peptide protected blood vessels: it stopped support cells from turning into scar-forming cells and restored a growth signal that helps vessel linings regrow. Given early, it reduced scarring and improved kidney function in mice, while later treatment helped less. In badly damaged tubule cells, though, the same peptide sped up cell death by blocking a separate survival pathway. The work warns that any future therapy would need early use and careful targeting.
plos-pone-0355509:
Jane Williams and seven others ask experienced horse retrainers what makes a retired racehorse's second career succeed, in this 2026 study. Thoroughbreds leaving racing face a wholesale change of life, and poor transitions harm welfare. The team surveyed one hundred people worldwide who retrain former racehorses, then ran a structured consensus exercise with twenty-seven retrainers and therapists.

Survey answers clustered around time allowed, the people involved, the horse's racing history, and the overall approach. The consensus panel agreed seven areas are key: feeding, rider skill, handler expertise, the exercises chosen, and assessing and adjusting the horse's shape, posture, and access to turnout. Thoroughbreds commonly moved on to eventing, dressage, and leisure riding. Participants asked for better owner education, easier access to expertise, and more money for retrainers.
plos-pone-0355609:
Minh Nguyen Viet and colleagues ran a randomized trial on ventilator settings for the most injured lungs. The patients were adults with moderate to severe respiratory failure after trauma or surgery. Their 2026 single-center study assigned eighty-six patients to one of two arms. One arm used standard pressure settings. The other used individualized settings guided by electrical impedance tomography. That is a bedside imaging belt that watches air move through the chest, region by region.

The guided strategy combined imaging, recruitment maneuvers, and gradual pressure titration. It lifted blood oxygen levels more over the first three days. Lung stiffness trajectories looked similar between groups. The trial was sized for these physiological measures rather than survival. The authors position imaging guidance as a promising way to personalize ventilation, where one pressure plainly does not fit all.
plos-pone-0356009:
Hui-ling Yan and colleagues reviewed tools that predict poor bowel cleaning before a colonoscopy. Dirty bowels can hide disease and waste the procedure, so clinics want to flag risky patients early. Their 2026 systematic review gathered studies from eight databases and pooled how well the prediction models performed.

The review covered thirty-one studies describing forty-six models. Common risk factors included constipation, diabetes, older age, body weight, and past bowel surgery. On average the models sorted patients moderately well, both in their own samples and in outside tests. But most studies carried a high risk of bias, and few checked whether predicted risks matched real rates. The authors call for bigger, independent validation studies.
plos-pone-0357009:
Maria Emfietzoglou leads a team of eight checking whether a broken cellular recycling gene reshapes the gut microbiome, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The gene, Lamp2, is needed to fuse recycling sacs with the cell's digestion chambers; its loss causes Danon disease in people. Male mice lacking the gene, and their normal littermates, gave fecal samples across their first year of life. Some cages held one genotype, others mixed both. The samples underwent deep shotgun sequencing of microbial DNA.

The headline is restraint. By the primary measures, the two groups' gut communities looked alike: similar diversity, similar overall composition. Whatever differences emerged were limited, as the paper's own framing stresses. Housing arrangement and cage effects loomed as the usual confounders to control. The careful negative matters: not every dramatic gene knockout echoes into the gut, and microbiome claims built on shallow sequencing deserve this study's deeper skepticism.
plos-pone-0357109:
Wei-Jia Kong and colleagues searched for a shared culprit between two conditions. One is sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection. The other is the delirium that often follows surgery. The two can feed each other. Their 2026 study merged gene activity datasets for both conditions. It carefully corrected a badly inflated sepsis dataset. It then looked for genes moving in the same direction in each.

Forty-four candidate genes overlapped, and twenty-two agreed in direction. Network analysis elevated one gene in particular, MAPK14. It is a stress and inflammation switch. It rose across sepsis and delirium cohorts alike. Computer docking further suggested the common blood pressure drug losartan interacts with it. The authors stress this is computer evidence only. It is a lead for experiments, not a treatment yet.
plos-pone-0357209: Fino and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on judging how well the kidneys filter blood. That rate, called GFR, is usually estimated from blood tests for creatinine or cystatin C, plus age and sex. The team studied how much estimates vary under this approach. Variation matters because one estimate can label a person healthy while another flags kidney disease.
plos-pone-0357309:
Zhiping Deng and coauthors published a 2026 engineering study in PLOS ONE on a greener concrete column. The column is a steel tube filled with concrete partly made from lithium slag, an industry waste, wrapped in carbon fiber polymer rings. Twenty short columns were crushed in the laboratory while the team varied lithium slag content, fiber ring spacing, and fiber layer count.

The columns failed gradually, ending with the steel tube buckling outward. More lithium slag raised load capacity but made behavior more brittle, with a middle replacement level performing best overall. Adding fiber layers improved both strength and ductility more than tightening the ring spacing did. The team distilled the tests into a strength formula and verified its accuracy against their data. Designers gain a tested recipe for using lithium waste in load-bearing columns rather than landfilling it.
plos-pone-0357409:
Yuichi Ninomiya and colleagues followed 752 adults in Japan who quit smoking. They tracked heart tracings over six years for signs of an enlarged left ventricle. Their 2026 retrospective study used annual health checkup records from people without hypertension. It compared the electrical voltage that signals heart enlargement at quitting and six years later.

The voltage eased downward. The share of people meeting the enlargement threshold fell too. That happened even though quitters gained weight and their blood pressure rose. Both of those usually push the heart the other way. Blood pressure medication independently predicted improvement. The findings add a concrete heart benefit to quitting. The overworked heart muscle can partly recover its normal electrical pattern over time.
plos-pone-0357709:
Andreea Cislaru led a team of eight authors studying sugar tags on blood proteins in liver failure, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. In decompensated cirrhosis, the liver can no longer keep up, and the sugar patterns on serum and antibody proteins change. The team linked those changes to the standard severity score, MELD-Na.

Cislaru's group mapped how the sugar profile shifts as cirrhosis worsens. Such signatures could sharpen forecasts for patients waiting for transplants, where timing is life or death. Blood sugar tags are cheap to read once the patterns are known, so a validated signature could spread widely. The study joins a growing field that reads protein sugars as early warnings of organ failure.
plos-pone-0357909:
Guanyu Yang and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on the state of behavioural research in the United Kingdom. That is the science of how people act, and it now informs policy on health, crime, climate, and more. Five workshops brought together close to sixty researchers and research users from universities, government, charities, and business. Using structured framework analysis, the authors mapped the field's strengths, its obstacles, and the fixes participants proposed.

Participants praised how visible behavioural research has become and how deeply it is embedded in some organizations. But they also listed public misunderstandings, thin funding, findings that fail to reach practice, teams working in silos, uneven training, and weak leadership backing. Remedies included making the research more accessible, reforming how it is funded, and training across sectors. Sustained investment, they conclude, is needed so behavioural evidence serves public priorities rather than sitting in journals.
plos-pone-0359109: Ranjan and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on dementia in Bangladesh, called the CARED study. They recorded the age at which people were diagnosed and which dementia subtype they had. Brain scans helped separate one subtype from another. In a country where dementia is often missed, such basic facts guide clinics and family support.
plos-pone-0359209:
Yeser Eroglu Eskicioglu and colleagues developed a measurement scale in 2026 for why people in Türkiye practice yoga. Consumer motivation matters to studios and instructors, but it also reveals how a practice imported from elsewhere takes on local meanings. Their scale development study builds and tests a questionnaire that can measure those motivations reliably.

A validated scale turns impressions about yoga's appeal, health, calm, fitness, community, or spirituality, into data that researchers and businesses can compare across groups and over time. The study also documents, through its items, the reasons Turkish practitioners themselves give. Work of this kind gives the young field of yoga research a firmer footing in a country where the practice is still spreading.
plos-pone-0359409:
Yixin Feng and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on city transit. It forecasts short-term metro passenger flow, how many riders stations will see in the near future. The modeling is decoupled spatio-temporal, treating patterns across places and across time as separate pieces before recombining them.

The design pairs a diffusion-convergence graph with a Swin-Enhanced LSTM, two machine learning components the authors credit for the forecast. Accurate short-term forecasts let metro operators add trains before platforms crowd. Transit planners in large cities are the audience for forecasting methods tested on metro data.
plos-pone-0359509: Chen and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on what wins bouts in elite amateur boxing. They compared winners and losers in matched pairs, so each pair was alike in most ways. The focus was on technical and tactical signs, such as punch patterns and ring control. Knowing which signs truly track with winning can sharpen coaching beyond raw punch counts.
plos-pone-0359809:
Rashid Mehmood and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a case-control analysis of end stage renal disease, kidney failure requiring dialysis or transplant. The authors test the impact of polymorphisms, common gene variants, in two genes, GST and TP53, on susceptibility to the disease.

TP53 is famous as a guardian gene against cancer, while GST genes help clear toxins from the body. Comparing patients with healthy controls shows whether certain variants cluster in kidney failure. Nephrologists and genetic researchers can use susceptibility evidence like this to understand why kidney disease strikes some families harder.
pmc-13328809: Kidney disease patients struggle with dietary self-management. The authors analyzed behavioral determinants through theory-informed analysis. The findings guide dietitian interventions. Theory-based approaches improve adherence. Behavioral science improves dietary adherence. Theory-informed analysis guides dietitians. Dietary behavior research aids kidney patients. Kidney nutrition research improves patient outcomes.
pmc-13358809: Ultrafast light inactivates S. epidermidis plasmonically. Mechanistic insights were revealed. The finding serves sterilization. Light kills bacteria. Sterilization needs light-based methods. Plasmonic inactivation offers chemical-free sterilization. Mechanistic insights guide light sterilization. Bacterial inactivation needs physical methods. Ultrafast pulses offer sterile surfaces.
pmc-13379509: Huntington's disease genetic testing presents families with agonizing choices. The authors explored perspectives on genetic testing, revealing a recommendation paradox. The qualitative findings guide counseling for at-risk families. Understanding ambivalence improves genetic services. Counseling research supports difficult family decisions. Qualitative insights improve genetic counseling.
pmc-13395509: Computer navigation guides a bone-preserving approach to an elbow cyst. Tasuku Miyake, Ryoya Shiode, and others detail the way. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is orthopedic way. It describes navigation-aided curettage of a humeral trochlea bone cyst via an extra-articular approach.
pmc-13398409: High-pressure dense matter physicists in full study pressure-induced effects on the crystal frame and Raman vibrational spectra of a layered van der Waals material. The team with care compress samples in diamond anvil cells. The 2026 Europe PMC paper in full studies the built changes. It a lot reveals pressure-driven phase changes. Hydrostatic pressure was slowly applied. The crystal frame fundamentally changed. Vibrational spectra markedly shifted.
pmc-13399509: Transcultural mental health the team discuss spirituality as a vital yet underutilized coping resource, advocating for its respectful mixing into mainstream mental health care plans. This conceptual paper with care argues for holistic inclusion. The 2026 Europe PMC paper clearly presents the integrative perspective. It strongly supports whole-person mental care. Spirituality truly helps many patients cope. It serves as a powerful coping resource. Medical mixing becomes proposed.
pmc-13401409: Movement disorder specialists apply deep learning pose estimation for phenotyping co-occurring hyperkinetic disorders. The team automate movement analysis. The 2026 Europe PMC paper validates the AI approach. It helps diagnostic precision. AI quantifies abnormal movements objectively. Phenotyping guides treatment. Technology aids neurology.

Schloss, Gevers, and Westcott address how PCR and sequencing artefacts distort studies based on the 16S rRNA gene. Next-generation sequencing sparked growth in research on microbial communities and their roles in health. Copying DNA before sequencing, though, introduces errors that can look like rare microbes.

The authors show how such artefacts inflate apparent diversity and how to reduce their effects. Cleaner pipelines protect studies of the gut, soil, and other communities from chasing phantom species. Their guidance shaped standard practice in microbiome analysis worldwide.  Mock communities with known contents let the authors measure the artefacts directly themselves.
pmc-5605509:
The GBD 2016 team reported in 2017 on illness and injury that do not kill, across the whole world. As death rates fall, life spans grow, and populations age, non-fatal outcomes form a larger share of the total burden of disease. Pain, disability, and mental illness shape daily life for huge numbers of people.

The study gives complete estimates of how often hundreds of diseases and injuries occur. It also counts how many people live with each one, and the years lived with disability, for nearly two hundred countries from 1990 to 2016. Such counts show where health systems must shift focus from saving lives to keeping people able and well. They guide plans for rehab, mental health, and chronic care.
pmc-6298009:
Nicole Davis, Diana Proctor, Susan Holmes, and coauthors presented a statistical fix for contaminant DNA in 2018. Microbe surveys often pick up DNA that was never in the sample. Contaminants sneak in from kits and lab reagents.

Their method, built into the decontam tool, spots sequences whose pattern matches contamination rather than biology. Sequences that appear more in blank controls or in dilute samples are flagged. Removing them sharpens results, above all for samples with few real microbes. The approach gave the field a shared, testable way to clean data instead of hand-waving the problem.
pmc-7026709:
The GBD 2017 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Collaborators published this global analysis in 2019. The burden of inflammatory bowel disease is rising worldwide. Levels and trends vary sharply between countries and regions.

The study reports cases and deaths for Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis across nearly two hundred countries. Rates remain highest in North America and Europe but climb fast in newly industrialized regions. An aging patient pool adds disability even where rates level off. Understanding that geography helps governments plan specialist care and drug budgets. The authors note that health systems in fast-growing regions face a double burden of old and new diseases.
pmc-7067809:
Johnny Fares, Mohamad Fares, Hussein Khachfe, and coauthors revisited the molecular principles of metastasis in 2020. Metastasis, the spread of cancer to distant organs, causes most cancer deaths. For all its importance, the process remains poorly understood.

The review follows cancer cells through escape, travel in blood, and colonization of new tissue. New views stress that spread can start early and that dormant cells can wake years later. Immune evasion and organ-specific niches get detailed treatment. Readers see why stopping spread, not just shrinking tumors, is oncology's hardest problem. Each stage of spread is paired with the therapies now being tested against it.
