Guanghui Xiong and colleagues launched ADMETlab 2.0 in 2021, an online platform that predicts how a candidate drug will behave in the body. Most drug projects fail because a compound is absorbed poorly, breaks down badly, or proves toxic. Testing those properties early, even by computer prediction, saves years and money.

The platform predicts the full set of such properties, known by the initials ADMET: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity. The authors describe the models behind the predictions and how the second version widened and sharpened them. Freely available tools of this kind let even small labs screen compounds before committing to costly experiments.
pound-exultations-1909:
Ezra Pound, a young American poet in London, published Exultations in 1909. It was his third small book in little more than a year. Pound was teaching himself poetry by raiding the past, and this collection leans hard toward the medieval troubadours of Provence.

The poems include translations and imitations of troubadour songs, full of spring mornings, distant ladies, and formal praise. Early original lyrics stand beside them, already showing Pound's drive toward exact, musical speech. The medievalist and the modernist in Pound are both visible here, side by side. Exultations is a workshop book: readers can watch a revolutionary poet gathering his tools from a thousand years of verse.
pound-personae-1909:
Ezra Pound published Personae in London in 1909, his first substantial collection and his bid for poetic mastery. The title means masks in Latin, and Pound explained that each poem speaks through an adopted character or voice. He was twenty-three, freshly arrived from America, and determined to remake English poetry.

The poems move from troubadour translations to dramatic monologues and sharp lyrics. Pound tries on Provençal singers, Italian courtiers, and his own brash modern self. The technique is already dazzling, though the great Imagist manifestos still lay ahead. Critics took notice of the young American at once. Personae is the root from which Imagism and much of modern poetry grew.
recherches-sur-le-systeme-nerveux-en-gen: Recherches sur le système nerveux, 1809. The nervous system research. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: Volume nine brings the valet's tale toward the fall of the Empire. Constant stands faithfully by his master through defeat and through doubt. The great household holds together bravely to the very last. Loyalty tested by history itself, and loyalty that never breaks.
saint-simon-memoirs-wormeley-vol-1-1909:
Louis de Rouvroy, duc de Saint-Simon, kept notes on the court of Louis XIV for thirty years. His years at Versailles ran from 1691 to 1723. The Mémoires were first published in 1829, long after his death. Volume one here opens Katharine Prescott Wormeley's English translation. Her version, made in 1899 to 1901, was printed in 1909 in four volumes.

Saint-Simon watched Versailles with a hawk's eye for rank, slight, and ambition. His pages swarm with dukes, ministers, mistresses, and spies, each drawn in a few unforgettable strokes. No other memoirist shows the Sun King's court from inside with such malice and brilliance. Volume one admits the reader to that gilded, dangerous world.
saint-simon-memoirs-wormeley-vol-2-1909:
Volume two of Wormeley's Saint-Simon continues the Mémoires of the duc de Saint-Simon in English. Saint-Simon wrote his memoirs from life at Versailles between 1691 and 1723, and they were first published in 1829. Wormeley's translation, made in 1899 to 1901 and printed in 1909, fills four volumes.

The court of Louis XIV fills these pages in all its ceremony and cruelty. Saint-Simon, a proud duke obsessed with rank, records every promotion, disgrace, and whisper of the palace. His portraits are so sharp that their subjects' descendants still wince. Historians treat the memoirs as a peerless source on the reign. Volume two keeps the court dancing under his merciless eye.
saint-simon-memoirs-wormeley-vol-3-1909:
Saint-Simon's Mémoires reach volume three in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation, the English set of 1899 to 1901, printed in 1909. Louis de Rouvroy, duc de Saint-Simon, composed his vast memoir from the years 1691 to 1723 at the court of France. Publication waited until 1829, when the book burst on a world that thought it knew Versailles.

Volume three holds more of the court's daily war of precedence, favor, and revenge. Saint-Simon hated the king's ministers and bastards, loved the old nobility, and wrote both loves and hatreds at full heat. The result is the greatest memoir of the age, half history and half settled scores. Its people live.
saint-simon-memoirs-wormeley-vol-4-1909:
Volume four completes Wormeley's English Saint-Simon, the translation of 1899 to 1901 printed in 1909. The duc de Saint-Simon's Mémoires, written from 1691 to 1723 and first published in 1829, close with the death of Louis XIV and the years that followed. Four volumes hold the English set entire.

The final volume keeps Saint-Simon's voice at full pitch: proud, funny, vindictive, and endlessly observant. His court portraits, from king to footman, form a whole society preserved in amber. Later writers from Proust onward have fed on these pages. To finish volume four is to leave Versailles at last, having seen it through the sharpest eyes in France.
scheible-das-kloster-vol09:
In 1848 Johann Scheible published band nine of Das Kloster, with cells thirty-three through thirty-six. Nine bands in, his cloister held more rescued print than any rival project of the age. The German reading public for old magic, story, and charm had found its supplier.

Grimoires stand thick in this band, and Faust books and Höllenzwänge hold their usual dark corner. Folk charms, some only lines long, are printed with the same care as the great spell books. Chapbooks round out the stock with tales meant for winter nights. Band nine proves the set never coasted: the flow of rare texts stayed strong to the end.
shahnama-warner-vol-4-1909:
Volume 4 of the Warner Shahnama appeared in 1909, the fourth of nine volumes. Firdausi's Book of Kings tells the story of Persia from the first mythical king to the Arab conquest. The Warner brothers' version was the first to give English readers the epic entire.

In this volume the heroic age rolls on, with champions whose strength and pride drive the tale. Court intrigue, single combat, and tragic error shape the action, as they do throughout the poem. The Warners kept close to the Persian while making the story readable. Readers who follow the set volume by volume watch a whole civilization's memory of itself pass in review.
shahnameh-warner-vol4-1909:
With the fourth book, from 1909, the Warner verse version of the Shahnama comes to its close. Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner gave English readers the first full verse form of Persia's epic. Ferdowsi spent years on the poem a thousand years ago. Its end deals with the last kings of old Persia.

Arab conquest closes the age of the shahs in these last tales. Kings look back on lost glory and warn those who come next. The poem ends in a tone of loss and pride. The full set still serves readers who want the whole epic in English.
shakespeare-sonnets-1609:
William Shakespeare's sonnets came out in 1609 in a set of 154 poems. The first edition is still the most famed sonnet cycle in English. Most poems speak to a fair young man, and later ones to a dark lady.

The poems praise the youth's beauty and urge him to have a child. Time, age, and death press hard on love in line after line. Some sonnets turn sharp, jealous, or weary, yet the craft stays superb. Lines like summer's day comparisons live in the minds of millions. Scholars still debate who the two loved figures were.
soddy-interpretation-radium-1909:
Frederick Soddy was a British chemist who worked with Rutherford on how atoms break apart. His 1909 book The Interpretation of Radium explains radioactivity to general readers with patience and flair. Radium was then a wonder substance, glowing in the dark and defying old chemistry.

Soddy shows that atoms of heavy elements decay step by step, throwing off rays and vast stored energy. He grasps early that this energy, if freed, could power cities or destroy them. His clear account seeded the atomic-age imagination long before the first reactor or bomb. He writes with wonder, but he checks every wonder against the lab bench.
spr-proceedings-vol21-1908-1909:
Parts fifty four, fifty five, and fifty six fill volume twenty one, for 1908 and 1909. The SPR enters its late Edwardian phase with new cases and old questions. Telepathy experiments run beside reports of hauntings and crisis apparitions. Trance mediumship still leads, with Piper's sittings drawing the closest study.

New mediums of the period, Thompson among the names in the files, get their hearings. The society prints failures of evidence as faithfully as successes. Volume twenty one keeps the central archive growing toward its 1930 horizon. Its reports fed books on survival for decades. Readers find the debate's texture here: careful, curious, unconvinced, unbowed.
stein-three-lives-1909:
Three Lives, published in 1909 at her own expense, was Gertrude Stein's first book. It tells the lives of three working women in the fictional city of Bridgepoint: two German servants and one young black woman.

'The Good Anna' and 'The Gentle Lena' follow servant girls through work, love, and early death in plain, repeating sentences. 'Melanctha', the longest, follows a restless young woman through a doomed love, in prose that loops and circles like thought itself. Stein's cubist sentences begin here, simple words arranged until they shimmer. The book announced a writer unlike any other.
stewart-origin-of-the-werewolf-superstit:
Caroline Taylor Stewart hunts the roots of a belief in The Origin of the Werewolf Superstition, her study of 1909. Stewart was a sage of tongues at a school in the United States. She traces the wolf man from old Greek tales and Rome's verse through wolf cults, trials, and tales of the north. Each age, she shows, bent the beast to its own fears and faiths.

Her tone is calm and learned, free of thrills. She treats the theme as a thread in man's tale, not a freak. The book is the base on which new study of the theme stands.
story-of-the-session-of-the-california-l: Hichborn, the muckraker, reports Sacramento’s 1909 session from inside. Reformers battle the railroad machine. A plain tale of graft and its foes, a plain tale of graft and its foes, reform versus the machine, inside story.
suess-face-of-earth-vol4-sollas-1909:
Volume 4 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1909. Eduard Suess turned to the Americas and the Atlantic in this volume of his global synthesis. The two American continents, north and south, get the same connected treatment he gave Asia.

Suess compared the Appalachians, Rockies, and Andes as parts of one crustal story, and he weighed the Atlantic's coasts and islands against each other. Matching rocks and fossils across the Atlantic fed his picture of former land links. Later plate tectonics explained those matches by moving continents instead. The volume is a prime record of how geology reasoned about the Americas and the Atlantic before that revolution came.
swanton-tlingit-myths-and-texts-1909:
John Reed Swanton recorded myths and texts among the Tlingit of southeastern Alaska for the Bureau of American Ethnology. This 1909 bulletin prints them in Tlingit with English translation. The stories came from Tlingit tellers who held them as clan property and history.

The Raven cycle leads the collection. Raven steals the sun, makes the tides, and tricks his way through the early world. Other texts cover crest stories tied to clan crests, shaman narratives, and accounts of spirits and the dead. Swanton's careful texts preserve both the language and the lore of the Tlingit. They remain basic sources for Northwest Coast study.
tauler-inner-way-1909: The Inner Way, sermons of Johannes Tauler in a 1909 translation. The 14th-century mystic guided souls toward God. This book preserves those spiritual teachings. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The ninth volume of Rousseau's Confessions wanders through bleak persecution. Driven from France and then Switzerland, he seeks a safe refuge. The hunted philosopher's nerves fray under constant pursuit. A hunted genius telling his own tale.
the-freelands-pg2309: John Galsworthy's 1915 novel about the Freelands: a family divided by a land dispute and a young radical's passion. The Forsyte author's England in microcosm, just before the war. Thoughtful and beautifully written. Galsworthy's England was changing, and he chronicled it faithfully.
the-two-gentlemen-of-verona-pg1509: Two friends and one lady tangle in this edition of Shakespeare's early comedy: Proteus forgets his vows and betrays Valentine to win Silvia. The clown Launce and his dog Crab steal every scene they sniff. Young Shakespeare trying out the themes he would later perfect.
the-wandering-jew-volume-09: Eugène Sue’s ninth volume of the Wandering Jew. The Rennepont heirs draw near to their fate. Jesuit plots thicken around them on all sides. Grand melodrama building to its great climax, Sue's best.
therigatha-rhys-davids-1909: Psalms of the Sisters, the Therigatha translated by Rhys Davids in 1909. These are among the earliest women's religious poetry, by Buddhist nuns. This edition preserves those remarkable voices. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
to-morrow-pg3609: To-morrow is a short story built around a single coming day. Its characters wait, hope, and plan for what the morning will bring. The tale turns on expectation and quiet suspense. Brief, poised, and quietly moving to the last line.
tob-0009:
R. H. Charles's translation of the Book of Enoch made an ancient apocalypse accessible to English readers. Enoch, Noah's great-grandfather, tours heaven and hell in visions and reports the coming judgment. The New Testament's letter of Jude quotes the book, yet most churches excluded it from the Bible; Ethiopia's church treasured and preserved it.

The fallen Watchers, angels who took human wives and taught forbidden arts, dominate the early chapters, filling gaps Genesis leaves about giants and corruption before the flood. Later sections unfold calendars, parables, and woes against the rich and unjust. Early Jewish and Christian ideas about angels, demons, and the end times run through it.
tob-0109:
An alchemist's last gift takes the form of the Last Will and Testament credited to Basil Valentine. Dying masters in legend often hid their final secrets for worthy hands, and this short work plays that role. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, it gathers Valentine's closing instructions.

Preparations of antimony, the fiery mineral at the heart of his medicine, stand beside directions toward the stone itself. The tone is cryptic by design; each recipe must be weighed like a riddle. Seekers prized the little testament out of proportion to its size. With the Twelve Keys, it forms the core of the Valentine legend.
tob-12909:
Swami Vivekananda, the Hindu monk who addressed the Chicago Parliament of Religions in 1893, gave the lectures printed as Raja Yoga in 1896. They teach the yoga of mind control, based on Patanjali's old Yoga Sutras. The book carried yoga thought to American readers.

Vivekananda explains concentration, meditation, and the control of breath and thought as a science of the mind anyone can test. He adds his own translation and notes on Patanjali's aphorisms. Raja Yoga became the most practical door into Vedanta for the West and still anchors courses on meditation and yoga philosophy.
tob-13509:
Charles F. Horne edited a fourteen-volume anthology, The Sacred Books and Early Literature of the East, and volume six covers medieval Arabic, Moorish, and Turkish material. Horne's project gave Western readers the essential texts of Asian civilizations in English dress, sampled widely across scripture, poetry, and wisdom. Volume six turns to the Islamic world's literary heritage.

Readers of Horne's era often met these traditions first through such anthologies, with introductions framing unfamiliar material. Selections rather than complete works are the method here, chosen to represent range. As with its companions, the volume now serves two uses: a taste of the literatures themselves, and evidence of how early twentieth-century America packaged the East.
tob-4009:
Tommaso Campanella, a Dominican friar, wrote The City of the Sun in a Naples prison around 1602, where he spent decades for heresy and conspiracy. Cast as a dialogue, his utopia imagines a city of shared property ruled by thinker-priests under the guidance of the stars. No private goods divide its citizens, and schooling is universal, painted on the city's walls.

Seven concentric walls, communal meals, and state-planned work organize the ideal commonwealth, governed by a chief metaphysician with officers for power, wisdom, and love. Campanella's dream shaped utopian thought for centuries. Readers can measure its appeal, and its total control, against More's Utopia, written a century earlier.
tob-4109:
T. W. Rhys Davids translated the Questions of King Milinda for the Sacred Books of the East, and part one of two appears here. King Milinda is Menander, the Indo-Greek ruler of the Punjab around 150 BC. He questions the Buddhist monk Nagasena with a duelist's relish.

Is there a self that passes from life to life? Nagasena answers with the famous image of the chariot, which is no part by itself yet rolls when parts combine. Rebirth, karma, and nirvana all come under the king's cross-examination. Rhys Davids, founder of the Pali Text Society, made the dialogue a classic. Verified from the 1919 edition.
tob-4309:
Hume's Thirteen Principal Upanishads returns in the 1921 revised printing, covering the Isa through the Prasna. Robert Ernest Hume, the Harvard Sanskritist, translated the thirteen texts that commentators treat as the principal ones, with notes drawn from the Indian tradition itself. His edition collects SBE material into one student volume.

Boy Nachiketa questions Death in the Katha; the Chandogya repeats thou art that like a bell. Hume's English stays close and clear through the riddles. Verified from the 1919 edition record, the printing carried the standard classroom Upanishads through a century of teaching. The sages' claims about Brahman and the Self stand complete here.
tob-9409:
Ovid, the Roman poet, wrote the Metamorphoses as one long poem made of stories about change. Gods, heroes, and ordinary people turn into animals, trees, stones, and stars, often as reward or punishment. The version here is Brookes More's English translation, published in 1919.

Readers meet Daphne turning into a laurel tree as she flees Apollo, and Arachne changed into a spider after she outweaves Athena. Story leads into story for fifteen books, from the making of the world down to Rome. For centuries, most writers and painters learned Greek and Roman myth from Ovid's telling, and his fast, witty style still carries readers through.
tyrrell-christianity-cross-roads-1909:
George Tyrrell was an Irish Jesuit whose doubts about scholastic theology led to his expulsion from his order and excommunication. His Christianity at the Cross-Roads appeared in 1909, the year of his death. The posthumous book calls for a living, developing Catholicism.

Tyrrell argues that the church must choose between treating its formulas as final cages and treating them as signs of a living experience. He looks to a future synthesis in which faith and modern knowledge correct each other. Modernist readers claimed the book as their testament, while Rome's condemnation gave it a martyr's fame.
un-doc-who-invitation-to-chinese-taipei-:
Chinese Taipei received an invitation in 2009 to attend the World Health Assembly as an observer, and this file records that step. The assembly is the yearly meeting of the World Health Organization. Taiwan had been shut out of the body for decades because of its dispute with Beijing.

The invitation let health officials from Taiwan sit in, under the name Chinese Taipei. It followed warmer ties across the Taiwan Strait at that time. Health experts welcomed the move, since disease control works best when all sides share data. The file marks a rare thaw in a long standoff.
un-ga-res-54-109:
General Assembly Resolution 54/109, adopted on December 9, 1999, approved the International Convention for the Suppression of the Financing of Terrorism. It grew from the Assembly's fifty-fourth session, though some catalog copies carry the year 2000. Lawmakers had learned that stopping attacks also meant cutting off the money behind them.

Under the treaty, giving or gathering funds for attacks on civilians counts as a crime in itself, even if no attack occurs. States must freeze suspect funds, share evidence, and try or extradite those accused. Banks gained duties to spot suspect transfers. The pact entered into force in 2002 and became a core tool after the September 2001 attacks.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Hosted under the Resolution 54/109 label, the text here is the International Convention for the Suppression of the Financing of Terrorism. The General Assembly adopted it through that resolution. The preamble states the treaty's core worry. The scale of terrorism turns on the money terrorists can raise. No older treaty dealt with that funding head on.

The articles make it a crime to give or collect funds for terrorist acts against civilians. The funds may be given directly or in a roundabout way. They must be meant to be used for such acts. States must punish the offence. They must hold firms liable when their managers are involved. They must freeze and seize funds meant for such acts. They must also help each other with cases and evidence.
un-sc-res-109:
On 14 December 1955 the Security Council recommended sixteen countries for membership in the United Nations. The vote was eight to none, with Belgium, China, and the United States abstaining. Albania, Jordan, Ireland, and Portugal were on the list. So were Hungary, Italy, Austria, Romania, and Bulgaria. Finland, Ceylon, Nepal, Libya, Cambodia, Laos, and Spain completed the group.

The Council said it had weighed each application on its own. It then sent all sixteen names to the General Assembly in one recommendation. The Assembly admitted the sixteen the next day. The package ended a long deadlock over new members. It also changed the size and the balance of the world body at a stroke.
un-sc-res-1309: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 1309, catalogued for 2000 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1409: Resolution 1409 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 2002. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades.
un-sc-res-1509:
In September 2003 the Security Council passed Resolution 1509, creating the United Nations Mission in Liberia, known as UNMIL. Liberia's long civil war had just ended with a peace deal and Charles Taylor's exile. The Council sent a large peacekeeping force to hold the calm.

The text sets out what the mission could do, from guarding the ceasefire to helping disarm fighters and protect civilians. It also covers support for elections and rebuilding state authority across the country. The resolution marks the moment Liberia's recovery became a shared world project, led on the ground by UN troops.
un-sc-res-1609: Under number 1609, the Council placed another formal decision in its record, and this collection keeps the record text via Wikisource. The preamble does the persuading, citing history and principle; the operative part does the governing. Students of the institution read both halves together, and this entry preserves them together, in order, as voted.
un-sc-res-1709: Security Council Resolution 1709, adopted in 2006, is held here in its official-record wording via Wikisource. The Council produces hundreds of pages of such text in a busy year, each piece voted and numbered. This piece is preserved entire, so its place in the year's business can be judged from the document itself.
un-sc-res-1809:
Peace and security in Africa are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1809, adopted on 16 April 2008. African leaders joined a high-level Council debate that day. The African Union was building its own peace and security system. Its missions often lacked steady money, gear, and transport.

The Council says funding for regional peacekeeping under a United Nations mandate must become steadier and more flexible. It backs a joint African Union and United Nations panel, to be set up within three months, to study how such support could work. The text urges the Union to grow its peacekeeping strength, its standby force, and its early warning work. Regional bodies, it notes, often grasp the roots of local conflicts best.
un-sc-res-2009:
For Libya, the Council's answer came in Resolution 2009, adopted on 16 September 2011. The old regime had fallen, and the National Transitional Council was taking charge. Frozen Libyan assets abroad were needed to restart the state. Loose weapons, above all shoulder-fired missiles, worried the whole region.

The Council creates a support mission, called UNSMIL, for an initial three months. It will back Libyan efforts on security, dialogue, a constitution, and elections. Two national oil firms come off the asset freeze at once. Freezes on the central bank and state funds are loosened under strict notice rules. The ban on Libyan flights ends, and monthly reports follow.
un-sc-res-209:
War between India and Pakistan over Kashmir drew an urgent cease-fire call on 4 September 1965. The Secretary-General had reported on 3 September, and both governments had spoken to the Council. Fighting along the cease-fire line in Kashmir was growing worse. The Council acted within days of the report, before the war widened further.

The Council called on India and Pakistan to take all steps at once for an immediate cease-fire. Both governments had to respect the cease-fire line and pull all their armed personnel back to their own side of it. They were told to cooperate fully with the United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan as it watched the truce. The Secretary-General had to report to the Council within three days on how the resolution was being carried out. The tight deadline shows how fast the Council feared the fighting could spread.
un-sc-res-309:
Namibia's future under South African rule came back to the Council in 1972. On 4 February 1972 it asked the Secretary-General to open contacts with all parties. Three Council members, from Argentina, Somalia, and Yugoslavia, would work with him. Their goal was to set the conditions for Namibians to choose their own future freely. The Council restated the people's right to self-determination and independence.

South Africa had to cooperate fully with the effort. The Secretary-General owed a report by 31 July 1972. The Council also restated Namibia's unity and territorial integrity. South Africa held the territory under an old League of Nations mandate. The United Nations had revoked that mandate in 1966, but Pretoria stayed.
un-sc-res-409:
Rhodesia's money channels abroad were closed by a Security Council decision of 27 May 1977. The sanctions committee had sent a special report on 31 December 1976 urging wider sanctions. The Council restated that the situation in Southern Rhodesia threatened international peace and security. It also reaffirmed that all earlier measures stayed in force.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ordered every member state to bar the use or transfer of funds in its territory by the illegal regime. The ban covered the regime's offices and agents and any person or body inside Southern Rhodesia. Only an office kept solely for pension purposes was exempt. States outside the United Nations were urged to comply as well. The Council set a meeting no later than 11 November 1977 to weigh further measures under Article 41, and told its committee to study such steps at once.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sixteen flags rose at UN headquarters thanks to this vote of 1955. On 14 December, the Council adopted Resolution 109. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. Belgium, China, and the United States held back. Cold War vetoes had blocked new members for years. A package deal finally broke the jam.

The Council weighed sixteen bids one by one. Albania and Jordan were on the list, as were Italy and Spain. Ireland, Nepal, and Libya also applied, among others. The Council urged the Assembly to admit them all. The Assembly voted them in the next day. The deal nearly doubled the body's reach in one stroke.

Western Sahara's long-promised referendum is again the business at hand on 25 July 2000. MINURSO, the United Nations mission set up to run a free vote on self-determination under an agreed Settlement Plan, faced deep gaps between the parties. Those gaps still blocked the plan.

Rather than end the mission, the Council extended it to 31 October 2000. It expected the parties to meet face to face under the Secretary-General's Personal Envoy. The talks were meant to clear the problems holding up the plan and find a political answer both sides could accept. A new report on the situation was due before the deadline.

Iraq's oil-for-food programme is renewed on 14 May 2002, this time with a new way of screening imports. The year before, the Council had agreed to a Goods Review List, meant to speed civilian goods while still checking items with military uses. The revised list was now ready.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the programme running for 180 days from 30 May 2002. It adopted the revised list and its procedures, to apply from the same date. States could then allow most civilian trade with Iraq, while listed sensitive goods faced review. The stated aim was a better flow of aid to Iraqi civilians under sanctions.

A peace agreement signed in Accra in August 2003 had ended Liberia's long civil war on paper, and on 19 September 2003 a United Nations mission is created to hold it. A West African force, ECOMIL, held the ground first. A United Nations stabilization force was now to follow.

UNMIL is set up for 12 months, with authority passing from ECOMIL on 1 October 2003. The mission could field up to 15,000 military personnel, plus up to 1,115 civilian police. Its mandate covers watching the ceasefire, protecting civilians and aid work, disarming fighters, and helping rebuild security and the rule of law, as Liberia moves toward elections and recovery.

Côte d'Ivoire's United Nations operation, UNOCI, is renewed and reshaped on 24 June 2005. The Pretoria Agreement of April 2005 had revived the peace process after a string of broken deals. The Secretary-General's June report and a study of cooperation among the West African missions informed the choices made.

UNOCI and the supporting French forces are extended, the mission's mandate is restated in full, and more troops are authorized to carry it out. Temporary cross-border support among the United Nations missions in Côte d'Ivoire, Liberia, and Sierra Leone is also arranged, so aircraft and personnel can be shared in emergencies. Disarmament, elections, and restoring state authority across the country stay at the centre of the mandate.

Only until 8 October 2006 is Sudan's mission, UNMIS, extended on 22 September 2006. Deep concern is noted at the limits placed on the mission's movements and supplies and at the worsening humanitarian situation in Darfur. The very short extension kept the mission in place while the fight over expanding it into Darfur, decided the previous month, remained unresolved.

Cooperation with regional organizations is the subject of Resolution 1809, adopted on 16 April 2008. The African Union was running peace operations across the continent, and transitions from AU missions in Burundi and Sudan to UN missions offered lessons. The Council noted a core problem: regional bodies, above all the AU, lacked predictable and flexible funding for peacekeeping.

The Council commits to closer work with regional organizations under Chapter VIII of the Charter, above all the AU Peace and Security Council. It backs the Ten-Year Capacity-Building Programme for the AU, the African Standby Force, the continental early warning system, and the Panel of the Wise for mediation. It welcomes the Secretary-General's plan for a joint AU-UN panel of distinguished persons to study how to fund AU peacekeeping under a UN mandate, including start-up funding, equipment, and logistics. Progress is to be reported regularly.

Resolution 1909, adopted on 21 January 2010, gives the UN Mission in Nepal, UNMIN, a short final stretch. Nepal's new constitution was due by 28 May 2010, and a high-level political body had formed to push the peace process to its end. An action plan signed on 16 December 2009 set out the discharge of Maoist army personnel who had been disqualified as minors. Nepal asked for UNMIN until 15 May 2010.

The Council renews UNMIN until 15 May 2010. It decides that UNMIN should arrange its withdrawal with the government and hand over any leftover monitoring duties by that date. It welcomes the shared pledge to produce a timed plan for integrating and settling Maoist army personnel by 15 May. A report on carrying out the resolution is due by 1 May 2010.

Post-war Libya gets a UN support mission and partial unfreezing in Resolution 2009, adopted on 16 September 2011. The National Transitional Council was forming a transitional government. The Secretary-General planned a deployment at the Libyan authorities' request. The Council had referred Libya to the International Criminal Court and frozen state assets in Resolutions 1970 and 1973 (2011).

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council establishes UNSMIL, the United Nations Support Mission in Libya, for an initial three months. It is to help restore public security and the rule of law, run inclusive political dialogue and constitution-making, extend state authority, protect human rights, and start economic recovery. It lifts the asset freeze on the Libyan National Oil Corporation and Zueitina Oil Company. It eases it for the Central Bank and other state funds under Committee-supervised exemptions, ends the flight-ban measures, and allows arms for security assistance to the Libyan authorities.

War between India and Pakistan over Kashmir produced Resolution 209, adopted unanimously on 4 September 1965. Fighting along the ceasefire line in Kashmir was getting worse, and the Secretary-General's report of 3 September described the slide. Both governments had addressed the Council.

The Council called on India and Pakistan to take all steps for an immediate ceasefire without delay. Both were to respect the ceasefire line and pull every armed person back to their own side of it. They were also told to cooperate fully with the UN observer group supervising the line. The Secretary-General had to report within three days on whether the order was being carried out, a sign of how fast events were moving.

Namibia's long road to freedom passes through this text of 1972. On 4 February, the Council adopted Resolution 309. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. South Africa still ruled Namibia in defiance of the UN. The world body had ended its mandate years before. The Council restated the people's fixed right to rule themselves.

The text asks the Secretary-General to open talks with all parties at once. A Council group of Argentina, Somalia, and Yugoslavia works with him. The goal is plain to state. Namibians must be free to choose their future, with full regard for human equality. South Africa is called on to help in full. A report is due by 31 July 1972. The talks failed, and freedom waited until 1990.

Resolution 409, adopted without a vote on 27 May 1977, tightens the financial screws on the illegal regime in Southern Rhodesia. Sanctions against Rhodesia had been building since its unilateral declaration of independence in 1965. A committee set up under the original sanctions resolution had now recommended expanding the measures, and the Council took up its special report at the end of 1976.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ordered all member states to block the use or transfer of funds in their territories by the Rhodesian regime, its offices, or its agents. The ban targeted money meant to run regime offices abroad, with a narrow exception for offices handling pensions alone. Non-member states were also urged to comply.

Estonia's restored statehood won the Council's nod in the autumn of 1991. On 12 September, it adopted Resolution 709 without a vote. The Republic of Estonia had restored its freedom the month before. Soviet power was collapsing at the time. Five decades of annexation had never won legal backing from most Western states.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Estonia. The Assembly did so days later, with Latvia and Lithuania beside it. For the Baltic states, the seat meant more than a chair. It proved in law that their statehood had lived on since 1940. The world body's welcome closed the long gap in their story.
vinogradoff-roman-law-mediaeval-europe-1:
Vinogradoff delivered the lectures printed as Roman Law in Mediaeval Europe in 1909. His subject is one of history's strangest resurrections: the law of ancient Rome, dead with the empire, coming back to life in medieval classrooms. The Oxford jurist tells the story with a storyteller's grace.

He traces how Justinian's books were rediscovered and taught at Bologna around 1100, where Irnerius and his school made Roman law a university science again. From Bologna the learned law spread to every court and chancery in Europe, mixing with local custom. Vinogradoff shows the professors, the glossators, at work on texts a thousand years old. Rome's afterlife in the lecture halls of the Middle Ages is his theme. The short book remains the most elegant introduction to the second life of Roman law.
wells-ann-veronica-1909: Ann Veronica, H, g. Wells's 1909 New Woman novel, the suffragette's tale. This book preserves that book. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol09:
Liverpool issued Volume IX of the Journal of Discourses in 1862, while war tore at the nation the Saints had left behind. Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve speak in these pages, their sermons preserved by shorthand reporters. The church in Utah watched the conflict from its mountain distance.

Pulpit counsel here joins doctrine to the duties of a people building Zion in wartime's shadow. The printed sermons let scattered Saints share one teaching voice. Volume IX carries the year-by-year doctrinal record forward, part of a set prized for its closeness to the living speakers.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-4-1909:
Tome four of Jean de Pauly's French Zohar appeared in 1909. The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the great Aramaic commentary at the heart of the Kabbalah, framed as the teaching of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. De Pauly gave the entire work in French between 1906 and 1911, the only complete public domain version.

The commentary moves through the Torah portion by portion. In each verse it finds the play of the sefirot. It tells of the wounds and healing of the Shekhinah, the presence of God in exile. Stories of the companions break the doctrine with sudden light. De Pauly's notes help the French reader through the symbols. The set advances here toward its close.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-5-1909:
The fifth tome of Jean de Pauly's Zohar also dates to 1909, as the translator pressed toward the end of his great task. The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the core book of Jewish mysticism, an Aramaic midrash on the Torah from the circle of Moses de Leon. De Pauly's French, in six tomes, is the only complete version in the public domain.

Portion by portion, the companions of Rabbi Shimon draw out the hidden life of God. They show the sefirot in their dance and the soul in its exile. Prayer becomes the repair of the worlds. Fierce debates and tender tales share the pages. De Pauly keeps the whole vast work in one steady French voice. One tome remains.
